title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Readings and sequence

Chouinard, “Theory Notes”

What belongs in the theory section of an empirical paper

Cheng, “How to Write Proofs: A Quick Guide”

How to make each step in an argument follow from what precedes it



This lecture follows the assigned readings in their schedule order. Chouinard establishes the role and organization of theory. Cheng provides a way to audit the logic within that organization.
[Sources] - Chouinard (2015) - Cheng (2004/Sources)

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Presenting the model in a paper
text:
Presenting the model in a paper
Lecture 4.1 developed a conceptual model of retailer authorization.
The next step is to present that reasoning in a paper

Explain why the theory is relevant to the research problem
Define the agents, choices, program rules, assumptions, and relationships
Show how the prediction follows from the model
Connect the prediction to the available evidence

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Recall the retailer participation model
For retailer ii

BiB_i is the benefit from SNAP authorization including SNAP-related sales
Ki(r)K_i(r) is the cost of meeting stocking standard rr
ai(r)a_i(r) records whether the retailer is authorized

ai(r)=1whenBi≥Ki(r)
a_i(r)=1 \quad \text{when} \quad B_i\geq K_i(r)

A stronger standard may raise Ki(r)K_i(r) by different amounts across retailers. If the cost rises above BiB_i the model predicts a change from authorized to unauthorized.

BiB_i is the benefit the retailer receives from authorization. It may include SNAP-related sales and access to SNAP customers. It is not a government payout. The revised standard applies to authorized retailers generally. The added cost may be zero or small for a store that already meets it and larger for a store that has to change its inventory.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Review the following claim

Because stricter stocking standards require healthier foods, they improve food access and diet quality.

Use the retailer model on the previous slide to assess the claim.

What does the model predict?
The standard may raise compliance costs and cause some retailers to lose authorization which can reduce the number of SNAP outlets in a community


What do the available data observe?
Whether stores remain authorized and how the authorized-store network changes


What requires additional evidence?
Changes in inventory food availability purchases diet and health


The quoted claim describes an intended policy pathway. The retailer participation model adds another pathway through compliance cost and authorization. Ask students to distinguish the model result from the later outcomes that would require separate measures and relationships.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Theory in an empirical paper
Chouinard emphasizes making the theory that motivates the research question and hypotheses explicit (Chouinard 2015).
For an empirical paper the theory section can

Explain the mechanism behind the research question
State the assumptions needed for that mechanism
Derive the hypotheses evaluated with data
Connect theoretical concepts to empirical measures
State the limits of the conclusions supported by the evidence

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: The role of theory depends on the contribution
text:
The role of theory depends on the contribution







Theoretical paper
Empirical paper




Develop or modify a model
Apply theory to explain the empirical question


Establish analytical results
Derive hypotheses and comparative predictions


Show what changes relative to prior theory
Connect concepts to observed measures


Treat the model as a central contribution
Use the model to organize the empirical argument



Both require explicit assumptions and a coherent sequence of reasoning.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Varying degrees of theory in a paper
text:
Varying degrees of theory in a paper
Apply established theory
Summarize the relevant result and explain how it applies to the research problem

Modify established theory
State the baseline model, identify the change, and show how the result changes


Develop new theory
Define the setting, assumptions, relationships, and results in sufficient detail to establish the contribution

The appropriate level of detail depends on how theory contributes to the paper.

Chouinard cautions against rederiving familiar theory when the contribution is an application. More detail is warranted when the paper changes the model or contributes new theory.
[Sources] - Chouinard (2015/Sources)

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Present the model in a logical order
text:
Present the model in a logical order
Chouinard recommends introducing the model components before presenting the complete argument.

Define the setting and relevant agents
Identify choices and institutional constraints
State the maintained assumptions
Introduce the relationships among model objects
Derive and interpret the conditional result
Connect the result to the empirical hypothesis

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Apply the sequence: setting, agents, choices, and constraints
text:
Apply the sequence: setting, agents, choices, and constraints
Setting and agents SNAP-authorized retailers respond to a revised stocking standard

Choice Each retailer decides whether authorization remains worthwhile


Institutional constraint A retailer must satisfy the stocking standard to remain eligible for SNAP authorization

The stocking rule limits the retailer’s feasible choices.
A compliance cost is a consequence of responding to that rule rather than the constraint itself.

Use constraint for a limit on choice imposed by the setting. Here the eligibility rule is the constraint. Do not use constraint as a synonym for an assumption or a cost.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Apply the sequence: assumptions, relationship, and result
text:
Apply the sequence: assumptions, relationship, and result
Maintained assumptions
These are conditions accepted for the model comparison

The stronger standard does not reduce compliance cost and may raise it by different amounts across retailers
BiB_i is held fixed when comparing the two standards
Retailers compare the benefit of authorization with the cost of compliance


Relationship ai(r)=1a_i(r)=1 when Bi≥Ki(r)B_i\geq K_i(r)


Conditional result Authorization changes when Ki(r)K_i(r) rises from no greater than BiB_i to greater than BiB_i

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Interpret the central terms consistently
For retailer ii

rr is the strictness of the stocking standard
BiB_i is the benefit of authorization including SNAP-related sales
Ki(r)K_i(r) is the cost of meeting standard rr
ai(r)a_i(r) is authorization status

The index ii allows benefits and costs to differ across retailers.

The benefit of authorization is not a direct government payout. It represents the private benefit to the retailer including SNAP-related revenue and access to customers who use SNAP benefits. Chouinard recommends recognizable notation defined without delay and used consistently.
[Sources] - Chouinard (2015/Sources)

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Pair the equation with its interpretation
text:
Pair the equation with its interpretation
The retailer remains authorized when the benefit of authorization covers the compliance cost
ai(r)={1if Bi≥Ki(r)0if Bi<Ki(r)
a_i(r)=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } B_i\geq K_i(r)\\
0 & \text{if } B_i<K_i(r)
\end{cases}

A change in the standard changes authorization only when compliance cost moves from at or below BiB_i to above BiB_i.

Define the symbols before or immediately after displaying the equation. Then give the economic interpretation. The equation and prose should make the same claim.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Separate the model result from the empirical hypothesis
text:
Separate the model result from the empirical hypothesis
Model result
Holding BiB_i fixed, a higher Ki(r)K_i(r) can cause a retailer to lose authorization

Empirical hypothesis
Retailers expected to face higher compliance costs are more likely to lose authorization after implementation


Evidence
Store-year authorization data can show whether losses differ by observable retailer characteristics

The evidence may support or challenge the hypothesis without revealing the unobserved compliance cost itself.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Discussion: apply Chouinard to your research
text:
Discussion: apply Chouinard to your research

What role does theory serve in your paper
Are you applying modifying or developing a model
Which concept must be defined before the reader sees an equation
Which assumption carries your principal result
What empirical hypothesis follows from that result


Use whole-class discussion. Students may answer using a dissertation chapter or another current project. Ask for the relationship among the five answers rather than separate summaries.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Cheng’s structure: premises reasoning and conclusion
text:
Cheng’s structure: premises reasoning and conclusion
Cheng describes a proof as a sequence of statements in which each statement follows from what came before (Cheng 2004).



Part
Function in an economic argument




Beginning
Definitions assumptions and accepted results


Middle
The steps connecting the premises to the result


End
The claim the argument was constructed to establish



The written argument makes the intermediate steps visible.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Develop the argument backward and present it forward
text:
Develop the argument backward and present it forward
When developing an argument it is useful to ask

What would have to be true for this conclusion to follow?


That question works backward from the intended result and helps identify the required assumptions and intermediate steps.


The written argument should then proceed forward from the stated premises to the result.


Cheng distinguishes the order in which a proof may be discovered from the order in which it should be written. The same distinction applies to an economic argument.
[Sources] - Cheng (2004/Sources)

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Apply Cheng’s structure to the retailer model
text:
Apply Cheng’s structure to the retailer model
Beginning
The revised standard may raise Ki(r)K_i(r) while BiB_i is held fixed

Middle
A retailer remains authorized only when Bi≥Ki(r)B_i\geq K_i(r)


End
For a retailer whose compliance cost rises above the benefit of authorization the model predicts a change from authorized to unauthorized

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Show the threshold crossing
Suppose the standard changes from r0r_0 to r1r_1 and
Ki(r0)≤Bi<Ki(r1)
K_i(r_0)\leq B_i<K_i(r_1)

Then
ai(r0)=1andai(r1)=0
a_i(r_0)=1
\quad\text{and}\quad
a_i(r_1)=0

The retailer was authorized under the earlier standard and is not authorized under the stronger standard.

This is a conditional model result. It does not establish that the cost increase occurred or caused an observed authorization loss in the data.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
“Handwaving”
Handwaving is a term that describes a step that may be plausible but is not established by the stated argument
The authorization model can support
higher compliance cost→possible authorization loss
\text{higher compliance cost}
\rightarrow
\text{possible authorization loss}

It does not by itself establish
authorization loss→food access change→diet or health change
\text{authorization loss}
\rightarrow
\text{food access change}
\rightarrow
\text{diet or health change}

That downstream pathway requires relationships and evidence about inventory availability purchases and health.

Handwaving does not mean the conclusion is impossible. It means that the premises and intermediate steps presented so far do not establish it. In this example the omitted steps include whether households used an affected retailer whether alternative retailers replace that access and whether purchases respond.
[Sources] - Cheng (2004/Sources)

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Two claims that require more support
text:
Two claims that require more support
Invalid converse

A retailer remained authorized therefore the revised requirement was slack

The retailer may instead have changed its inventory to comply.

Unsupported causal attribution

A retailer lost authorization after implementation therefore the revised rule caused the loss

The analysis needs to distinguish policy exposure from closure, reclassification, and other changes over time.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Discussion: trace a claim in your research
text:
Discussion: trace a claim in your research
Choose one claim your conceptual framework is intended to support

What conclusion follows from the model
Which maintained assumption is needed for that conclusion
What observed result would be consistent with the conclusion
What stronger claim would require another relationship or additional evidence


Students may use a dissertation chapter another current project or one of the assigned papers. Ask for one explicit inference in the form “Given A and B, C follows because…” and examine whether another premise is missing.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Organizing a written conceptual framework

State the research problem that requires explanation
Identify the relevant economic theory
Define agents, choices, institutional constraints, and key terms
State the maintained assumptions
Introduce the relationships among model objects
Derive the result and empirical hypothesis
State what the model and available evidence do not establish

The sequence should make the relationship between theory, prediction, and evidence clear.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Use the framework to inform the empirical design
text:
Use the framework to inform the empirical design








Step
Question
SNAP application




Framework
What mechanism produces the prediction?
A stronger standard may change authorization through compliance cost


Measurement
Which variables represent the concepts?
Authorization, retailer type, location, and local SNAP participation


Identification
What comparison isolates the policy response?
A comparison to what authorization would have been without the change




Identification is the argument that the empirical comparison separates the policy response from other changes over time. This slide introduces the concept. Identification strategies and threats receive fuller treatment in Unit 6.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
SNAP example: problem and structure
Research problem
Revised stocking standards may change the number, type, and location of SNAP-authorized retailers
Economic theory
Retailer participation is a threshold choice in which the benefit of authorization is compared with the cost of compliance
Agent and choice
Retailer ii decides whether the benefit of authorization justifies the cost of meeting the standard
Institutional constraint
The retailer must satisfy stocking standard rr to remain authorized

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
SNAP example: assumptions and result
Maintained assumptions

A stronger standard does not reduce Ki(r)K_i(r) and may raise it by different amounts across retailers
BiB_i is held fixed when comparing standards
Retailers compare the benefit of authorization with the cost of compliance

Relationship ai(r)=1a_i(r)=1 when Bi≥Ki(r)B_i\geq K_i(r)
Conditional result
Ki(r0)≤Bi<Ki(r1)⇒ai(r0)=1 and ai(r1)=0
K_i(r_0)\leq B_i<K_i(r_1)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
a_i(r_0)=1 \text{ and } a_i(r_1)=0

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: SNAP example: hypothesis, evidence, and audit
text:
SNAP example: hypothesis, evidence, and audit
Empirical hypothesis
Authorization losses increase after implementation among retailers expected to face larger compliance-cost increases
Observable evidence
Store-year data show authorization changes by retailer type, location, and local SNAP participation
Takeaways
The argument establishes a conditional prediction about authorization
Changes in inventory, household food access, purchases, diet, or health require additional relationships and evidence

These three slides provide an example of a complete workshop submission. Together they define the problem, agent, choice, constraint, maintained assumptions, result, empirical hypothesis, available evidence, and boundary. Emphasize that the boundary identifies a missing part of the argument rather than declaring the downstream outcomes impossible.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
SNAP example: in paragraph form

The revised standard may raise the cost of continued SNAP authorization, with the increase varying across retailers. Let BiB_i denote the benefit a retailer receives from authorization, including SNAP-related sales, and let Ki(r)K_i(r) denote the compliance cost. Holding BiB_i fixed, the model predicts an authorization loss when Ki(r)K_i(r) exceeds BiB_i. This prediction motivates an analysis of authorization changes by store type and local SNAP participation. The available data do not establish changes in inventory, household access, purchases, diet, or health.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
SNAP example: paragraph checklist

States the maintained assumptions
Separates model results from empirical hypotheses
Distinguishes observed from unobserved outcomes
Limits the conclusion to what the evidence can support

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: SNAP example: boundaries on the scope of the evidence
text:
SNAP example: boundaries on the scope of the evidence
The framework supports a conditional prediction about retailer authorization.
The data can describe changes in the number, type, and location of authorized retailers.
The study cannot directly establish

Which retailers changed inventory and by how much
How household access to qualifying food changed
How household purchases changed
Whether diet or health improved

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: In your groups: build a framework
text:
In your groups: build a framework
Choose one volunteer whose research question the group will workshop

State the research problem and outcome
Identify the relevant economic theory
Define the agents, choices, and institutional constraints
State the maintained assumptions and relationships
Derive a conditional prediction and empirical hypothesis

15 minutes · groups of 3–4

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: As a class: present and audit
text:
As a class: present and audit
Group report

The research problem and conditional prediction
One empirical hypothesis
One step requiring an additional premise or evidence

Class audit

Check whether each step follows from the preceding step
Identify a missing premise, unsupported inference, or outcome outside the evidence

Output: A preliminary framework that connects the premises to the conditional prediction

Ask for a volunteer in each group whose current research question will be workshopped. The volunteer should explain the research problem briefly and then participate as a group member rather than defend a finished framework. During the report-out ask each group to present its conditional prediction and the step that required the strongest assumption or additional evidence.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Apply the reporting sequence to your research
text:
Apply the reporting sequence to your research
For your paper, ask

What mechanism connects the cause or policy to the outcome?
Which maintained assumptions are required for the prediction?
Which theoretical concepts have observable counterparts?
What empirical comparison would isolate the proposed effect?
Which conclusions remain outside the model or available evidence?

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Summary of readings
Chouinard identifies the components and order of a theory section
Cheng requires each conclusion to follow from stated premises
Both provide guidelines to turn a model into a written argument whose scope a reader can evaluate.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
References


Cheng, Eugenia. 2004. How to Write Proofs: A Quick Guide. Department of Mathematics, University of Chicago.


Chouinard, Hayley H. 2015. Theory Notes. EconS 529 course notes.

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Reading and sequence
Dominitz and Manski, “More Data or Better Data? A Statistical Decision Problem” (Dominitz and Manski 2017)

Retrieve four types of data in R

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
APIs deliver secondary data
The organization responsible for the source determines

What is measured
Which people, places, or activities are covered
When observations are collected and released
How uncertainty, missing values, and revisions are recorded

An application programming interface provides a documented way for R (or other programming languages) to request selected records from that source

Lecture 5.1 introduced primary and secondary data. An API is one way to receive secondary data collected and maintained by another organization.

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
section: What happens when R calls an API
text:
What happens when R calls an API








Step
What happens
Streamflow example




1. R function
You call a package function and list what you want
read_waterdata_daily() with a station, a parameter, and dates


2. Request
The package adds those parameters to the service’s web address, called the endpoint
api.waterdata.usgs.gov/...?monitoring_location_id=USGS-06752260&parameter_code=00060


3. Data service
The agency’s server finds the matching records
USGS Water Data


4. Response
The server returns the records in a format the service chooses: JSON or CSV for tables, GeoTIFF or NetCDF for grids
JSON text, one record per day


5. R object
The package reads that format and returns a data frame, raster, or map layer
183 rows, one per day

Four applications








Application

Returned to R

Install the R packages
Run once in the RStudio Console. The list matches the top of api_examples.R

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
A retrieval workflow

Read the source documentation
Define the place, time period, variables, and unit of observation
Run a small request
Inspect column names, values, units, and missingness
Save the returned file or object
Record the request and retrieval date
Expand the request after the checks are complete


A small request might cover one county, one station, or one month. This keeps errors visible and makes it easier to learn the returned structure.

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Example 1: land use
Question
Which crop and land-cover classes does the Cropland Data Layer assign in Larimer County in 2024?
Source
USDA NASS Cropland Data Layer through the CropScape service
Observation
Each raster cell has a modeled crop or land-cover class for a particular year
CropScape documentation | CropScapeR documentation

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
section: Request a Cropland Data Layer map
text:
Request a Cropland Data Layer map
library(CropScapeR)

larimer_cdl <- GetCDLData(
  aoi = "08069",
  year = 2024,
  type = "f",
  save_path = "data/raw/cdl_larimer_2024.tif"
)

raster::plot(larimer_cdl)
08069 is the five-digit Census code for Larimer County
The saved GeoTIFF contains a grid of land-cover codes and the information needed to locate those cells on a map

Map crop locations

Compare annual crop patterns
Define land-use exposure near water infrastructure or development

text:
Example 2: water
Question
What was the daily flow of the Cache la Poudre River during the 2024 growing season?
Source
USGS Water Data API
Observation
Each row reports a daily statistic for one parameter at one monitoring location
USGS monitoring location 06752260 | dataRetrieval tutorial

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Request daily streamflow
library(dataRetrieval)

poudre_flow <- read_waterdata_daily(
  monitoring_location_id = "USGS-06752260",
  parameter_code = "00060",
  time = c("2024-04-01", "2024-09-30")
)

names(poudre_flow)
head(poudre_flow)
00060 is the USGS parameter code for discharge
The returned columns include date, value, unit, approval status, qualifiers, station geometry, and a time-series identifier

text:
Assess the streamflow series

Confirm the monitoring location and parameter
Read the unit attached to each series
Examine provisional and approved status
Identify missing dates and changes in the operating record
Learn whether reservoirs, diversions, or return flows affect the gauge
Define the geographic relationship between the gauge and the study area

The gauge measures conditions at one point on a river network. A study of irrigation access may also require diversion service areas, water rights, or delivery records

Request daily weather
library(nasapower)

fort_collins_weather <- get_power(
  community = "AG",

head(fort_collins_weather)

The three requested measures are maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs

Example 4: Census ACS
Question
How does median household income vary across census tracts in Larimer County?
Source
American Community Survey five-year estimates
Observation

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Store the Census API key
Open the user-level environment file from R
install.packages("usethis")
usethis::edit_r_environ()
Add one line, save the file, and restart R (Session > Restart R)
CENSUS_API_KEY=paste_your_key_here

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Request tract estimates and geometry
library(tidycensus)

larimer_income <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(median_income = "B19013_001"),
  state = "CO",
  county = "Larimer",
  year = 2024,
  survey = "acs5",
  geometry = TRUE,
  key = Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY")
)

head(larimer_income)
The result contains a geographic identifier, name, estimate, margin of error, and tract geometry

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Map the ACS estimates
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(larimer_income) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = estimate), color = NA) +
  labs(
    fill = "Median income",
    title = "Median household income by census tract"
  )
The default margin of error describes a 90 percent confidence interval

\text{estimate} \pm \text{margin of error}

Treatment of revised, suppressed, and missing values

The combined analytic sample includes the observations that satisfy all source coverage and matching rules

Connect this point to Lecture 5.1. Adding a secondary source can change the analytic sample because locations or years with complete matches may differ from the intended study population.

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
section: The reading: allocating the collection budget
text:
The reading: allocating the collection budget
Dominitz and Manski ask how to allocate a fixed budget across collection processes that differ in cost and information (Dominitz and Manski 2017)
API access reduces the time required to retrieve additional observations
Research time is also required to

Verify definitions and units
Examine coverage, missing values, flags, and uncertainty
Select spatial and temporal aggregation rules
Validate joins across sources
Archive metadata and retrieval records

Question: How should a researcher allocate one additional week across these tasks?

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Select the access method







Project need
Useful access method




A defined subset repeated across places or periods
API request


Most records in a fixed release
Bulk download


A few values needed once
Web table or manual download


Repeated data cleaning and analysis
Scripted retrieval with archived raw files



Choose the method after reviewing the source documentation update schedule and request limits

Class share: where are you in the process?

Before class

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
section: Make the project understandable to others
text:
Make the project understandable to others
A collaborator needs to know:

What identifies an observation.
What each transformation does.
How tasks and changes are coordinated.
How to reproduce the result.

Version control supports this work; it does not replace a clear design.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Keys define the observations
A key is a field or combination of fields that uniquely identifies a row








Data structure
One row represents
Possible key




Household survey
One household in one wave
household_id, wave


County panel
One county in one year
county_fips, year


Parcel transactions
One recorded sale
transaction_id



Cleaned tables should have keys that are unique and nonmissing

Source: Gentzkow and Shapiro (2014), Section 5

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Check the key before joining
stopifnot(!anyNA(data[c("county_id", "year")]))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(data[c("county_id", "year")]))
Before merging:

State the expected matching relationship.
Inspect unmatched keys.
Compare row counts before and after.

Keep identifiers as text when leading zeros matter.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Exercise: find the merge problem
A county-year table is joined to a county-industry-year table using county and year.

Should the row count increase?
What becomes the unit of observation?
What happens if county population is later summed?
How would you prevent double counting?

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Abstraction: write the idea once
Use a function or loop for repeated transformations.
rate_per_1000 <- function(events, population) {
  stopifnot(all(population > 0))
  1000 * events / population
}
State assumptions about missing values, units, and valid inputs.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Discussion: when does abstraction help?

When is a function clearer than repeated code?
When does a general solution become harder to understand?
What would make a function easier to check?
Which repeated step in your project is worth simplifying?

Source: Gentzkow and Shapiro (2014), Section 6.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Documentation explains decisions
Use names and structure to show what code does.
Use comments for:

Why a choice was made.
A source or definition.
An unexpected but intentional rule.
A limitation a future user might miss.

A codebook should define units and missing-value conventions.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
A task needs an owner
A useful task record contains:

A concrete deliverable.
One responsible person.
Inputs and dependencies.
A definition of completion.
A place to record decisions.

What goes wrong in the reading’s email exchange about robustness checks?
Source: Gentzkow and Shapiro (2014), Section 8.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
section: A branch for a focused change
text:
A branch for a focused change
In the practice repository:
git switch -c clarify-codebook
# Edit the README, then:
git add README.md
git commit -m "Clarify missing-value codes"
git switch main
git merge clarify-codebook
Use the actual default branch name if it is not main.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
A conflict requires a decision

Read both versions and understand their intentions.
Edit the file to the agreed result.
Remove conflict markers.
Check the result, stage it, and complete the merge.

Do not choose a version solely because it is newer.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Code style supports review

Give scripts and functions one clear purpose
Use names that identify the concept and unit
Make function inputs and outputs explicit
Separate key calculations from setup code
Write logical conditions in the form a reader would describe them
Use consistent naming and indentation across the project
Return informative errors for invalid inputs


Source: Gentzkow and Shapiro (2014), Code Style appendix

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Workshop: hand off the project
Ask a partner to identify:

The key in one dataset.
How to reproduce one output.
Where a variable is defined.
Who owns an unfinished task.
Why the most recent change was made.

Record the first point where they need your help.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Before you leave
Show one of the following

A branch created for a current research task
A commit that records a coherent change
A draft pull-request description for a proposed change

Also identify the key of one dataset used in that task

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Start with four questions

What relationship are you trying to learn about?
What would the ideal experiment look like?
What identification strategy is feasible?
How will you quantify uncertainty?

Source: Angrist and Pischke (2009).

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Structural and reduced-form approaches







Structural
Reduced-form / design-based




Specifies behavioral relationships
Focuses on variation identifying an effect


Recovers parameters within a model
Often targets a treatment or policy effect


Can support model-based counterfactuals
Often speaks most directly to the studied setting



Both require assumptions. Their usefulness depends on the question.
Source: Timmins and Schlenker (2009).

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
What a structural model adds

Agents, objectives, constraints, and interactions.
Parameters with a behavioral interpretation.
A way to trace feedback and equilibrium responses.
A framework for welfare or unobserved policy counterfactuals.

Identification still requires informative data and defensible restrictions.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Example: vehicle policy
The source slides use fuel-economy regulation versus fuel taxation.
A model may need:

Firms’ new-vehicle decisions.
Household vehicle choice and driving.
Used-vehicle markets and scrappage.
Interactions across these decisions.

Which effects would a simple comparison of new-car fuel economy miss?

Adapted from Unit 6, slides 6–8 and the discussion of Jacobsen in Timmins and Schlenker. Focus on the mechanism rather than presenting uncited numerical results.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Structural tradeoffs
Potential gains: explicit mechanisms, feedbacks, welfare analysis, counterfactual simulation.
Challenges: specification, computational demands, identification, and sensitivity to behavioral assumptions.
A counterfactual prediction is conditional on the model remaining appropriate.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
What reduced-form designs emphasize

A clearly defined outcome and treatment.
A credible comparison.
Institutional knowledge about assignment.
Variation that isolates the relationship of interest.

Fixed effects, thresholds, instruments, and random assignment are possible tools, not automatic guarantees.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Discussion: Timmins and Schlenker
For your proposed question:

Is the goal an effect in an observed setting or a new policy counterfactual?
Which behavioral responses must be represented?
Which assumptions would each approach require?
Could the approaches provide complementary evidence?

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Outcomes we cannot observe together
Let Yi(1)Y_i(1) be an individual’s outcome under treatment and Yi(0)Y_i(0) under no treatment.
Yi=DiYi(1)+(1−Di)Yi(0)
Y_i=D_iY_i(1)+(1-D_i)Y_i(0)

We observe only one potential outcome for each individual.
The missing counterfactual is the central problem.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Selection contaminates a raw comparison
E[Y∣D=1]−E[Y∣D=0]=E[Y(1)−Y(0)∣D=1]+E[Y(0)∣D=1]−E[Y(0)∣D=0].
\begin{aligned}
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
&=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid D=1]\\
&\quad+E[Y(0)\mid D=1]-E[Y(0)\mid D=0].
\end{aligned}

The first term is the average treatment effect on the treated. The remaining difference is selection bias.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Example: hospitals and health
People who visit hospitals may have worse health than those who do not.

Does that establish that hospitals worsen health?
What would their health have been without treatment?
Which selection process makes the raw comparison misleading?

Source: Angrist and Pischke (2009).

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
What random assignment gives us
Under random assignment:
D⟂(Y(0),Y(1)).
D\;\perp\;(Y(0),Y(1)).

With consistency and no interference, the population difference in means identifies the average treatment effect.
Randomization makes groups comparable in expectation; a realized sample can still be imbalanced.

Corrects Unit 6, slide 24: assignment is independent of potential outcomes, not necessarily of the observed outcome. Imperfect compliance and attrition require additional analysis.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
section: Regression does not remove selection by itself
text:
Regression does not remove selection by itself
In a model such as
Yi=α+τDi+Xi′β+εi,Y_i=\alpha+\tau D_i+X_i'\beta+\varepsilon_i,
a causal interpretation of τ\tau needs assumptions about treatment assignment and the error term.
Controls can help with comparability or precision. They can also introduce problems if chosen without a causal argument.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Read the experimental table



Table from Mostly Harmless Econometrics comparing estimated small-class effects across specifications with additional controls.


Source: Angrist and Pischke; retained from Unit 6, slide 26.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Discussion: what changes across columns?

Which coefficients are stable?
What happens to standard errors?
How can controls improve precision in an experiment?
What would a large change in the treatment coefficient prompt you to investigate?

Start with the table’s sample, units, and assignment process.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Omitted-variable bias
Suppose the population model is
Y=α+βX+γZ+u,Y=\alpha+\beta X+\gamma Z+u,
but we omit ZZ. Under the usual exogeneity conditions,
plim⁡β̂short=β+γCov⁡(X,Z)Var⁡(X).
\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta_{\text{short}}
=\beta+\gamma\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.

Both the outcome relevance of ZZ and its association with XX matter.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Discussion: Jurajda
Choose one identification example from the notes.

Where does the relevant variation come from?
Why is a simple group comparison insufficient?
What institutional detail supports the design?
What alternative explanation remains?

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
section: Can you describe the ideal experiment?
text:
Can you describe the ideal experiment?
Specify treatment, population, assignment, outcome, and follow-up period.
If the treatment itself is ambiguous, refine the question first.

Preserves the source speaker-note example: changing school-start age may also change schooling duration or age at testing. Ask students which effect their hypothetical experiment would isolate.

text:
Workshop: your identification statement
Complete:

“The relationship of interest is …”
“The ideal experiment would …”
“The feasible comparison is …”
“Its causal interpretation requires …”
“The largest remaining threat is …”

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Before class

Athey and Imbens, “The State of Applied Econometrics: Causality and Policy Evaluation” (Athey and Imbens 2017)

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Begin with the task
Are we trying to:

Predict an outcome?
Describe patterns?
Estimate a causal effect?
Learn how effects vary?

The task determines how success should be evaluated.

Source: Athey and Imbens (2019).

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Prediction and causality
A model can predict outcomes well using variables that do not cause them.
A causal question asks how outcomes change under an intervention.
Predictive accuracy alone does not justify changing a policy variable.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Supervised and unsupervised learning

Supervised: learn a relationship between inputs and observed outcomes.
Unsupervised: find structure without an outcome label.

Examples: predicting demand versus grouping similar observations.
Both can contribute to economic research when the role is explicit.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Overfitting
A flexible model can fit noise in its training sample.

Evaluate performance on observations not used to fit the model.
Keep the final test set separate from model selection.
Respect the dependence structure when splitting data.

For forecasting, information from the future should not enter training.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Bias and variance
Greater flexibility may reduce approximation bias while increasing variability.
Regularization constrains the fit to improve performance outside the training sample.
The best training fit is not necessarily the best predictive model.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
LASSO
A common form minimizes
1n∑i=1n(Yi−α−Xi′β)2+λ∑j=1p|βj|.
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\alpha-X_i'\beta)^2
+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|.


The penalty shrinks coefficients and may set some to zero.
The tuning parameter controls the penalty.
Cross-validation can guide predictive tuning.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Trees and forests
A regression tree splits observations into groups with different predicted outcomes.
A random forest averages predictions across many randomized trees.



Illustrative regression tree with splitting rules and terminal-node predictions, retained from the source deck.



Source: Unit 6, slide 43.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Exercise: identify leakage
A model predicts whether a household will miss a payment.
One input is “number of collection calls made during the following month.”

Why might this variable predict well?
Could it be known at prediction time?
How would you redesign the evaluation?

This is a hypothetical example.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Model selection and confounding
Selecting variables only for predicting the outcome can omit variables important for treatment assignment.
The reading discusses selecting predictors of both outcome and treatment, then using their union in an appropriate estimation procedure.
This still depends on the underlying identification assumptions.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Machine learning within a causal design
text:
Machine learning within a causal design
Flexible methods may estimate nuisance relationships such as:

Expected outcomes conditional on covariates.
Treatment probabilities.

Sample splitting and specialized inference can help manage overfitting.
Machine learning does not supply exogenous variation by itself.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Discussion: Athey and Imbens

Where can prediction tools improve an economic research workflow?
Why is ordinary predictive validation insufficient for a causal claim?
What is the difference between selecting controls and identifying treatment effects?
Which example in the reading would be useful for your project?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Workshop: evaluation plan
Specify:

Your task and target.
Available predictors.
A simple baseline.
A training/validation/test strategy.
A performance measure.
One plausible leakage path.

text:

Boonpramote, Writing for Economics Journals: Elements of Publication Success (Boonpramote 2000).
Choi, “Rejection and Revision” (Choi n.d.).
Fryer, “A Response to Steven Durlauf and James Heckman” (Fryer 2020).

Readings and course handouts are available on Canvas.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
section: Read the decision before drafting a response
text:
Read the decision before drafting a response

What did the editor decide?
Which concerns are central?
What revision is invited or required?
What deadline and submission instructions apply?

A revision invitation is an opportunity, not a guarantee of acceptance.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
What rejection can teach us
Possible problems include:

Unclear contribution.
A gap between evidence and claims.
Weak organization or exposition.
Poor fit with the journal.
A substantive methodological flaw.

Separate presentation problems from problems requiring new analysis.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Discussion: Boonpramote
The reading approaches publication from editors’ and referees’ perspectives.

What makes a contribution recognizable?
How can weak communication obscure useful research?
Which concerns can be addressed through writing?
Which require changing the research itself?

Find an example in the reading for each kind of revision.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Choi: persist and listen

Read the criticism carefully.
Look for useful information even in an unwelcome report.
Treat misunderstanding as a reason to improve clarity.
Respond to substance without attacking the reviewer.


Source: Choi (n.d.).

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Build a revision plan









Comment
Planned response
Manuscript change
Status




Outcome definition unclear
Define units and timing
Data section
Pending


Comparison group questionable
Investigate exposure
Analysis and limitations
Pending


Conclusion too broad
Narrow claim
Abstract and conclusion
Pending



Illustrative plan. Assign responsibility and resolve dependencies.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Answer each comment directly
For every substantive comment:

State the concern.
Explain your response.
Describe the change or provide a reasoned disagreement.
Identify where the manuscript changed.
State any remaining limitation.

Make the reviewer able to verify your answer.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
When you agree

We agree that the outcome definition was ambiguous. We now specify the reference period and units in the Data section and use the same definition in Table 1.

Why is this more useful than “Fixed” or “Thank you”?
Hypothetical response example.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
When you disagree

Restate the concern fairly.
Explain why the requested change would not resolve it or would change the question.
Supply evidence or reasoning.
Clarify the manuscript where misunderstanding is plausible.
Acknowledge what remains unresolved.

Disagreement should be specific and verifiable.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Discussion: Choi’s recommendations

Which recommendations improve the substance of a revision?
Which concern tone and persistence?
Which advice is context-dependent?
How would you respond if two reviewers made incompatible requests?

Distinguish general advice from a particular editor’s instructions.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Fryer: map the response
The response organizes the debate around:

What the analysis claims about racial differences and discrimination.
Selection into police-civilian interactions.
The reliability of police narratives.

Identify where the author agrees, disagrees, or clarifies the scope of a claim.

Source: Fryer (2020).

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Discussion: evaluate the response
Choose one of those three issues.

What criticism is being answered?
What evidence or reasoning is offered?
Does the response change the analysis, narrow the claim, or defend the original approach?
What question would you still want answered?

Read this as an exercise in evaluating argument, not as evidence that the underlying debate is settled.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Communicate other substantive changes
Tell the editor and reviewers about important changes beyond their requests:

New data.
A different specification.
Additional checks.
Revised interpretation.

Explain why the change was made and how it affects the conclusions.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Should review correspondence be public?
The source deck raises transparency in peer review.
Discuss possible effects on:

Accountability and learning.
Candor.
Confidentiality.
Willingness to review.

What publication policy would balance these concerns?

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Workshop: write a response
Use the major comment from Lecture 7.1.
Produce:

A response paragraph.
A proposed manuscript revision.
A precise location for the change.
An explanation of what remains uncertain.

Exchange with your reviewer. Can they verify that the concern was addressed?

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Before you leave
Identify your first revision task and the evidence that would show it is complete.

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Getting access
Services use one of three arrangements

Open: no registration, as with USGS Water Data, NASA POWER, and the World Bank
Agency key: a free key from one agency, as with Census, BLS, BEA, FRED, and NASS
Shared key: one api.data.gov key works across many federal services, including ERS and FoodData Central

A key is a personal credential. Store it in your user environment file and keep it out of shared code and repositories

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
APIs change and disappear

NOAA moved station data from the Climate Data Online API to a new data service, and the rnoaa package left CRAN in 2024
EPA removed EJScreen and its map services in February 2025; reconstructions are now hosted outside EPA
USGS plans to retire the services behind the readNWIS functions in 2027

Save the raw response and the retrieval date so the data can be reproduced after a service changes

This sets up Lecture 5.3: raw files, retrieval records, and version control are the protection against a source that changes after the analysis is written.

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Working in R and RStudio
R is the programming language that sends each request and holds the returned data. RStudio is the application where you write R code in a script, run it, and see the results
Collecting data with code has three advantages over clicking through a website

The script records exactly what was requested: place, period, and variables
Rerunning the script repeats the request, for you or a coauthor
Changing one value extends the request to more counties or years

Today we will run API requests in RStudio and try short exercises inside these slides

Stata and Python have packages for many of the same APIs. The course uses R because of its Census, water, and geospatial packages.

{"time": "2024-07-01", "value": 86.4, "unit_of_measure": "ft^3/s", "approval_status": "Approved"}

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Before using the land-use data
Questions to answer from the CDL documentation

How does the CDL define each crop class, and did the definitions change across years?
How accurate is the classification for this crop and state? (NASS publishes accuracy tables by state)
What do the 30-meter pixels and the map projection imply for small fields?
How are double-cropped fields classified?
Does the study boundary stay the same across years?

The CDL records modeled land-cover classes. Parcel ownership, zoning, and management practices require additional sources

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Before using the streamflow series
Questions to answer from the USGS record

Is this the right monitoring location and parameter (00060, discharge)?
What unit does the series use (cubic feet per second)?
Which values are provisional or revised? In the 2024 download, 72 of 183 days carry the qualifier REVISED
Are any dates missing?
Do reservoirs, diversions, or return flows upstream affect the gauge?
How does one gauge relate to the study area?

The gauge measures conditions at one point on a river network. A study of irrigation access may also require diversion service areas, water rights, or delivery records

Use the read_waterdata functions for the current USGS Water Data APIs. USGS plans to decommission the services used by readNWIS functions in 2027.

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Before using the weather data
Questions to answer from the POWER documentation

How large is the grid cell? (About 0.5° by 0.625°, roughly 55 by 53 km near Fort Collins)
Which coordinates represent each farm, county, or market in the study?
How is each variable defined, and in what unit?
Which time standard defines a day? (POWER daily values use local solar time)
Which data version was retrieved, and can values be revised?

Every location in a grid cell receives the same values, so conditions at individual fields can differ from the cell estimate

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Before using the ACS estimates
Questions to answer from the ACS documentation

The 2024 five-year estimate pools responses from 2020 to 2024. Does a pooled period suit the question?
How large is each margin of error relative to its estimate?
Which tracts have estimates too uncertain to use?
Are geographic identifiers stored as text, so leading zeros survive?
Which tract boundaries apply? (2020 boundaries for the 2024 release)
Are dollar values adjusted to a common year when comparing periods?

ACS data describe the population and socioeconomic setting; exposure measures come from other sources

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:

Write one line for each item, specific enough that a classmate could start the same search

Outcome or exposure: the behavior or condition you need to observe

Sources and access: the two catalog sources you marked, with the access type (API, file download, or license) and whether a key is required
Unit of observation: what one row represents, such as county-year or gauge-day
Open question: the part of collection you are still working through
Next step: one concrete action and when you will take it

Share your plan in about one minute. Template: docs/data-plan.md in the follow-along repository

Allow about one minute per student. Record recurring sources and problems on the board. Use the final few minutes to identify classmates who are using related data or tools and may be able to exchange documentation or code.

Allocating the collection budget
Dominitz and Manski ask how to allocate a fixed budget across collection processes that differ in cost and information (Dominitz and Manski 2017)

Validate joins across sources

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
section: Example: a JSON response becomes a data frame
text:
Example: a JSON response becomes a data frame
The USGS service returns text like this for each day (simplified)
{"time": "2024-07-01", "value": 86.4, "unit_of_measure": "ft^3/s", "approval_status": "Approved"}
dataRetrieval reads the JSON and turns the records into rows of a data frame
  time       value unit_of_measure approval_status
  2024-07-01  86.4 ft^3/s          Approved
  2024-07-02 162   ft^3/s          Approved
You then work with the data frame; the JSON is never saved unless you save it

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
section: Which format did the server send?
text:
Which format did the server send?

Documentation lists the formats and the parameter that picks one. NASA POWER takes format=JSON, CSV, or NETCDF
The response header names the format in Content-Type: application/json, text/csv, image/tiff, application/x-netcdf
Saving the raw response keeps the file exactly as sent, before any package converts it

The packages in today’s examples choose a format for you. nasapower, for example, requests CSV

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
section: Extension: the weather data as a NetCDF grid
text:
Extension: the weather data as a NetCDF grid
Question
How did maximum temperature vary across northern Colorado during the July 2024 heat wave?
Why a different request
The point request returns one grid cell. A regional request returns every cell in a box, over every day requested, in one NetCDF file
Request
NASA POWER, daily maximum temperature, 39.5 to 41.5 N and 104.5 to 106.5 W, July 10 to 16, 2024

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
section: Without an API: downloading by hand
text:
Without an API: downloading by hand
From the POWER Data Access Viewer

Choose the user community (Agroclimatology) and the temporal level (daily)
Select a region on the map, or type the corner coordinates
Enter the start and end dates
Check each parameter: maximum temperature
Choose the output format (NetCDF) and submit
Download the file, move it into data/raw, and rename it
Write down every choice, so the file can be explained later

Another year, region, or variable means repeating all seven steps

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
section: With an API: one request in a script
text:
With an API: one request in a script
library(httr2)
library(terra)

request("https://power.larc.nasa.gov/api/temporal/daily/regional") |>
  req_url_query(parameters = "T2M_MAX", community = "AG",
                `latitude-min` = 39.5, `latitude-max` = 41.5,
                `longitude-min` = -106.5, `longitude-max` = -104.5,
                start = "20240710", end = "20240716", format = "NETCDF") |>
  req_perform(path = "data/raw/power_tmax_2024-07.nc")

tmax <- rast("data/raw/power_tmax_2024-07.nc")
tmax   # 15 grid cells (5 rows x 3 columns), 7 daily layers, degrees C
Each argument replaces a click. The file is saved exactly as the server sent it

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
What the NetCDF file holds





Three dimensions: longitude, latitude, and day
15 cells x 7 days = 105 values in one 21 KB file
Units (degrees C) and variable names travel inside the file
terra reads each day as one layer of a raster

Fort Collins sits in one of the two hottest cells on July 12. The cells to its west, over the mountains, ran 8 to 9 degrees cooler

title: Lecture 5.3: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git I
text:
What version control adds
Version control gives a project a documented history. At selected points, it records the state of the project’s files together with the author, date, and reason for the change.
That history allows a researcher to compare versions, recover earlier work, and identify the exact project state used for an analysis or manuscript.

Source: Bryan (2017)

The team repository
Your fork

A person with merge permission in the target repository

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
section: Clone creates the local working repository
text:
Clone creates the local working repository
Cloning creates a complete local Git repository from a remote repository

The clone includes the files and commit history
Git names the source repository origin
A commit records a version in the local repository
Fetch and pull bring later updates from origin
Push copies local commits to origin when your GitHub account has write access

The clone records the remote repository as origin so Git knows where to fetch, pull, and push
The remote repository’s permissions determine whether GitHub accepts a push

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
section: Fork creates a GitHub repository you control
text:
Fork creates a GitHub repository you control
Forking creates a linked copy of a GitHub repository under your account

Your account can push branches to the fork
Your account can change settings and add collaborators
Sync fork brings accepted changes from the original repository
Cloning the fork creates the local working repository
A pull request proposes changes to the original repository

Updates arrive in the fork when you use Sync fork
Forking does not create a local copy on your computer. Clone the fork when you are ready to work in RStudio

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:

1. Do I need to push changes?

If no, clone the original repository and pull later updates when needed
If yes, ask whether you have write access to the original repository

2. Do I have write access to the original repository?

If yes, clone the original repository and push a branch there
If no, fork the original repository on GitHub, then clone your fork and push there

Your local origin is the repository you cloned

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
section: Branches and merges belong to Git
text:
Branches and merges belong to Git

A local repository can create branches and merge them into local main
A team collaborator can push a branch to the shared repository and open a pull request
A fork owner can push a branch to the fork and open a pull request
The pull request can target the fork’s main or the original repository’s main
A person with permission in the target repository completes the merge

A fork changes which remote repository you control and where your branches are pushed

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
section: Decide where the version history should live
text:
Decide where the version history should live
A commit records version history on your computer
A push copies those commits to GitHub
1. Should my commits also be stored on GitHub?

If no, the local repository keeps the version history
If yes, ask whether you have write access to the original repository

2. Do I have write access to the original repository?

If yes, clone the original repository and push a branch there
If no, fork the original repository on GitHub, then clone your fork and push there

Your local origin is the repository you cloned

title: Lecture 5.3: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git I
section: Branches move while tags stay fixed
text:
Branches move while tags stay fixed









Branch
Tag




What it identifies
The current commit in an ongoing line of work
One selected commit


What happens after a new commit
The branch name advances to the new commit
The tag remains with the selected commit


Common use
Developing and reviewing changes
Marking a release, data freeze, or submitted version



A tag such as v1.0 gives one commit a durable name that is easier to recognize than its commit hash

Git permits a tag to be deleted and recreated, but the usual practice is to treat a published tag as fixed. A tag does not create a separate line of development. To continue developing from a tagged commit, create a branch from that tag.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
section: Choose how the project reaches your computer
text:
Choose how the project reaches your computer


Start with the desired destination for future commits. A clone creates the local repository in every pathway involving an existing GitHub repository. A fork adds a personal GitHub repository before that clone.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
section: A fork is your GitHub copy of the original repository
text:
A fork is your GitHub copy of the original repository
GitHub creates the fork under your account and records which repository it came from

Clone the fork to create the local working repository
The local name origin points to your fork
Push sends your local commits to your fork
A pull request asks the original repository’s owners to accept your commits
Sync or fetch can bring later changes from the original repository into your work

Your fork and the original remain separate repositories

Changes travel in two directions








Direction
Path
Result




Your changes
Local branch, then push to origin
Your fork is updated


Proposed contribution
Fork branch, then pull request
The original changes if its owner merges the request


Original updates with GitHub
Sync fork, then pull from origin
Your fork and local copy are updated


Original updates with Git
Fetch upstream, merge, then push to origin
Your local copy and fork are updated



Push targets the repository named origin. In this pathway, origin is your fork

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
section: Update a fork through the terminal
text:
Update a fork through the terminal
Add the original repository as upstream once
git remote add upstream https://github.com/laurenchenarides/arec_570_demo.git
git remote -v
Bring later updates into local main, then update the fork
git fetch upstream
git switch main
git merge --ff-only upstream/main
git push origin main

The --ff-only option updates main only when Git can move it directly to the newer upstream commit. It stops when local main contains competing commits. Keeping project work on separate branches makes this update path easier to maintain.

section: When Git reports a merge conflict
text:
When Git reports a merge conflict
A conflict occurs when the branches being combined changed the same part of a file in different ways

Git pauses the pull or merge
The Git pane identifies each conflicted file
The file contains both versions between conflict markers
The researcher decides what the final file should contain

Git preserves both versions because it cannot determine which edit is correct for the project

Conflict markers begin with <<<<<<<, separate the versions with =======, and end with >>>>>>>. HEAD identifies the version on the branch currently checked out. The other label identifies the incoming branch or commit.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:

Open every file marked as conflicted
Find each set of conflict markers
Compare the current and incoming versions
Keep one version, combine them, or write a new final version
Delete all conflict markers and save the file
Run the checks affected by the change
Stage the resolved files and complete the merge commit

The commit message should summarize the resolution when the choice affects the research record

text:
Research question and testable hypotheses


Research question

How did grocery retailers adjust prices and dollar margins during COVID-19 states of emergency, when anti-price-gouging laws, demand, and wholesale costs changed at the same time?


Framework-derived hypotheses

Retail prices and dollar margins differ across the pre-SOE, SOE, and post-SOE periods
Within-chain price differences vary with state enforcement status if APG protections affect pricing
Retail prices respond to wholesale acquisition costs, and pass-through may change during the SOE
More frequent promotions can reduce net transaction prices while posted prices remain similar



The framework allows several mechanisms to operate at the same time. Higher demand and wholesale costs can create upward price pressure. APG protections can constrain price increases. Chain-level pricing can limit cross-state price differences. Promotions can lower the price paid at the register.
