title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The empirical strategy section turns a prediction from your framework into an estimating equation
text:
The empirical strategy section turns a prediction from your framework into an estimating equation

Conceptual framework (Unit 4) gives you guidance on developing testable predictions
Data (Unit 5) gives you guidance on describing your data, the unit of observation, and the measures that make your data fit for use
Methods (this unit) explains how to turn the conceptual model into an equation with estimable parameters, and why the data identify them


This slide places the section in the paper. The rest of the lecture follows the order of the section itself: the estimation strategy (equation, estimator, inference), then the identification strategy (assumption, threats, robustness), then one research question answered three ways.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Bellemare splits the section into what you estimate and why it identifies a causal effect
text:
Bellemare splits the section into what you estimate and why it identifies a causal effect
Estimation strategy
The equations, the estimator, and how inference is done
Identification strategy
The feature of the data that supports a causal interpretation, or, the manner in which a researcher uses observational data to approximate a real experiment
Use these as the two parts of your section (Bellemare 2020).

This is the structure from the Bellemare reading in Lecture 2.3, Section 5. His Section 5.1 covers the equation, the estimator, hypothesis tests, and standard errors. Section 5.2 covers identification and the threats to it.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Answer four questions before you write the section
text:
Answer four questions before you write the section







Angrist and Pischke ask
The section reports




What is the causal relationship of interest?
The parameter of interest


What experiment would ideally capture it?
The estimand


What is your identification strategy?
The identifying assumption and the variation


What is your mode of statistical inference?
The population, the sample, and the standard errors



Source: Angrist and Pischke (2009), Chapter 1.

Angrist and Pischke call these the four research FAQs. Ask: which of the four is hardest to answer for your proposal right now? Most students will say the second or third.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The ideal experiment tells you which parameter you are after
text:
The ideal experiment tells you which parameter you are after
Question: How will climate change affect US agriculture?

Ideal experiment: give some counties a permanently warmer climate, then wait decades
Farmers would change crops, irrigation, and planting dates
The target is a long-run effect that includes adaptation
A single hot year is a different experiment with a different answer


Angrist and Pischke argue that describing the ideal experiment “helps you formulate causal questions precisely.” Here it separates two estimands that are easy to confuse: the effect of climate and the effect of weather.
Ask: in your proposal, what would you randomize, and how long would you wait to measure the outcome?

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The identifying assumption says which comparison is free of selection
text:
The identifying assumption says which comparison is free of selection

A raw comparison mixes the effect with differences that existed anyway
Jurajda treats identification as a search for variation unrelated to those differences
The variation can come from across places, within a place over time, a threshold, or assignment
Write the assumption in one plain sentence, with no notation


Angrist and Pischke, Chapter 2: the observed difference in means equals the average effect on the treated plus selection bias, the difference in untreated outcomes between the two groups. Jurajda’s Example 1.1 makes the same point with veterans’ earnings: are veterans earning more because of service, or are high earners more likely to enlist?
Students do not need the decomposition in their paper. They need the sentence that says why selection bias is zero for the comparison they use.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: One climate question produces three different empirical strategy sections
text:
One climate question produces three different empirical strategy sections


Open the methods map in a new tab

This is the only slide that shows the methods map. Students should use it as a reference while writing, not as content to memorize. The next six slides walk through the three paths: same question, different variation, different assumption, different estimand.
Timmins and Schlenker frame the tradeoff: a cross-section uses differences in long-term averages that units have adapted to, while a panel uses period-to-period variation and so measures a short-run response.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The Ricardian model compares farmland values across counties with different climates
text:
The Ricardian model compares farmland values across counties with different climates


Estimation strategy
Vc=α+f(Tc,Pc)+Xc′γ+εc
V_c = \alpha + f(T_c, P_c) + X_c'\gamma + \varepsilon_c


VcV_c: farmland value per acre in county cc
Tc,PcT_c, P_c: long-run average temperature and precipitation
f(⋅)f(\cdot): a quadratic; its slope in TcT_c is the parameter of interest
XcX_c: soil quality and other county characteristics
Standard errors allow neighboring counties’ errors to be correlated


Identification strategy

Identifying assumption: counties with different climates do not differ in other ways that affect land values
Main threat: irrigated farms in drier, hotter counties draw water from elsewhere and have higher land values; Schlenker, Hanemann, and Fisher re-estimate the model for dryland counties (Schlenker et al. 2005)
What the coefficient measures: the long-run effect of climate on land values, including adaptation




The logic: land markets capitalize the expected profit from farming in a given climate, so land values already reflect how farmers have adapted.
Irrigation is Bellemare’s “unobserved heterogeneity” threat, and the response is a design choice: change the sample so the omitted factor no longer varies.
Discussion: which variable in your proposal could play the role of irrigation? Expect answers such as access to markets, local policy, or management practices that vary across space with the treatment.
Transition: any fixed county characteristic like irrigation access could be removed by comparing each county with itself. That is the next design.



Source: Mendelsohn et al. (1994).

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Irrigation shows what a violated Ricardian assumption looks like
text:
Irrigation shows what a violated Ricardian assumption looks like

Irrigated farms draw water from outside the county, so local rainfall matters less
Irrigation is concentrated in drier, hotter counties and raises land values
Pooling irrigated and dryland counties omits a variable correlated with climate
Schlenker, Hanemann, and Fisher re-estimate the model for dryland counties (Schlenker et al. 2005)

Discussion: Which variable in your proposal could play the role of irrigation?

This is a clean example of Bellemare’s “unobserved heterogeneity” threat and of a design response: change the sample so the omitted factor no longer varies.
Expect answers such as access to markets, local policy, or management practices that vary across space with the treatment.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The panel model compares each county with itself in hotter and cooler years
text:
The panel model compares each county with itself in hotter and cooler years
yct=g(Wct)+γc+δt+εct
y_{ct} = g(W_{ct}) + \gamma_c + \delta_t + \varepsilon_{ct}


ycty_{ct}: log crop yield or farm profit in county cc, year tt
WctW_{ct}: growing-season weather, such as degree days and precipitation
g(⋅)g(\cdot): the weather–outcome relationship; its slope is the parameter of interest
γc\gamma_c: county effects; δt\delta_t: year effects

Identifying assumption: within a county, year-to-year deviations in weather are as good as random (Deschênes and Greenstone 2007; Schlenker and Roberts 2009).

Deschênes and Greenstone use farm profits; Schlenker and Roberts use yields and allow temperature effects to be nonlinear. Both rely on the same variation.
Ask: why is weather a more believable source of variation than climate? Farmers cannot choose it, and it is hard to forecast at planting.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Fixed effects make the comparison more credible and change the estimand to a short-run response
text:
Fixed effects make the comparison more credible and change the estimand to a short-run response

County effects remove everything fixed about a county, including soils and its long-run climate
What remains is year-to-year deviation in weather
Farmers cannot fully adapt to one hot year
So the estimate is a short-run response, not the long-run effect of climate

Timmins and Schlenker: the long-run effect can be larger or smaller than the short-run effect (Timmins and Schlenker 2009).

Timmins and Schlenker give both directions. Long-run responses face fewer constraints, so long-run damages can be smaller (Le Chatelier principle). But some short-run responses cannot be sustained; their example is groundwater pumping during a drought, which works for one dry year and not for a permanently drier climate.
The point for the paper: a credibility gain is also a change in what you estimate. The section has to say which one you estimate.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Long differences compare slow changes in climate over decades
text:
Long differences compare slow changes in climate over decades
Δy‾c=αs+βΔW‾c+Δε‾c
\Delta \bar{y}_c = \alpha_s + \beta\, \Delta \bar{W}_c + \Delta \bar{\varepsilon}_c


Δy‾c\Delta \bar{y}_c: change in county cc’s multi-year average outcome between two periods
ΔW‾c\Delta \bar{W}_c: change in its multi-year average weather over the same periods
αs\alpha_s: state fixed effects; β\beta: the parameter of interest

1. Relationship of interest: the response to gradual climate change, including adaptation (Burke and Emerick 2016)

Burke and Emerick use recent temperature and precipitation trends.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Each design states a different assumption, estimand, and main threat
text:
Each design states a different assumption, estimand, and main threat










Ricardian
Panel weather
Long differences




Variation
Across counties
Within a county, across years
Across counties’ trends, within a state


Identifying assumption
No omitted factor correlated with climate
Weather deviations as good as random
Climate trends unrelated to other outcome trends


Estimand
Long-run effect, including adaptation
Short-run response to weather
Response to gradual change, including adaptation


Main threat
Omitted factors such as irrigation
Responses that do not last
Other trends correlated with climate trends



Your section needs one column of this table, stated for your design.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Name each threat and say how the design or a robustness check handles it
text:
Name each threat and say how the design or a robustness check handles it







Threat
In the panel weather model




Reverse causality
Farm output does not change the weather


Unobserved heterogeneity
County effects absorb fixed differences; year effects absorb national shocks


Measurement error
Gridded weather misses farm conditions; check a second weather data set


Spillovers
Year effects absorb national price changes, so the estimate excludes them



This is question 5 in detail. Each row needs an answer: the threat does not apply, the design handles it, or a robustness check tests it.

The four threats are Bellemare’s list (Section 5.2): reverse causality, unobserved heterogeneity, measurement error, and spillovers. Dalheimer and Bellemare’s Section 2.2 (shown earlier) walks through the first three in this order.
Classical measurement error in weather attenuates the estimate toward zero.
The record on this design shows why data checks matter: Fisher, Hanemann, Roberts, and Schlenker (2012) identified errors in the weather and climate data used by Deschênes and Greenstone, and Deschênes and Greenstone (2012) replied with corrected estimates.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Write the equation so a referee never has to ask what a symbol means
text:
Write the equation so a referee never has to ask what a symbol means

Latin letters for variables (aa, bb, cc, …), Greek letters (α\alpha, β\beta, γ\gamma, …) for parameters
Subscripts run from the smallest unit to the largest
Define every term directly below the equation
Give each specification its own coefficient labels
The unit of observation matches the key in your data section


Source: Bellemare (2020), Section 5.1.


Bellemare also asks for the estimator by name (OLS, linear probability model, probit, maximum likelihood) and for the standard errors to say what they are robust to. “Robust standard errors” is not enough; “robust to heteroskedasticity” is.
The next slide explains the last rule. Lecture 6.2 opens with the first two.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: In pairs, write the assumption that each climate equation requires
text:
In pairs, write the assumption that each climate equation requires
Count off 1, 2, 3. Pair 1 takes the Ricardian slide, 2 the panel slide, 3 the long-differences slide.

Write the identifying assumption in one sentence, in your own words
State the estimand in words
Name the main threat and one design choice or robustness check that addresses it
Trade with a pair holding a different design and check whether their assumption matches their equation

Two pairs read their assumption aloud at the end.

20 minutes: 10 to write, 5 to trade and check, 5 to share. Listen for assumptions that describe the equation’s variables rather than the variation. “Temperature affects yields” is a prediction, not an identifying assumption.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Four terms come up in every empirical strategy section
text:
Four terms come up in every empirical strategy section

Parameter of interest: the coefficient that answers your research question
Estimator: the method that turns data into an estimate of that parameter, such as OLS, maximum likelihood, or a difference in means
Inference: how you measure the uncertainty in the estimate, through standard errors, clustering, and hypothesis tests
Identifying assumption: the condition under which the parameter you estimate equals the relationship you want to learn about


Students often use “estimator” and “identification” interchangeably. They are separate choices. The same identifying assumption can be paired with different estimators, and a correct estimator cannot fix a comparison that is not identified.
Ask: which of the four is hardest to write down for your proposal right now?

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
text:
Five questions organize the section







Question
Where the answer appears in your section




What is the relationship of interest?
The estimating equation and the parameter of interest


Is that relationship causal?
Whether the parameter is causal, and if not, what it describes


What experiment would ideally measure it?
The effect you are trying to estimate


What is your identification strategy?
The identifying assumption and the variation behind it


How will you measure uncertainty?
The standard errors, the clustering level, and why



Adapted from Angrist and Pischke (2009), Chapter 1.

Angrist and Pischke ask “What is the causal relationship of interest?” Not every paper estimates a causal relationship. A descriptive paper or a forecasting paper still needs an estimating equation; it states what the parameter describes and does not claim more. That is why the causal question is separate here.
The rest of the lecture uses these five questions as its outline.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The identifying assumption says why the groups you compare are comparable
text:
The identifying assumption says why the groups you compare are comparable

Comparing treated and untreated units measures the treatment effect plus any difference that existed between the groups before treatment
Example: veterans may earn more because of military service, or because people with higher earnings potential were more likely to enlist (Angrist 1990)
That pre-existing difference is selection bias
The identifying assumption states why selection bias is zero for your comparison
The coefficient receives a causal interpretation because we successfully control for all mutually determining factors, or exploit variation orthogonal to the error term, ensuring the groups are identical on average except for the treatment itself


The identifying assumption is the explicit claim that your statistical strategy has successfully killed off selection bias.
Angrist and Pischke, Chapter 2, write this as a decomposition: the observed difference in means equals the average effect on the treated plus selection bias, the difference in untreated outcomes between the two groups. Students do not need the decomposition in their paper. They need the sentence that explains why the untreated outcomes of the two groups would have been the same.
Jurajda’s notes describe identification as a search for variation that is unrelated to these pre-existing differences.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The ideal experiment tells you which effect you are after
text:
The ideal experiment tells you which effect you are after
Question: How will a warmer climate affect U.S. agriculture?

Ideal experiment: give some counties a permanently warmer climate, then wait decades
Farmers would change crops, irrigation, and planting dates
The target is a long-run effect that includes this adaptation
A single hot year is a different experiment with a different answer


Angrist and Pischke argue that describing the ideal experiment “helps you formulate causal questions precisely.” Here it separates two effects that are easy to confuse: the effect of climate and the effect of weather.
Ask: in your proposal, what would you randomize, and how long would you wait to measure the outcome?

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The Ricardian assumption fails if anything that varies with climate is omitted, and irrigation does
text:
The Ricardian assumption fails if anything that varies with climate is omitted, and irrigation does

2. Uncertainty: neighboring counties share soils, markets, and climate, so their errors are correlated
3. Causal? Yes, if the identifying assumption in 5 holds
4. Experiment it approximates: counties assigned different climates long ago
5. Identifying assumption: counties with different climates do not differ in other ways that affect land values
6. Threat to identification: irrigated farms in drier, hotter counties draw water from elsewhere and have higher land values; Schlenker, Hanemann, and Fisher re-estimate the model for dryland counties (Schlenker et al. 2005)


Irrigation is Bellemare’s “unobserved heterogeneity” threat, and the response is a design choice: change the sample so the omitted factor no longer varies.
Discussion: which variable in your proposal could play the role of irrigation? Expect answers such as access to markets, local policy, or management practices that vary across space with the treatment.
Transition: any fixed county characteristic like irrigation access could be removed by comparing each county with itself. That is the next design.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The panel model removes fixed county differences by comparing each county with itself across years
text:
The panel model removes fixed county differences by comparing each county with itself across years
yct=g(Wct)+γc+δt+εct
y_{ct} = g(W_{ct}) + \gamma_c + \delta_t + \varepsilon_{ct}


ycty_{ct}: log crop yield or farm profit in county cc, year tt
WctW_{ct}: growing-season weather, such as degree days and precipitation
g(⋅)g(\cdot): the relationship between weather and the outcome; its slope is the parameter of interest
γc\gamma_c: county fixed effects; δt\delta_t: year fixed effects

1. Relationship of interest: the short-run response of yields or profits to weather (Deschênes and Greenstone 2007; Schlenker and Roberts 2009)

Deschênes and Greenstone use farm profits; Schlenker and Roberts use yields and allow temperature effects to be nonlinear. Both rely on the same variation.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Fixed effects solve the irrigation problem and change what is estimated
text:
Fixed effects solve the irrigation problem and change what is estimated

Variation used: year-to-year deviations in weather within a county
Identifying assumption: those deviations are as good as random
Relationship estimated: the short-run response to weather, because farmers cannot fully adapt to one hot year
Main threat: short-run responses that would not last under a permanent change

Timmins and Schlenker: the long-run effect can be larger or smaller than the short-run effect (Timmins and Schlenker 2009).

This fills in the panel column. County fixed effects remove everything fixed about a county, including irrigation access and long-run climate. What is left is weather.
Timmins and Schlenker give both directions. Long-run responses face fewer constraints, so long-run damages can be smaller. But some short-run responses cannot be sustained; their example is groundwater pumping, which works for one dry year and not for a permanently drier climate.
The point for the paper: gaining credibility also changed what is estimated, and the section has to say which effect it estimates.
Transition: to recover adaptation without going back to a cross-section of levels, compare slow changes instead of yearly shocks.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Long differences recover the adaptation that the panel model misses
text:
Long differences recover the adaptation that the panel model misses

2. Uncertainty: one observation per county leaves far fewer observations than the panel, and errors are still correlated across neighboring counties
3. Causal? Yes, for the effect of gradual change, if the identifying assumption in 5 holds
4. Experiment it approximates: a climate that warms slowly over decades
5. Identifying assumption: within a state, counties that warmed more did not change in other ways that affect yields
6. Threat to identification: other trends, such as technology adoption, that move with climate trends


Comparing the long-differences estimate with the panel estimate for the same weather variable shows how much farmers adapted over the period. That comparison is only possible because the two designs estimate different relationships.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Where the empirical strategy section lives in your paper
text:
Where the empirical strategy section lives in your paper

Introduction
Background or Literature Review
Conceptual Framework
Data and Summary Evidence
Empirical Strategy & Identification Strategy
Results
Discussion (or Policy Implications, or Managerial Implications)
Conclusion

Bellemare calls this section the Empirical Framework, and some papers place it before the data section (Bellemare 2020).

Bellemare’s outline for an applied paper: Introduction, Theoretical Framework, Data and Descriptive Statistics, Empirical Framework, Results and Discussion, Summary and Concluding Remarks. He notes that the data and empirical sections are often swapped; the Dalheimer and Bellemare paper on the next slides puts the empirical framework first.
Two differences from his outline. He argues that a separate literature review is “almost always entirely unwarranted” in a journal article and recommends a short review of the five to ten closest studies in the introduction; a separate review fits a thesis or dissertation chapter. He recommends a background section when the reader needs institutional detail, such as the provisions of a law.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: A published AJAE paper opens its estimation strategy with the equation and defines every term
text:
A published AJAE paper opens its estimation strategy with the equation and defines every term

Source: Dalheimer and Bellemare (2026), Section 2.1 (accepted version posted on Bellemare’s website).

Point out the sequence: the relationship in words, the equation, a definition of every term, then one sentence naming the parameter of interest. The next paragraph explains why they first-difference the equation, which is the estimator choice.
Two small inconsistencies are worth noticing: the text defines pitp_{it} for “county ii” in a country-level paper, and the equation uses e1ite_{1it} while the text defines eite_{it}. Referees catch these, and they are why every term should be defined with the same notation used in the equation.
Footnote 5 in the paper explains why the authors do not cluster standard errors after first-differencing. That is an inference decision stated with a reason.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Its identification strategy names the threats before explaining how the design addresses them
text:
Its identification strategy names the threats before explaining how the design addresses them

Source: Dalheimer and Bellemare (2026), Section 2.2 (accepted version posted on Bellemare’s website).

The section walks through Bellemare’s threats in order: reverse causation, omitted variables, and measurement error. Only after naming them does it explain the shift-share instrumental variable design that addresses them. We return to this structure when we reach threats later today.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
text:
Six questions organize the section







Question
Where the answer appears in your section




1. What is the relationship of interest?
The estimating equation and the parameter of interest


2. Is that relationship causal?
Whether the parameter is causal, and if not, what it describes


3. What experiment would ideally measure it?
The effect you are trying to estimate


4. What variation identifies it, and what must be true of that variation?
The identifying assumption


5. What could make the identifying assumption fail?
The threats to identification and how the design or a robustness check addresses each


6. How will you measure uncertainty?
The standard errors, the clustering level, and why



Adapted from Angrist and Pischke (2009), Chapter 1, and Bellemare (2020), Section 5.

Angrist and Pischke ask four questions, starting with “What is the causal relationship of interest?” Not every paper estimates a causal relationship. A descriptive paper or a forecasting paper still needs an estimating equation; it states what the parameter describes and does not claim more. That is why question 2 is separate here.
Question 5 comes from Bellemare’s Section 5.2, which asks authors to discuss each threat to identification and how the paper deals with it.
The rest of the lecture uses these six questions as its outline.

Your empirical strategy section answers these six questions for your design, in prose. It does not need a table like this one; the slide on writing with comments shows how to keep the questions in front of you while drafting.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: A threat to identification biases the estimate; a problem with inference misstates its precision
text:
A threat to identification biases the estimate; a problem with inference misstates its precision

Threat to identification: the estimate is centered on the wrong value, and a larger sample does not fix it
Problem with inference: the estimate may be centered correctly, but the standard errors are too small, so confidence intervals are too narrow and tests reject too often
Panel weather example: neighboring counties share weather shocks, so treating their errors as independent overstates precision; cluster at a level that contains that correlation and say why
Either problem leads a referee to doubt the result, so the section addresses both

Source: Bellemare (2020), Sections 5.1 and 5.2.

Students often list clustering as a threat. It is not a threat to identification: clustering does not change the point estimate. It changes how confident we are in it.
Robustness checks can address either problem: alternative samples or controls test the identifying assumption; alternative clustering levels test the inference choice.
We return to inference later in the unit, including how to handle a small number of clusters.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Robustness checks vary your choices; sensitivity analyses relax your assumptions
text:
Robustness checks vary your choices; sensitivity analyses relax your assumptions

Robustness check: re-estimate with another defensible outcome measure, treatment measure, estimator, functional form, or sample, and show the conclusion holds (Bellemare 2020, sec. 6.2)
Sensitivity analysis: ask how far the identifying assumption would have to fail before the conclusion changes, for example how strong an omitted variable would have to be (Athey and Imbens 2017)
Placebo test: estimate an effect that should be zero; Bellemare counts these as robustness checks, and Athey and Imbens list them separately
Why papers include them: researchers try many specifications before choosing one, so readers need evidence that the result was not selected for (Athey and Imbens 2017)

A robustness check asks whether your choices matter. A sensitivity analysis asks how wrong your assumption could be.

Athey and Imbens call these “supplementary analyses”: their purpose is not a better estimate of the main effect but evidence on the credibility of the primary analysis. They cite Leamer on the gap between the single model that classical inference assumes and the many specifications researchers actually try. The sensitivity approaches they discuss include Rosenbaum and Rubin, Imbens, Altonji and coauthors, and Oster.
Bellemare frames robustness checks as a response to higher standards of evidence after the credibility revolution: authors “have to work hard to convince readers that their results were not cherrypicked.”
This is why papers have a robustness section. Each check should name the threat or the choice it tests. Lecture 6.5 returns to this.
Note that “robust” in “robust standard errors” is a different use of the word: those standard errors are robust to a specific feature of the errors, such as heteroskedasticity.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Latin letters mark what you observe; Greek letters mark what you estimate
text:
Latin letters mark what you observe; Greek letters mark what you estimate









Latin letters
Greek letters




Examples
yy, xx, WW, PP, VV
α\alpha alpha, β\beta beta, γ\gamma gamma, δ\delta delta, ε\varepsilon epsilon


Used for
Variables you observe in the data
Parameters you estimate, and the error term you never observe




Latin letters are the letters of the English alphabet
Fixed effects are parameters, so they get Greek letters: γc\gamma_c, δt\delta_t
A reader who sees a Greek letter knows it is estimated, not measured

Source: Bellemare (2020), Section 5.1.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Subscripts tell the reader the level at which each term varies
text:
Subscripts tell the reader the level at which each term varies
ycst=βPst+γc+δt+εcst
y_{cst} = \beta P_{st} + \gamma_c + \delta_t + \varepsilon_{cst}


One letter per dimension, used the same way throughout the paper: cc county, ss state, tt year
Order from the smallest unit to the largest, with time last
A term carries only the subscripts it varies over: a state policy is PstP_{st}, not PcstP_{cst}
A fixed effect’s subscript says what it holds constant: γc\gamma_c county, δt\delta_t year
The outcome’s subscripts state the unit of observation: a county in a year


Smallest to largest is Bellemare’s rule. Time last is a common convention rather than a rule from the reading.
The subscript on the treatment also tells the reader where the identifying variation is. In this example the policy varies by state and year, which is also a natural starting point for the clustering level.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The unit of observation describes a row; the key identifies it in the file
text:
The unit of observation describes a row; the key identifies it in the file
The unit tells the reader what each row means. The key lets you check that there is exactly one row per unit before you estimate (Gentzkow and Shapiro 2014).









Unit of observation
Key




What it is
What one row represents, in words
The field or fields whose values are unique for every row


Panel weather model
A county in a year
County FIPS code and year


Price-gouging data (Lecture 5.5)
One product at one store in one week
Store, product, and week identifiers


Where it appears
The data section and the equation’s subscripts
The code that builds and merges the data




The two are the same idea at different levels: the unit is the description for the reader, and the key is how the computer enforces it. If two rows share the same key, either the key is incomplete or the data contain duplicates, and the estimate will weight some units twice. Gentzkow and Shapiro’s chapter on keys (Lecture 5.4) covers how to check this.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Put the six questions in your draft as comments, then answer each in prose
text:
Put the six questions in your draft as comments, then answer each in prose
\section{Empirical Strategy}

\subsection{Estimation Strategy}
% What is the relationship of interest?
%   equation, every term defined, parameter of interest
% How will you measure uncertainty?
%   standard errors, clustering level, and why

\subsection{Identification Strategy}
% Is that relationship causal?
% What experiment would ideally measure it?
% What variation identifies it, and what must be true of that variation?
% What could make the identifying assumption fail?
%   each threat, and the design choice or robustness check that handles it
Lines that start with % do not appear in the compiled PDF. In Word, use comments; in Quarto or Markdown, use <!-- -->.

The comments keep the six questions in front of you while you draft, and a coauthor can check that each one has an answer. Delete them before submission or leave them; they do not print. This follows Bellemare’s split: inference belongs in the estimation strategy, and the threats belong in the identification strategy.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: A published paper states the equation, then defines every term
text:
A published paper states the equation, then defines every term



Point out the sequence: the relationship in words, the equation, a definition of every term, then one sentence naming the parameter of interest. The next paragraph explains why they first-difference the equation, which is the estimator choice.
Two small inconsistencies are worth noticing: the text defines pitp_{it} for “county ii” in a country-level paper, and the equation uses e1ite_{1it} while the text defines eite_{it}. Referees catch these, and they are why every term should be defined with the same notation used in the equation.
Footnote 5 in the paper explains why the authors do not cluster standard errors after first-differencing. That is an inference decision stated with a reason.


Source: Dalheimer and Bellemare (2026), Section 2.1 (accepted version posted on Bellemare’s website).

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Its identification strategy names the threats before the design
text:
Its identification strategy names the threats before the design



The section walks through Bellemare’s threats in order: reverse causation, omitted variables, and measurement error. Only after naming them does it explain the shift-share instrumental variable design that addresses them. We return to this structure in the identification strategy section. First, what does identification mean?

Examples
yy, xx, WW, PP, VV

Used for
Variables you observe in the data
Parameters you estimate, and the error term you never observe




Latin letters are the letters of the English alphabet
Fixed effects are parameters, so they get Greek letters: γc\gamma_c, δt\delta_t
A Greek letter tells the reader the term is estimated


Source: Bellemare (2020), Section 5.1.


Check the equation you wrote at the end of Lecture 6.1 against this slide and the next one.

text:
Subscripts tell the reader the level at which each term varies
ycst=βPst+γc+δt+εcst
y_{cst} = \beta P_{st} + \gamma_c + \delta_t + \varepsilon_{cst}


One letter per dimension, used the same way throughout the paper: cc county, ss state, tt year
Order from the smallest unit to the largest, with time last
A term carries only the subscripts it varies over: a state policy is PstP_{st}

The outcome’s subscripts state the unit of observation: a county in a year


Smallest to largest is Bellemare’s rule. Time last is a common convention.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: But first, where the empirical strategy section lives in your paper
text:
But first, where the empirical strategy section lives in your paper

Introduction
Background or Literature Review
Conceptual Framework
Data and Summary Evidence
Empirical Strategy & Identification Strategy
Results
Discussion (or Policy Implications, or Managerial Implications)
Conclusion

Bellemare calls this section the Empirical Framework, and some papers place it before the data section (Bellemare 2020).

Bellemare’s outline for an applied paper: Introduction, Theoretical Framework, Data and Descriptive Statistics, Empirical Framework, Results and Discussion, Summary and Concluding Remarks. He notes that the data and empirical sections are often swapped; the Dalheimer and Bellemare paper on the next slides puts the empirical framework first.
Two differences from his outline. He argues that a separate literature review is “almost always entirely unwarranted” in a journal article and recommends a short review of the five to ten closest studies in the introduction; a separate review fits a thesis or dissertation chapter. He recommends a background section when the reader needs institutional detail, such as the provisions of a law.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: A parameter is identified when only one value of it fits the data you could observe
text:
A parameter is identified when only one value of it fits the data you could observe

Imagine an unlimited sample: could you recover the number you want?
If not, the parameter is not identified, and more data or a better estimator will not fix it
Identification depends on assumptions about how the data were generated, not on the sample size
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) draws those assumptions: each arrow is a causal effect, and each missing arrow is an assumption


Bellemare (Section 5.2) uses “identification” in the sense most applied papers now use: causal identification, when a coefficient reflects a causal relationship rather than a partial correlation. He refers to Pearl’s notation for this, the effect of setting a variable rather than observing it.
The next two slides use one question from the readings, the effect of military service on earnings, to show a parameter that is not identified and two ways to identify it.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: When an unobserved factor drives both treatment and outcome, the effect is not identified
text:
When an unobserved factor drives both treatment and outcome, the effect is not identified

A comparison of veterans and nonveterans picks up both the effect and the path through earnings potential. With unlimited data it still cannot separate them (Angrist 1990).
In regression terms, military service is endogenous: earnings potential is part of the error term and also affects who serves, so service is correlated with the error term.

Angrist (1990) studies this question; Jurajda poses it as his Example 1.1: “Are the (minority) vets earning more because of the military service or are the high-earners more likely to enroll in the army?” The dashed path through earnings potential is selection bias, the term defined two slides from now.
Endogeneity is the regression name for the same problem. In Yi=α+βDi+εiY_i = \alpha + \beta D_i + \varepsilon_i, the treatment DD is endogenous when it is correlated with the error term. Here earnings potential is not in the regression, so it sits in ε\varepsilon; because it also drives who serves, service and the error term move together, and the OLS coefficient mixes the effect of service with the effect of earnings potential. Selection bias, endogeneity, and the dashed path are three descriptions of one problem.
The four threats map onto this picture. Unobserved heterogeneity is the dashed node. Reverse causality would be an arrow from earnings back to service. Measurement error means the service box is recorded with error. Spillovers would be an arrow from one person’s service to another person’s earnings.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The effect becomes identified when you measure the common causes or find variation they do not drive
text:
The effect becomes identified when you measure the common causes or find variation they do not drive

A: Angrist (1998), discussed in Angrist and Pischke (2009), Chapter 3. B: the Vietnam-era draft lottery, Angrist (1990), in Jurajda (2007), Example 3.11.

Panel A is selection on observed characteristics. The military screens applicants on age, schooling, and test scores, so comparing veterans and nonveterans with the same values identifies the effect, if nothing else drives both. Angrist and Pischke note that this is “clearly not guaranteed”: applicants who drop out at the last minute may differ in earnings potential.
Panel B is an instrument. The lottery number changes who serves but is assigned at random, so earnings potential cannot affect it, and it should affect earnings only through service. It identifies the effect for men whose service depended on their lottery number.
The identifying assumption in each panel is the “Requires” line. That is the sentence a paper states in words.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Six questions organize the section, in the order they appear in a paper
text:
Six questions organize the section, in the order they appear in a paper








Subsection
Question
Where the answer appears




Estimation strategy
1. What is the relationship of interest?
The estimating equation and the parameter of interest



2. How will you measure uncertainty?
The estimator, the standard errors, the clustering level, and why


Identification strategy
3. Is that relationship causal?
Whether the parameter is causal, and if not, what it describes



4. What experiment would ideally measure it?
The effect you are trying to estimate



5. What variation identifies it, and what must be true of that variation?
The identifying assumption



6. What could make the identifying assumption fail?
The threats, and the design choice or robustness check that handles each



Adapted from Angrist and Pischke (2009), Chapter 1, and Bellemare (2020), Section 5.

Angrist and Pischke ask four questions, starting with “What is the causal relationship of interest?” Not every paper estimates a causal relationship. A descriptive paper or a forecasting paper still needs an estimating equation; it states what the parameter describes and does not claim more. That is why the causal question is separate here.
The order follows Bellemare: the estimation strategy (equation, estimator, inference) comes first, then the identification strategy (assumption, threats, robustness). The rest of the lecture follows the same order.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The estimation strategy also names the estimator and says how inference is done
text:
The estimation strategy also names the estimator and says how inference is done

The estimator by name, such as OLS, a linear probability model, probit, or maximum likelihood, and why
The hypothesis being tested
What the standard errors are robust to, such as heteroskedasticity
Whether and how standard errors are clustered, at what level, and why
Whether sampling weights are used, and how they were constructed


Source: Bellemare (2020), Section 5.1.


“Robust standard errors” alone is not enough, instead say “We used cluster-robust standard errors, clustering at the state level, to account for within-state correlation over time.”
The clustering level usually follows the level at which the treatment varies or at which errors are correlated. In the panel weather example later today, neighboring counties share weather shocks.
We return to inference later in the unit, including how to handle a small number of clusters.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Bellemare asks every paper to address four threats to identification
text:
Bellemare asks every paper to address four threats to identification








Threat
What it means
Common responses




Reverse causality
The outcome affects the treatment
Measure treatment before the outcome; use an instrument


Unobserved heterogeneity
An omitted factor affects both treatment and outcome
Fixed effects, controls, or a design that holds the factor constant


Measurement error
The treatment is recorded with error; classical error biases the estimate toward zero
A second measure; an instrument


Spillovers
One unit’s treatment affects another unit’s outcome, now or later
Define units so spillovers stay within them; test for them



Bellemare calls the first three sources of endogeneity: each makes the treatment correlated with the error term (Bellemare 2020, sec. 5.2).

Bellemare asks authors to discuss each threat in turn, say whether it applies, and explain how the paper handles it. The response column lists common approaches; it is not from Bellemare.
His wording is “the three following sources of statistical endogeneity: (i) reverse causality, (ii) unobserved heterogeneity, and (iii) measurement error.” Each puts something into the error term that moves with the treatment: the outcome feeding back into the treatment, an omitted factor that drives both, or the part of the treatment that was mismeasured. He treats spillovers separately because they are not endogeneity; they mean the effect on one unit depends on others’ treatment, so the effect itself is not well defined.
Endogeneity is one way identification fails. A parameter can also fail to be identified because of spillovers, or because a model has more parameters than the variation can determine. In Lecture 6.2, “endogenous variable” also has a structural meaning: a variable determined inside the model, such as price. It becomes an estimation problem when it is correlated with the error term, as with price and unobserved product quality in BLP.
He adds: “If your results are not causally identified, do not lie about what they can and cannot do.”
The DAG from earlier shows each threat as a feature of the graph. The climate example later applies this table to three designs.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: In the panel weather model, each threat has an answer
text:
In the panel weather model, each threat has an answer







Threat
In the panel weather model




Reverse causality
Farm output does not change the weather


Unobserved heterogeneity
County effects absorb fixed differences; year effects absorb national shocks


Measurement error
Gridded weather misses farm conditions; check a second weather data set


Spillovers
Year effects absorb national price changes, so the estimate excludes them



This applies the four threats to one design. Each row needs an answer: the threat does not apply, the design handles it, or a robustness check tests it.

The four threats are Bellemare’s list (Section 5.2): reverse causality, unobserved heterogeneity, measurement error, and spillovers. Dalheimer and Bellemare’s Section 2.2 (shown earlier) walks through the first three in this order, and the generic version is in the identification strategy section.
Classical measurement error in weather attenuates the estimate toward zero.
The record on this design shows why data checks matter: Fisher, Hanemann, Roberts, and Schlenker (2012) identified errors in the weather and climate data used by Deschênes and Greenstone, and Deschênes and Greenstone (2012) replied with corrected estimates.

section: The effect is identified if you measure the common causes or use variation they do not drive
text:
The effect is identified if you measure the common causes or use variation they do not drive



Panel A is selection on observed characteristics. The military screens applicants on age, schooling, and test scores, so comparing veterans and nonveterans with the same values identifies the effect, if nothing else drives both. Angrist and Pischke note that this is “clearly not guaranteed”: applicants who drop out at the last minute may differ in earnings potential.
Panel B is an instrument. The lottery number changes who serves but is assigned at random, so earnings potential cannot affect it, and it should affect earnings only through service. It identifies the effect for men whose service depended on their lottery number.
The identifying assumption in each panel is the “Requires” line. That is the sentence a paper states in words.


A: Angrist (1998), discussed in Angrist and Pischke (2009), Chapter 3. B: the Vietnam-era draft lottery, Angrist (1990), in Jurajda (2007), Example 3.11.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The identification strategy explains what in the data supports a causal interpretation
text:
The identification strategy explains what in the data supports a causal interpretation



The section walks through Bellemare’s threats in order: reverse causation, omitted variables, and measurement error. Only after naming them does it explain the shift-share instrumental variable design that addresses them. We return to this structure in the identification strategy section.


Source: Dalheimer and Bellemare (2026), Section 2.2 (accepted version posted on Bellemare’s website).

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Identification asks whether your data and assumptions determine the parameter you want to estimate
text:
Identification asks whether your data and assumptions determine the parameter you want to estimate

Suppose you had data on the entire population. The parameter is identified if only one value of it is consistent with those data
If more than one value fits, the parameter is not identified, and a larger sample or a different estimator will not fix it
Whether a parameter is identified depends on assumptions about how the data were generated

A directed acyclic graph (DAG) draws those assumptions: each arrow is a causal effect, and each missing arrow is an assumption

Example: a paper wants to estimate the effect of military service on later earnings (Angrist 1990; posed in Jurajda 2007, Example 1.1)


Bellemare (Section 5.2) uses “identification” in the sense most applied papers now use: causal identification, when a coefficient reflects a causal relationship. He refers to Pearl’s notation for this, which denotes the effect of setting a variable to a value.
The next two slides use this question to show a parameter that is not identified and two ways to identify it.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: A hypothesis test asks whether β\beta differs from zero; identification asks what β\beta measures
text:
A hypothesis test asks whether β\beta differs from zero; identification asks what β\beta measures

Hypothesis test: given sampling variation, can the data reject H0:β=0H_0: \beta = 0? The answer depends on the estimator and the standard errors
Identification: does β\beta measure the causal effect, or the effect plus selection bias? The answer depends on the identifying assumption
Rejecting H0H_0 is evidence of a causal effect only if β\beta is identified; otherwise it shows only that the comparison picks up something
A larger sample makes the test more precise but does not change what β\beta measures
Some identifying assumptions have testable implications, such as placebo, pre-trend, or balance tests; passing them adds credibility but does not prove the assumption

The identification strategy subsection makes the case that β\beta measures the effect you want.

Bellemare (Section 5.1) notes that “a hypothesis test always tests for an equality sign.” The paper’s theoretical hypothesis may be that a treatment causes an increase in the outcome, but the statistical null is that the association between the two is not significantly different from zero. Identification is what connects the two.
The chain from earlier units: the conceptual framework gives a testable prediction (Unit 4); identification makes the coefficient a valid measure of that prediction; the hypothesis test says whether the data reject the null. A significant result supports the prediction only if the middle step holds.
Athey and Imbens call placebo and related checks “supplementary analyses”: they test implications of the identifying assumption, not the assumption itself. Core assumptions such as an exclusion restriction usually cannot be tested directly.
If the assumptions a paper can defend only bound the effect rather than pin down one value, the test asks whether the bounds exclude zero. Lecture 6.5 returns to statistical and economic significance with Gibson and Kim.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Hypothesis testing and identification answer different questions
text:
Hypothesis testing and identification answer different questions

Hypothesis test: is β\beta different from zero? This depends on the estimator and the standard errors
Identification: does β\beta measure the causal effect? This depends on the identifying assumption
A significant β\beta is evidence of a causal effect only if β\beta is identified
More data makes the test more precise, but it does not change what β\beta measures

The identification strategy subsection explains why β\beta measures the effect you want.

Bellemare (Section 5.1) notes that “a hypothesis test always tests for an equality sign.” The paper’s theoretical hypothesis may be that a treatment causes an increase in the outcome, but the statistical null is that the association between the two is not significantly different from zero. Identification is what connects the two.
The chain from earlier units: the conceptual framework gives a testable prediction (Unit 4); identification makes the coefficient a valid measure of that prediction; the hypothesis test says whether the data reject the null. A significant result supports the prediction only if the middle step holds.
Some identifying assumptions have testable implications, such as placebo, pre-trend, or balance tests; passing them adds credibility but does not prove the assumption. Athey and Imbens call placebo and related checks “supplementary analyses”: they test implications of the identifying assumption, not the assumption itself. Core assumptions such as an exclusion restriction usually cannot be tested directly.
If the assumptions a paper can defend only bound the effect rather than pin down one value, the test asks whether the bounds exclude zero. Lecture 6.5 returns to statistical and economic significance with Gibson and Kim.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Threats to identification and problems with inference are different
text:
Threats to identification and problems with inference are different

Problem with inference: the estimate may measure the right thing, but its standard errors are too small, so the result looks more certain than it is
Threat to identification: the estimate measures the wrong thing, and more data will not fix it
Clustering standard errors is an inference choice: it changes the standard errors and leaves the estimate unchanged


Source: Bellemare (2020), Sections 5.1 and 5.2.


Example for inference: in the panel weather model, neighboring counties share weather shocks, so their errors are correlated. Treating them as independent makes the standard errors too small; clustering at a level that contains the correlation fixes the standard errors and leaves the estimate unchanged.
Students often list clustering as a threat. Clustering is an inference choice: it leaves the point estimate unchanged and changes how confident we are in it.
Robustness checks can address either problem: alternative samples or controls test the identifying assumption; alternative clustering levels test the inference choice.
We return to inference later in the unit, including how to handle a small number of clusters.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Each design has to answer all four threats
text:
Each design has to answer all four threats









Threat
Ricardian
Panel weather
Long differences




Reverse causality
Land values do not change the climate
Farm output does not change the weather
Farm output does not change climate trends


Unobserved heterogeneity
The main threat: irrigation and other factors that vary with climate
County and year fixed effects absorb fixed differences and national shocks
The main threat: other trends that move with climate trends


Measurement error
Reported land values may differ from sale prices
Gridded weather misses conditions on the farm
Averaging over several years reduces noise in weather


Spillovers
Land values reflect current crop prices, which warming everywhere would change
Year effects absorb national price changes
State effects absorb price changes common within a state



Each cell needs an answer: the threat does not apply, the design handles it, or a robustness check tests it.

The four threats are Bellemare’s list (Section 5.2). This table applies the general table from the identification strategy section to each design. Unobserved heterogeneity is the main threat for the Ricardian and long-differences designs; the panel design’s fixed effects handle it, which leaves measurement error and spillovers as its main concerns.
Classical measurement error in weather attenuates the panel estimate toward zero. The Ricardian spillover row is a common critique: land values reflect current crop prices, and a warmer climate everywhere would change those prices.
The record on this design shows why data checks matter: Fisher, Hanemann, Roberts, and Schlenker (2012) identified errors in the weather and climate data used by Deschênes and Greenstone, and Deschênes and Greenstone (2012) replied with corrected estimates.

One page checklist, parallel to the data checklist from Lecture 5.5

Each row is tagged with the lecture that covers it; today covers rows 1 to 9
Built from Bellemare’s Section 5, Angrist and Pischke’s Chapter 1, and the AJAE Author Guidelines

Research FAQs
Social science is interested in cause-and-effect relationships
Before starting your research, ask:

What is the causal relationship of interest?
What experiment could ideally be used to capture the causal effect of interest?
What is your identification strategy?
What is your mode of statistical inference?

These questions are answered throughout the paper, but formally written up in the methods (or empirical strategy) section

Their question about the ideal experiment is a planning question (the Research FAQs slide), so it is not one of the questions the written section answers.
The order follows Bellemare: the estimation strategy (equation, estimator, inference) comes first, then the identification strategy (assumption, threats, robustness). The rest of the lecture follows the same order.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Note: Hypothesis testing and identification answer different questions
text:
Note: Hypothesis testing and identification answer different questions

Hypothesis test: is β\beta different from zero? This depends on the estimator and the standard errors
Identification: does β\beta measure the causal effect? This depends on the identifying assumption
A significant β\beta is evidence of a causal effect only if β\beta is identified
More data makes the test more precise, but it does not change what β\beta measures; more data -> smaller standard error -> more precise

The identification strategy subsection explains why β\beta measures the effect you want.

Bellemare (Section 5.1) notes that “a hypothesis test always tests for an equality sign.” The paper’s theoretical hypothesis may be that a treatment causes an increase in the outcome, but the statistical null is that the association between the two is not significantly different from zero. Identification is what connects the two.
The chain from earlier units: the conceptual framework gives a testable prediction (Unit 4); identification makes the coefficient a valid measure of that prediction; the hypothesis test says whether the data reject the null. A significant result supports the prediction only if the middle step holds.
Some identifying assumptions have testable implications, such as placebo, pre-trend, or balance tests; passing such a test adds credibility, and the assumption itself remains unproven. Athey and Imbens call placebo and related checks “supplementary analyses”: they test implications of the identifying assumption. Core assumptions such as an exclusion restriction usually cannot be tested directly.
If the assumptions a paper can defend yield only bounds on the effect, the test asks whether the bounds exclude zero. Lecture 6.4 returns to statistical and economic significance with Gibson and Kim.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: To show one thing causes another (the effect is identified) you must either control for shared causes, or isolate an exogenous source of variation
text:
To show one thing causes another (the effect is identified) you must either control for shared causes, or isolate an exogenous source of variation

Both remove the endogeneity. A takes the shared causes out of the error term by controlling for them. B uses only the variation in service that the lottery creates, which is exogenous: unrelated to the error term.


Panel A is selection on observed characteristics. The military screens applicants on age, schooling, and test scores, so comparing veterans and nonveterans with the same values identifies the effect, if nothing else drives both. Angrist and Pischke note that this is “clearly not guaranteed”: applicants who drop out at the last minute may differ in earnings potential.
Panel B is an instrument. The lottery number changes who serves but is assigned at random, so earnings potential cannot affect it, and it should affect earnings only through service. It identifies the effect for men whose service depended on their lottery number.
The identifying assumption in each panel is the “Requires” line. That is the sentence a paper states in words. In regression terms, A assumes that after controlling for X, service is uncorrelated with the error term; B assumes the lottery is uncorrelated with the error term (Cov(Z, ε) = 0) and affects earnings only through service.


A: Angrist (1998), discussed in Angrist and Pischke (2009), Chapter 3. B: the Vietnam-era draft lottery, Angrist (1990), discussed in Jurajda (2007), Example 3.11.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
text:
Robustness check or sensitivity analysis?
Robustness checks vary your choices

Re-estimate your model with another defensible outcome measure, treatment measure, estimator, functional form, or sample, and show the conclusion holds (Bellemare 2020, sec. 6.2)
A placebo test estimates an effect that should be zero; Bellemare counts these as robustness checks, and Athey and Imbens list them separately

Sensitivity analyses relax your assumptions

Purpose is to ask how far the identifying assumption would have to fail before the conclusion changes, for example how strong an omitted variable would have to be (Athey and Imbens 2017)

Why papers include them: researchers try many specifications before choosing one, so readers need evidence that the result was not selected for (Athey and Imbens 2017)

Athey and Imbens call these “supplementary analyses”: their purpose is to provide evidence on the credibility of the primary analysis. They cite Leamer on the gap between the single model that classical inference assumes and the many specifications researchers actually try. The sensitivity approaches they discuss include Rosenbaum and Rubin, Imbens, Altonji and coauthors, and Oster.
Bellemare frames robustness checks as a response to higher standards of evidence after the credibility revolution: authors “have to work hard to convince readers that their results were not cherrypicked.”
This is why papers have a robustness section. Each check should name the threat or the choice it tests. Lecture 6.4 returns to this.
Note that “robust” in “robust standard errors” is a different use of the word: those standard errors are robust to a specific feature of the errors, such as heteroskedasticity.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Two published papers answer the same climate question with different empirical strategy sections
text:
Two published papers answer the same climate question with different empirical strategy sections
Question: How will a warmer climate affect U.S. agriculture?

The ideal experiment: give some counties a permanently warmer climate, then wait decades while farmers adapt
No paper can run that experiment, so each one approximates it with a different comparison
The comparison determines what the coefficient measures
Read each design as the empirical strategy section its paper would write: estimation strategy, then identification strategy


Purpose of the example: one research question, two empirical strategy sections, two different parameters. Students should leave with the point that choosing the identifying variation also chooses what the coefficient means, and that the section has to say which one it estimates.
Angrist and Pischke argue that describing the ideal experiment “helps you formulate causal questions precisely.” Here it separates two effects that are easy to confuse: the effect of climate and the effect of weather. The ideal experiment is a planning question (the Research FAQs slide); it is not a separate part of the written section.
Ask: in your proposal, what would you randomize, and how long would you wait to measure the outcome?

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The panel model compares each county with itself across years, which removes irrigation but changes what is estimated
text:
The panel model compares each county with itself across years, which removes irrigation but changes what is estimated


Estimation strategy
yct=g(Wct)+γc+δt+εct
y_{ct} = g(W_{ct}) + \gamma_c + \delta_t + \varepsilon_{ct}


ycty_{ct}: log crop yield or farm profit in county cc, year tt
WctW_{ct}: growing-season weather, such as degree days and precipitation
g(⋅)g(\cdot): its slope is the parameter of interest
γc\gamma_c, δt\delta_t: county and year fixed effects
Standard errors allow neighboring counties’ errors to be correlated, because they share weather shocks


Identification strategy

Identifying assumption: within a county, hotter and cooler years do not differ in other ways that affect yields
Main threats: measurement error in gridded weather, and price changes that spill over across counties
What the coefficient measures: the short-run response to weather; farmers cannot fully adapt to one hot year, so the long-run effect can be larger or smaller (Timmins and Schlenker 2009)




Deschênes and Greenstone use farm profits; Schlenker and Roberts use yields and allow temperature effects to be nonlinear. Both rely on the same variation.
County fixed effects remove everything fixed about a county, including irrigation access and long-run climate. What is left is weather.
Timmins and Schlenker give both directions. Long-run responses face fewer constraints, so long-run damages can be smaller. But some short-run responses cannot be sustained; their example is groundwater pumping, which works for one dry year and not for a permanently drier climate.
The point for the paper: gaining credibility also changed what the coefficient measures, and the section has to say which effect it estimates.
Transition: to recover adaptation without going back to a cross-section of levels, compare slow changes over long periods.



Sources: Deschênes and Greenstone (2007); Schlenker and Roberts (2009).

Your empirical strategy section makes the same statements for your design, in prose. It does not need a table like this one; the slide on writing with comments shows how to keep the questions in front of you while drafting.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Put the five questions in your draft as comments, then answer each in prose
text:
Put the five questions in your draft as comments, then answer each in prose
\section{Empirical Strategy}

\subsection{Estimation Strategy}
% What is the relationship of interest?
%   equation, every term defined, parameter of interest
% How will you measure uncertainty?

\subsection{Identification Strategy}

Lines that start with % do not appear in the compiled PDF. In Word, use comments; in Quarto or Markdown, use <!-- -->.

The comments keep the five questions in front of you while you draft, and a coauthor can check that each one has an answer. Delete them before submission or leave them; they do not print. This follows Bellemare’s split: inference belongs in the estimation strategy, and the threats belong in the identification strategy.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Three published papers answer the same climate question with different empirical strategy sections
text:
Three published papers answer the same climate question with different empirical strategy sections
Question: How will a warmer climate affect U.S. agriculture?

The ideal experiment: give some counties a permanently warmer climate, then wait decades while farmers adapt
No paper can run that experiment, so each one approximates it with a different comparison
The comparison determines what the coefficient measures
Read each design as the empirical strategy section its paper would write: estimation strategy, then identification strategy


Purpose of the example: one research question, three empirical strategy sections, three different parameters. Each design responds to a weakness in the one before it. Students should leave with the point that choosing the identifying variation also chooses what the coefficient means, and that the section has to say which one it estimates.
Angrist and Pischke argue that describing the ideal experiment “helps you formulate causal questions precisely.” Here it separates two effects that are easy to confuse: the effect of climate and the effect of weather. The ideal experiment is a planning question (the Research FAQs slide).

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Long differences compare slow changes in climate over decades, which recovers the adaptation the panel model misses
text:
Long differences compare slow changes in climate over decades, which recovers the adaptation the panel model misses


Estimation strategy
Δy‾c=αs+βΔW‾c+Δε‾c
\Delta \bar{y}_c = \alpha_s + \beta\, \Delta \bar{W}_c + \Delta \bar{\varepsilon}_c


Δy‾c\Delta \bar{y}_c: change in county cc’s multi-year average outcome between two periods
ΔW‾c\Delta \bar{W}_c: change in its multi-year average weather over the same periods
αs\alpha_s: state fixed effects; β\beta: the parameter of interest
Standard errors allow neighboring counties’ errors to be correlated; one observation per county leaves far fewer observations than the panel


Identification strategy

Identifying assumption: within a state, counties that warmed more did not change in other ways that affect yields
Main threat: other trends, such as technology adoption, that move with climate trends
What the coefficient measures: the response to gradual climate change, including the adaptation farmers made over the period




Burke and Emerick use recent temperature and precipitation trends. Comparing the long-differences estimate with the panel estimate for the same weather variable shows how much farmers adapted over the period. That comparison is only possible because the two designs estimate different relationships.
State fixed effects mean the comparison is between counties in the same state, so anything that changed for the whole state is removed.



Source: Burke and Emerick (2016).
