title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: A structural model recovers the parameters of behavior
text:
A structural model recovers the parameters of behavior

Definition: any empirical model that recovers the parameters of behavioral functions, such as demand and supply equations, utility functions, or cost structures
It starts from a theoretical model and states what the researcher can and cannot observe
What cannot be observed becomes a structural error, backed out of observed behavior
The parameters are estimated with a procedure such as GMM or maximum likelihood


Source: Timmins and Schlenker (2009), Section 2.


Nevo and Whinston (page 69): “Structural modeling attempts to use data to identify the parameters of an underlying economic model, based on models of individual choice or aggregate relations derived from them.” Their footnote 1 (page 70) adds that a structural model is “an economic behavioral model that defines the relationship between exogenous and endogenous variables, both observed and unobserved by the researcher.” They distinguish this from the econometrics textbook meaning of “structural.”
Link to Unit 4: for Ethridge, a conceptual framework is an analysis of a specific problem using relevant theory and concepts. A theoretical model is a conceptual framework written in mathematics, with stated objectives, constraints, functional forms, and an equilibrium. Any paper can have a conceptual framework. A structural paper needs the mathematical version, because its equations are what get estimated.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: “Reduced form” has two meanings, and the recent one is the one you will read
text:
“Reduced form” has two meanings, and the recent one is the one you will read

Textbook meaning: solve a system of equations so the outcome depends only on exogenous variables
Recent meaning: program evaluation or treatment effects, with attention to how the exogenous variable was assigned
The goal is to avoid as many structural assumptions as possible
Reduced-form studies still require assumptions of their own

The designs from Lecture 6.1 are reduced form in the recent sense: fixed effects, quasi-experiments, regression discontinuity, and randomization.
Source: Timmins and Schlenker (2009), Section 3.

Timmins and Schlenker’s example of the textbook meaning: demand and supply both depend on price; the reduced form eliminates price and writes equilibrium quantity as a function of the demand and supply shifters.
Where the climate designs from 6.1 fit: the panel weather model and long differences are reduced form in the recent sense. The Ricardian model estimates a hedonic-style relationship with an economic argument behind it; the methods map places it between the two.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: The two approaches differ in what they estimate and what they assume
text:
The two approaches differ in what they estimate and what they assume









Reduced form
Structural




Estimates
High-level response parameters
Behavioral parameters, such as preferences and costs


Credibility comes from
The source of variation
The source of variation and the economic model


Best suited to
Establishing causality for a change in the data
Feedback loops, large policy changes, and welfare


Main assumptions
How treatment was assigned
Functional form, unobservables, and how agents behave (such as profit maximization)


Counterfactual
A comparison group, for a change in the data
A simulation of the model, including changes not in the data


Main limit
Harder to extend to changes not observed
Conclusions depend on the model being right




Source: Timmins and Schlenker (2009), Sections 1 and 4.


Timmins and Schlenker say each approach “may be better suited to answering particular types of questions.” The choice follows from the question.
Counterfactual and simulation are different ideas. A counterfactual is the scenario: what would happen under conditions we do not observe. A simulation is a calculation: solving a model under stated conditions. Reduced-form designs also estimate a counterfactual, because the control group stands in for what would have happened to the treated group. Timmins and Schlenker’s point is about out-of-sample counterfactuals: “Counter-factual policy simulations that include out-of-sample predictions by definition require structural parameters.”

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Structural models answer questions that reduced-form designs cannot
text:
Structural models answer questions that reduced-form designs cannot

Feedback loops: people and firms re-optimize, and markets re-equilibrate
Large or new policies: the change has not happened, or not at this scale
Welfare: effects are converted to dollars through a utility function
Who bears the cost: heterogeneity in preferences changes the distributional answer
Unintended consequences: simulate the world with one piece of the policy turned off

Source: Timmins and Schlenker (2009), Section 2.1.

Examples from Timmins and Schlenker for each point, if students ask.
Who bears the cost: Jacobsen (2008) models fuel-economy standards together with the used-car market and finds the cost falls on poorer households who buy used cars, not on new-car buyers.
Unintended consequences: Ryan (2006) models entry in the cement industry and finds the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments raised sunk entry costs, which reduced competition and left consumers worse off while incumbent firms gained.
Link to the methods map: these are the methods at the top of the map, where the outcome is not in the data.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Structural analysis has two steps, and it still needs credible identification
text:
Structural analysis has two steps, and it still needs credible identification

Match observed behavior to a theoretical model to recover parameters such as preferences and technology
Use the model to predict responses to changes, assuming those parameters do not change


Nevo and Whinston: structural analysis and credible identification are complements
Identification tells you what the data reveal; the model extends it to settings not observed
Timmins and Schlenker: the most convincing evidence comes from contrasting approaches

Sources: Nevo and Whinston (2010), pages 70 to 71; Timmins and Schlenker (2009), Section 4.

Nevo and Whinston: “Structural analysis is not a substitute for credible inference. Quite to the contrary, in general, structural analysis and credible identification are complements.” The second step is the extrapolation that a treatment effect alone does not provide.
The complement runs both ways. Timmins and Schlenker note that reduced-form estimates of a response can be used inside a structural model to simulate policy.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Merger analysis shows what each approach can and cannot answer
text:
Merger analysis shows what each approach can and cannot answer









Treatment effect of a past merger
Merger simulation




Method
Compare prices near and far from the merging firms, before and after
Estimate demand and pricing, then simulate joint pricing


Strength
Clear identification for that merger
Predicts a proposed merger, with welfare


Limit
Other mergers may not be similar; no welfare measure
Holds products, firms, and pricing behavior fixed; instruments are often imperfect



Nevo and Whinston’s conclusion: each is useful in some cases and fails in others, depending on the question and the data.
Source: Nevo and Whinston (2010), pages 73 to 77.

The treatment-effect example is Hastings (2004) on the ARCO acquisition of Thrifty gasoline stations. Nevo and Whinston call it careful design, then ask what it says about a merger of two large branded firms, or a merger in another region.
Their conclusion on page 80: “the future of econometrics and applied microeconomic work is in combining careful design, credible inference, robust estimation methods, and thoughtful modeling.”
Transition: merger simulation is one use of a structural model. The next slide shows the range of models students will see.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: A structural section states the same four choices as any empirical section
text:
A structural section states the same four choices as any empirical section







Choice
In a structural paper




Model
The primitives: preferences, technology, and how agents interact


Estimation and inference
The estimator in one paragraph, with details in an appendix


Identification
Which variation identifies which parameter


Reported results
Fit or validation, and the counterfactuals the model is used for




This is the one slide drawn from the methods map’s “Four choices” section. The next slides go through these four choices for BLP. BLP is one structural model; the choices apply to all of them, from demand systems to dynamic models.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Demand for many products needs a model because there are too many cross-prices
text:
Demand for many products needs a model because there are too many cross-prices

With 100 products, a log-log demand system has at least 10,000 parameters
BLP describes each product by its characteristics, so the number of parameters depends on the characteristics, not the number of products
It uses market-level data on prices and quantities, and it allows for endogenous prices
Running question: how much would prices rise if two cereal firms merged?

Sources: Nevo (2000), pages 514 to 515; Berry et al. (1995).

BLP stands for Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (1995), who estimate demand for automobiles. Nevo applies the method to ready-to-eat cereal (2001). Food demand is a common application in agricultural economics, so the method may be useful for proposals on food retail or consumer demand.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Model: each consumer chooses the product that gives the highest utility
text:
Model: each consumer chooses the product that gives the highest utility
uijt=αi(yi−pjt)+xjtβi+ξjt+εijt
u_{ijt} = \alpha_i(y_i - p_{jt}) + x_{jt}\beta_i + \xi_{jt} + \varepsilon_{ijt}


uijtu_{ijt}: utility of consumer ii from product jj in market tt (a city in a quarter)
yiy_i: income; pjtp_{jt}: price; xjtx_{jt}: observed characteristics, such as sugar content
ξjt\xi_{jt}: characteristics the researcher does not observe, such as brand quality or promotions
αi\alpha_i, βi\beta_i: tastes that vary across consumers with demographics and unobserved traits
εijt\varepsilon_{ijt}: a mean-zero shock; consumers can also buy nothing (the outside good)

Summing individual choices gives each product’s predicted market share. The data are the observed shares.
Source: Nevo (2000), pages 517 to 520.

The parameters of interest are the taste parameters. Everything the paper reports (elasticities, markups, welfare) is computed from them.
Latin letters are data, Greek letters are estimated. ξjt\xi_{jt} is Greek because it is never observed: it is the structural error in Timmins and Schlenker’s definition, backed out of observed shares.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Estimation: invert shares to recover the unobserved term, then use GMM
text:
Estimation: invert shares to recover the unobserved term, then use GMM
In plain logit, where tastes do not vary, shares invert to a linear regression:
ln⁡sjt−ln⁡s0t=xjtβ−αpjt+ξjt
\ln\, s_{jt} - \ln\, s_{0t} = x_{jt}\beta - \alpha p_{jt} + \xi_{jt}


sjts_{jt}: market share of product jj; s0ts_{0t}: share of the outside good
This is a linear instrumental-variables regression (Berry 1994)
With random coefficients, the same idea is solved numerically for each guess of the taste parameters
The estimator is GMM: instruments must be uncorrelated with ξjt\xi_{jt}

In a paper, this gets one paragraph. The steps go in an appendix.

This is the only slide on the algorithm. The methods map walks through it step by step for anyone who needs it.
Inference: report GMM standard errors for the parameters, and standard errors for the quantities the paper is about, such as elasticities.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Numerical estimation means the appendix has to report how you solved it
text:
Numerical estimation means the appendix has to report how you solved it








Same model, same data
Mean price coefficient
Mean own-price elasticity




Replication of the published estimates
−32.4
−3.70


Tighter optimizer tolerance
−62.7
−3.62


Best practices
−27.5
−3.69




Report the optimizer, tolerances, starting values, and integration method
Try several optimizers and starting values, and check that they agree
Report the quantities that matter for the question, because individual coefficients can move a lot

Source: Conlon and Gortmaker (2020), Table 7.

Conlon and Gortmaker re-estimate Nevo’s model on his simulated data. Changing one optimizer setting (the gradient tolerance from 1E-4 to 1E-5) nearly doubles the price coefficient, while the elasticity barely moves. “Best practices” adds further changes, including a tighter tolerance and better approximations to the instruments.
They also find that with these practices, estimates are stable across starting values and optimizers, which is better news than earlier work suggested (Knittel and Metaxoglou, 2014, as discussed in Conlon and Gortmaker 2020).

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Identification: firms set prices knowing what the researcher cannot see
text:
Identification: firms set prices knowing what the researcher cannot see

Ideal experiment: randomly assign prices to consumers and record purchases
In the data, firms set prices knowing ξjt\xi_{jt}, so price is endogenous
Price needs an instrument, and each choice rests on its own assumption:

Cost shifters, if cost data vary by brand
Characteristics of rival products (BLP)
Prices of the same brand in other cities (Hausman)

A threat to the last one: a national demand shock moves prices in every city

Source: Nevo (2000), pages 528 and 534 to 536.

This is the same endogeneity as the veterans DAG in Lecture 6.1: ξjt\xi_{jt} is in the error term and also affects the treatment, here price.
Nevo’s example of a threat to the other-city instrument: a finding that fiber may reduce the risk of cancer raises demand for high-fiber cereals in every city. Coordinated advertising across city borders would also violate it. Nevo says resolving this requires comparing sets of instruments, additional data, and knowledge of the industry.
Nevo and Whinston (page 76) say that in many cases the instruments are less than ideal. That is a limitation to state, not to hide.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Identification: which products gain share when one price rises reveals substitution
text:
Identification: which products gain share when one price rises reveals substitution

Plain logit forces substitution to follow market shares, not how similar the products are
If Cap’n Crunch and Grape Nuts have similar shares, plain logit says a rise in the price of Lucky Charms helps both equally
Random coefficients let similar products be closer substitutes
The taste parameters are identified by how shares actually shift when prices or the set of products change
Tastes linked to demographics require markets with different demographics

Source: Nevo (2000), pages 523 and 529.

Nevo’s cereal example (page 523): Lucky Charms and Cap’n Crunch are both children’s cereals, Grape Nuts is not, so we expect more consumers to switch to Cap’n Crunch. His three-product example (page 529) is the identification argument: if A and B are similar and B and C have the same share, the relative change in the shares of B and C after a rise in the price of A separates plain logit from random coefficients.
This is what “state which variation identifies which parameter” means in a structural paper.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Reported results: state what the counterfactual holds fixed, and how you validated the model
text:
Reported results: state what the counterfactual holds fixed, and how you validated the model

Merger simulation: set the prices of the merging firms jointly and solve for new prices
Report results under a range of assumptions
State what is held fixed: current merger simulations hold products, firms, and pricing behavior fixed
Validate the model: check that it predicts outcomes not used to estimate it

Sources: Nevo and Whinston (2010), pages 75 to 77; Timmins and Schlenker (2009), Section 2.

Nevo and Whinston give the validation example: Peters (2006) compares merger simulations with what actually happened after airline mergers and finds the simulations missed the size of several price changes. Retrospective studies are how the two approaches check each other.
Timmins and Schlenker suggest estimating with a subset of the data and checking the model’s ability to predict behavior in the rest.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Demo: one script estimates cereal demand in steps, then simulates a merger
text:
Demo: one script estimates cereal demand in steps, then simulates a merger

Data: Nevo’s simulated cereal data, 24 products in 94 markets (47 cities, 2 quarters)
Nevo: the data are “not real and should not be used for any analysis,” so these numbers teach the method, not cereal
Steps: plain logit by OLS, add product fixed effects, add instruments, add random coefficients, simulate a merger of firms 1 and 2
Software: PyBLP in Python; the script runs in under a minute

Download the demo script
Sources: Nevo (2000), page 538; Conlon and Gortmaker (2020).

We read results here rather than running code in class. Students who want to run it can install PyBLP and run the script on their own. The script also works from R through the reticulate package.
Firms 1 and 2 are the two largest firms in the simulated data, with about 75 percent of sales.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Comparing each product with itself triples the price coefficient, because quality is the omitted variable
text:
Comparing each product with itself triples the price coefficient, because quality is the omitted variable



Specification (plain logit)
Price coefficient




OLS, no product fixed effects
−10.1


OLS, product fixed effects
−29.0


Instrumental variables, product fixed effects
−30.0




Better cereals cost more, so without fixed effects a high price partly signals high quality
Product fixed effects absorb a product’s fixed quality, which is part of ξjt\xi_{jt}
In these simulated data, the instruments change little once fixed effects are included


This is the selection problem from Lecture 6.1 in a demand setting: price and unobserved quality move together, so the comparison across products mixes the effect of price with the effect of quality.
The small change from adding instruments is a feature of these simulated data. It does not show that instruments are unnecessary in real data. Instruments address the part of ξjt\xi_{jt} that varies within a product across markets.

Change in consumer surplus
−11.6%
−13.6%



The counterfactual depends on how the model lets consumers substitute, which is an assumption the section has to state and defend.

Row two: when one product’s price rises, plain logit makes every rival respond in the same proportion (ratio of 1). With random coefficients, the most affected rival responds about 6 times as much as the least affected, in the median case, in one market.
Why the merger result doubles: merging firms raise prices more when their products are close substitutes for each other, because more of the lost sales stay within the merged firm. Plain logit cannot represent that closeness.
The takeaway for writing: two models can fit one summary statistic and still disagree on the counterfactual. That is why a structural section states its assumptions and reports results under alternatives.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: The term “reduced form” has two meanings
text:
The term “reduced form” has two meanings

Textbook meaning: solve a system of equations so the outcome depends only on exogenous variables
Recent meaning: program evaluation or treatment effects, with attention to how the exogenous variable was assigned
Avoids as many structural assumptions as possible, and still requires assumptions of its own
The two approaches overlap, and many papers combine them

The designs from Lecture 6.1 are reduced form in the recent sense: fixed effects, quasi-experiments, regression discontinuity, and randomization.

Sources: Timmins and Schlenker (2009), Section 3; Woerman (2022), slide 12.


Woerman uses the term “nonstructural” for the same idea. Nonstructural models are usually grounded in theory, which decides what goes in yy and xx, but the estimated relationship need not have an economic interpretation.
Timmins and Schlenker’s example of the textbook meaning: demand and supply both depend on price; the reduced form eliminates price and writes equilibrium quantity as a function of the demand and supply shifters.
Where the climate designs from 6.1 fit: the panel weather model and long differences are reduced form in the recent sense. The Ricardian model estimates a hedonic-style relationship with an economic argument behind it; the methods map places it between the two.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Structural models are used for feedback effects, new policies, and welfare
text:
Structural models are used for feedback effects, new policies, and welfare

Feedback loops: people and firms re-optimize, and markets re-equilibrate
Large or new policies: the change has not happened, or not at this scale
Welfare: effects are converted to dollars through a utility function
Who bears the cost: heterogeneity in preferences changes the distributional answer
Unintended consequences: simulate the world with one piece of the policy turned off

Source: Timmins and Schlenker (2009), Section 2.1.

Examples from Timmins and Schlenker for each point, if students ask.
Who bears the cost: Jacobsen (2008) models fuel-economy standards together with the used-car market and finds the cost falls on poorer households who buy used cars.
Unintended consequences: Ryan (2006) models entry in the cement industry and finds the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments raised sunk entry costs, which reduced competition and left consumers worse off while incumbent firms gained.
Link to the methods map: these are the methods at the top of the map, where the outcome is not in the data.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Structural analysis recovers parameters, then simulates counterfactuals
text:
Structural analysis recovers parameters, then simulates counterfactuals

Match observed behavior to a theoretical model to recover parameters such as preferences and technology
Use the model to predict responses to changes, assuming those parameters are unchanged

Sources: Nevo and Whinston (2010), pages 70 to 71; Timmins and Schlenker (2009), Section 4.

Nevo and Whinston describe structural analysis and credible identification as complements: identification establishes what the data reveal, and the model extends those results to settings not observed.
Nevo and Whinston: “Structural analysis is not a substitute for credible inference. Quite to the contrary, in general, structural analysis and credible identification are complements.” The second step is the extrapolation that a treatment effect alone does not provide.
The complement runs both ways. Timmins and Schlenker note that reduced-form estimates of a response can be used inside a structural model to simulate policy. We return to this at the end of the lecture.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: BLP addresses the large number of cross-price effects in differentiated-product demand
text:
BLP addresses the large number of cross-price effects in differentiated-product demand
A log-log demand system estimates one equation for each product jj, with every price on the right side:
ln⁡qjt=γj+∑k=1100ηjkln⁡pkt+εjt
\ln\, q_{jt} = \gamma_j + \sum_{k=1}^{100} \eta_{jk} \ln\, p_{kt} + \varepsilon_{jt}


ηjk\eta_{jk}: the percent change in the quantity of jj when the price of kk rises 1 percent
With 100 products, a log-log demand system has at least 10,000 parameters
BLP describes each product by its characteristics, so the number of parameters depends on the number of characteristics
It uses market-level data on prices and quantities, and it allows for endogenous prices

Sources: Nevo (2000a), pages 514 to 515; Berry et al. (1995).

BLP stands for Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (1995), who estimate demand for automobiles.
A log-log demand system regresses the log quantity of each product on the logs of all prices, so each coefficient is an own-price or cross-price elasticity: 100 equations with 100 prices each. It has no utility function, so it looks like a regression a reduced-form paper would run. It is a demand equation, though, and it needs an exogenous source of variation for each price. A reduced-form design can estimate a few elasticities, for example from a tax or price change that affects one product. The problem on this slide is estimating all of them at once.
Nevo describes this system in words; the equation writes out his description. Nevo also notes that the symmetry and adding-up restrictions from theory still leave too many parameters.

Source: Conlon and Gortmaker (2020), Table 7.

Conlon and Gortmaker re-estimate Nevo’s model on his simulated data. Changing one optimizer setting (the gradient tolerance from 1E-4 to 1E-5) nearly doubles the price coefficient, while the elasticity barely moves. “Best practices” adds further changes, including a tighter tolerance and better approximations to the instruments.
They also find that with these practices, estimates are stable across starting values and optimizers, which is better news than earlier work suggested (Knittel and Metaxoglou, 2014, as discussed in Conlon and Gortmaker 2020).

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Identification of the price coefficient: price is endogenous, so it needs instruments
text:
Identification of the price coefficient: price is endogenous, so it needs instruments

Price is an equilibrium outcome: firms set markups knowing demand, so pjtp_{jt} is correlated with ξjt\xi_{jt}
OLS biases the price coefficient toward zero, because high-ξjt\xi_{jt} products have both higher prices and higher shares
Identification requires instruments ZjtZ_{jt} that shift price and satisfy E[ξjt∣Zjt]=0E[\xi_{jt} \mid Z_{jt}] = 0









Instrument
Why it moves price
Exclusion restriction




Cost shifters
Shift marginal cost
Uncorrelated with demand shocks


Characteristics of rival products (BLP)
Close rivals lower markups
Product characteristics are set before demand shocks are realized


Prices of the same brand in other markets (Hausman)
Same brand shares marginal cost across markets
Demand shocks are independent across markets




Source: Nevo (2000a), pages 528 and 534 to 536.


This is the classic supply and demand identification problem: to trace out a demand curve, you need variation that shifts supply and leaves demand unchanged. The instruments play that role. It is the same endogeneity as the veterans DAG in Lecture 6.1: ξjt\xi_{jt} is in the error term and also affects the treatment, here price.
Nevo and Whinston (page 76) say that in many cases the instruments are less than ideal. State that limitation in the section.
Transition: Nevo uses the third row, and checks it against the first.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Identification of substitution patterns: taste parameters need variation across markets
text:
Identification of substitution patterns: taste parameters need variation across markets

Plain logit implies substitution proportional to market shares (independence of irrelevant alternatives)
Random coefficients let substitution depend on product characteristics
The taste distribution is identified by how shares respond across markets with different choice sets, characteristics, and prices
Parameters linking tastes to demographics are identified by variation in the distribution of demographics across markets
Identification improves with more markets and more variation in the set of products

Source: Nevo (2000), pages 523 and 529 to 530.

Nevo’s cereal example (page 523): Lucky Charms and Cap’n Crunch are both children’s cereals and Grape Nuts is a nutrition cereal. If Cap’n Crunch and Grape Nuts have similar shares, plain logit says a rise in the price of Lucky Charms raises both shares by the same amount. We expect more consumers to switch to Cap’n Crunch.
His three-product example (page 529): products A and B are similar, and B and C have the same market share. When the price of A rises, plain logit predicts equal increases in the shares of B and C. The relative change in the two shares identifies the parameters that govern the distribution of tastes.
This is what “state which variation identifies which parameter” means in a structural paper.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Pairing reduced-form evidence with a structural model is good practice
text:
Pairing reduced-form evidence with a structural model is good practice

A credible design shows that the response exists in the data
Reduced-form estimates can serve as inputs to the model or as targets it must reproduce
Retrospective studies check the accuracy of model predictions
Reporting why the approaches agree or disagree gives the reader more confidence than either one alone

Sources: Timmins and Schlenker (2009), Sections 1 and 4; Nevo and Whinston (2010), page 77.

Timmins and Schlenker: “the most convincing evidence stems from contrasting various approaches.” They give the example of reduced-form estimates of the effect of amenities on infant health or crop yields being used in structural models to simulate policy responses.
Nevo and Whinston’s example of a retrospective study is Peters (2006) on airline mergers. On the methods map, this approach appears as “Reduced-form estimates as model targets” and “Out-of-sample validation.”

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: What to think about when using a structural model
text:
What to think about when using a structural model

The question: does it require a model? Name the reason: feedback, a new policy, welfare, or distribution
The parameters: which ones does the model recover, and what variation identifies each one?
The assumptions: which ones drive the counterfactual, and how do results change under alternatives?
The reduced-form evidence: what credible estimate supports the model?
The validation: does the model predict outcomes not used to estimate it?


Students whose proposal is reduced form can use the first question to explain why their design answers the question without a model, and to name one counterfactual the design does not answer.

title: Cereal Demand Demo
text:
This demo estimates demand for ready-to-eat cereal in steps, computes what the estimates imply for substitution and costs, and then simulates a merger. It goes with the BLP section of Lecture 6.2. Each step shows the code, the output, and how to read the result. The derivation notes show where the equations come from.
The demo compares two models. In the logit model, every consumer has the same tastes. In the random-coefficients logit, the model in BLP, tastes vary across consumers. Steps 1 to 3 estimate the logit model, Step 4 estimates the random-coefficients logit, and Steps 5 to 7 use both.

title: Cereal Demand Demo
text:
The data
The data are the simulated cereal data from Nevo (2000), which ship with PyBLP. Nevo writes that the data are “not real and should not be used for any analysis,” so the numbers below illustrate the method and say nothing about actual cereal markets.
One row is a product in a market, and a market is a city in a quarter. The file holds 24 products in 94 markets (47 cities in 2 quarters), which gives 2,256 rows. Each row records the market share, the price, two characteristics (sugar content and whether the cereal gets soggy in milk, called mushy), and 20 columns of instruments. A second file holds simulated consumers, with income, age, and an indicator for children.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pyblp

products = pd.read_csv(pyblp.data.NEVO_PRODUCTS_LOCATION)
agents = pd.read_csv(pyblp.data.NEVO_AGENTS_LOCATION)
The logit model turns market shares into a linear regression (Berry 1994). The dependent variable is the log share of each product minus the log share of the outside good (buying no cereal):
ln⁡sjt−ln⁡s0t=xjtβ−αpjt+ξjt
\ln\, s_{jt} - \ln\, s_{0t} = x_{jt}\beta - \alpha p_{jt} + \xi_{jt}

outside_share = 1 - products.groupby("market_ids").shares.transform("sum")
y = np.log(products.shares) - np.log(outside_share)

title: Cereal Demand Demo
text:
Step 1: plain logit by OLS
This regression treats price as exogenous and controls only for a constant, sugar, and mushy.
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(products)), products.prices, products.sugar, products.mushy])
ols_no_fe = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0][1]
Price coefficient: -10.12

title: Cereal Demand Demo
text:
Step 2: add product fixed effects
Product fixed effects absorb each product’s fixed quality, which is part of ξjt\xi_{jt}. The comparison is now each product with itself across markets.
price_within = products.prices - products.groupby("product_ids").prices.transform("mean")
y_within = y - y.groupby(products.product_ids).transform("mean")
ols_fe = (price_within @ y_within) / (price_within @ price_within)
Price coefficient: -28.95
The coefficient roughly triples. Better cereals cost more, so in Step 1 a high price partly signals high quality, and the estimate is biased toward zero. This is the omitted-variable problem from Lecture 6.1 in a demand setting.

title: Cereal Demand Demo
text:
Step 3: add instruments for price
This step instruments for price in the logit model. It addresses the endogeneity of price and does not yet involve random coefficients.
logit_problem = pyblp.Problem(
    pyblp.Formulation("0 + prices", absorb="C(product_ids)"), products
)
logit = logit_problem.solve(method="2s")
Price coefficient: -30.05 (standard error 1.01)
First-stage R-squared within products: 0.97
The instruments are the 20 columns named demand_instruments0 to demand_instruments19. The file does not label them. In the real cereal data, Nevo (2001) uses two kinds of instruments: regional average prices of the same brand in other cities, which share its marginal cost, and proxies for distribution costs, such as city density and earnings in the supermarket sector.
The instruments change the estimate by about 4 percent. That small change is a feature of these simulated data: the 20 columns explain 97 percent of the variation in price within a product, so the instrumented price is close to the actual price. In real data, the instruments can change the estimate by much more.

title: Cereal Demand Demo
text:
Step 4: add random coefficients
Random coefficients let tastes for price and characteristics vary with income, age, and children, and with traits the researcher does not observe. The model now has no closed-form solution, so PyBLP searches numerically over the taste parameters.
rc_problem = pyblp.Problem(
    (
        pyblp.Formulation("0 + prices", absorb="C(product_ids)"),
        pyblp.Formulation("1 + prices + sugar + mushy"),
    ),
    products,
    pyblp.Formulation("0 + income + income_squared + age + child"),
    agents,
)
rc = rc_problem.solve(
    initial_sigma,
    initial_pi,
    optimization=pyblp.Optimization("bfgs", {"gtol": 1e-5}),
    method="1s",
)
The script defines the starting values initial_sigma and initial_pi.
Mean price coefficient: -62.73 (standard error 14.80)
Optimizer converged after 51 iterations; run time 16 seconds
This matches the “Tighter Tolerance” column of Table 7 in Conlon and Gortmaker (2020). The mean coefficient is not comparable with the logit coefficient on its own, because each consumer’s price sensitivity also depends on the interactions with demographics. Their table is worth reading alongside this result: with a looser stopping rule for the optimizer, the same model on the same data gives a mean price coefficient of -32.4, and their best-practice estimate is -27.5, while the mean own-price elasticity stays between -3.62 and -3.70. They report nearly identical elasticities and markups across these runs. Individual coefficients move, partly because the price and income interaction terms are nearly collinear in the data, so report the optimizer, tolerances, starting values, and integration method in an appendix, along with the quantities that matter for your question.

The last step asks what each model implies for substitution, then simulates a merger of firms 1 and 2, the two largest firms in the data (about 75 percent of sales). The simulation recovers each product’s marginal cost from the pricing model, assigns the two firms joint ownership, and solves for new prices.
merged_firms = products.firm_ids.replace(2, 1).to_numpy()
new_prices = results.compute_prices(firm_ids=merged_firms, costs=results.compute_costs())

The two models agree on own-price elasticities and differ on the merger. The second row explains why. When one product’s price rises, plain logit makes every rival respond in the same proportion, so the ratio is 1. title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Structural models are used for feedback loops, new policies, and welfare
text:
Structural models are used for feedback loops, new policies, and welfare

Feedback loops: an outcome changes the conditions that produced it, so agents re-optimize and markets re-equilibrate
Large or new policies: the change has not happened, or not at this scale
Welfare: effects are converted to dollars through a utility function
Who bears the cost: heterogeneity in preferences changes the distributional answer
Unintended consequences: simulate the world with one piece of the policy turned off

Source: Timmins and Schlenker (2009), Section 2.1.

Examples from Timmins and Schlenker for each point, if students ask.
Feedback loops: they use “feedback loops” and “feedback effects” for the same idea. Their example is a fishery: fish stocks affect fishing effort, and effort affects stocks through the harvest. A change in either sets in motion “the re-equilibration of the entire system.” A merger has the same structure, although Timmins and Schlenker do not use it as an example: the merged firm raises prices, consumers switch, rivals reset their prices, and those prices change the merged firm’s demand.
Who bears the cost: Jacobsen (2008) models fuel-economy standards together with the used-car market and finds the cost falls on poorer households who buy used cars.
Unintended consequences: Ryan (2006) models entry in the cement industry and finds the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments raised sunk entry costs, which reduced competition and left consumers worse off while incumbent firms gained.
Link to the methods map: these are the methods at the top of the map, where the outcome is not in the data.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Comparing reduced-form and structural approaches to merger analysis
text:
Comparing reduced-form and structural approaches to merger analysis









Reduced form: treatment effect of a past merger
Structural: merger simulation




Method
Compare prices near and far from the merging firms, before and after
Estimate demand and pricing, then simulate joint pricing


Strength
Clear identification for that merger
Predicts a proposed merger, with welfare


Limit
Other mergers may not be similar; no welfare measure
Holds products, firms, and pricing behavior fixed; instruments are often imperfect



Source: Nevo and Whinston (2010), pages 73 to 77.

The treatment-effect example is Hastings (2004) on the ARCO acquisition of Thrifty gasoline stations. Nevo and Whinston call it careful design, then ask what it says about a merger of two large branded firms, or a merger in another region.
Nevo and Whinston’s conclusion: each is useful in some cases and fails in others, depending on the question and the data.
Their conclusion on page 80: “the future of econometrics and applied microeconomic work is in combining careful design, credible inference, robust estimation methods, and thoughtful modeling.”
Transition: merger simulation is one use of a structural model. The next slide shows the range of models students will see.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: The theoretical model behind BLP: consumers, firms, and equilibrium
text:
The theoretical model behind BLP: consumers, firms, and equilibrium









Consumers
Firms




Choice
One product, or none
Prices of their own products


Objective
Maximize utility
Maximize profit: ∑j∈Ff(pj−mcj)Msj(p)\sum_{j \in F_f} (p_j - mc_j)\, M s_j(p)


Take as given
Income, products, and prices
Demand, marginal costs, and rivals’ prices




Equilibrium: Bertrand-Nash; each firm’s prices are optimal given rivals’ prices, and shares equal what consumers choose at those prices
Researcher observes: market shares, prices, and product characteristics
Researcher does not observe: unobserved quality, individual tastes and shocks, and marginal cost

Sources: Berry et al. (1995), Sections 2 and 3; Nevo (2001).

This is what a conceptual framework looks like when it is written as a model. It names the same items as Unit 4: agents, choices, objectives, constraints, and relationships. Here FfF_f is the set of products owned by firm ff, and MM is the size of the market.
BLP’s own summary (Section 8): the model is “four primitives and a Nash equilibrium assumption in prices.” The primitives are the utility function, the cost function, the distribution of consumer characteristics, and the distribution of product characteristics.
The next slides write out the consumer side. The firm side returns for the merger simulation. Nevo (2000, page 543) notes that a paper can use the supply side only to motivate instruments, without estimating it.
Transition: every structural paper turns its theoretical model into the same four choices.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Model: each consumer chooses the option that gives the highest utility
text:
Model: each consumer chooses the option that gives the highest utility
uijt=αi(yi−pjt)+xjtβi+ξjt+εijt
u_{ijt} = \alpha_i(y_i - p_{jt}) + x_{jt}\beta_i + \xi_{jt} + \varepsilon_{ijt}


uijtu_{ijt}: utility of consumer ii from product jj in market tt (a city in a quarter)
yi−pjty_i - p_{jt}: income left after buying jj; αi\alpha_i: marginal utility of income
xjtx_{jt}: observed characteristics, such as sugar content
ξjt\xi_{jt}: characteristics the researcher does not observe, such as brand quality or promotions
βi\beta_i: tastes for those characteristics; αi\alpha_i and βi\beta_i vary across consumers
εijt\varepsilon_{ijt}: a mean-zero shock
Buying nothing is the outside good: ui0t=αiyi+εi0tu_{i0t} = \alpha_i y_i + \varepsilon_{i0t}

Summing individual choices gives each product’s predicted market share. The data are the observed shares.
Source: Nevo (2000a), pages 517 to 520.

Why income minus price: the consumer spends yi−pjty_i - p_{jt} on everything else, and each dollar of it is worth αi\alpha_i. Nevo notes this form comes from quasilinear utility, with no wealth effects, which is reasonable for cereal and unreasonable for cars.
The parameters of interest are the taste parameters. Everything the paper reports (elasticities, markups, welfare) is computed from them.
Latin letters are data, Greek letters are estimated. ξjt\xi_{jt} is Greek because it is never observed: it is the structural error in Timmins and Schlenker’s definition, backed out of observed shares.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Logit and random-coefficients logit differ in whether tastes vary across consumers
text:
Logit and random-coefficients logit differ in whether tastes vary across consumers









Logit
Random-coefficients logit (BLP)




Tastes
Same for everyone: α\alpha, β\beta
Vary across consumers: αi\alpha_i, βi\beta_i


How consumers differ
Only through the shock εijt\varepsilon_{ijt}
Through tastes and the shock


Market shares
A closed-form formula
An average over consumers, computed numerically


Substitution
In proportion to market shares
Toward products with similar characteristics


Estimation
Linear instrumental-variables regression
GMM with a numerical search



Logit is the special case of random coefficients in which every consumer has the same tastes.

Source: Nevo (2000a), pages 522 to 526.


Nevo’s example (page 523): when the price of Lucky Charms rises, logit predicts equal gains for Cap’n Crunch and Grape Nuts if they have similar shares. We expect more consumers to switch to Cap’n Crunch, another children’s cereal. Logit cannot say that, because consumers differ only through an independent shock, so those who leave a product split across rivals in proportion to market shares.
Students will see “BLP” used for the random-coefficients logit estimated with instruments for price. BLP (1995) also add a supply side.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: From the model to the estimating equation, in the logit case
text:
From the model to the estimating equation, in the logit case

Choices depend on utility differences, and αyi\alpha y_i appears in every option, so income cancels
With the same tastes, utility is uijt=δjt+εijtu_{ijt} = \delta_{jt} + \varepsilon_{ijt}, where mean utility is δjt=xjtβ−αpjt+ξjt\delta_{jt} = x_{jt}\beta - \alpha p_{jt} + \xi_{jt}
Extreme-value shocks give a formula for shares:

sjt=exp⁡(δjt)1+∑kexp⁡(δkt)s0t=11+∑kexp⁡(δkt)
s_{jt} = \frac{\exp(\delta_{jt})}{1 + \sum_{k} \exp(\delta_{kt})} \qquad s_{0t} = \frac{1}{1 + \sum_{k} \exp(\delta_{kt})}


Dividing the two and taking logs gives a linear equation in data and parameters:

ln⁡sjt−ln⁡s0t=xjtβ−αpjt+ξjt
\ln s_{jt} - \ln s_{0t} = x_{jt}\beta - \alpha p_{jt} + \xi_{jt}

Open the derivation notes
Sources: Berry (1994); Nevo (2000a), pages 522 and 532.

Answer the two questions students ask. Why yi−pjty_i - p_{jt}: it is the money left for everything else. Where yiy_i went: it is in the outside good too, so it does not affect which option is best. Income can still matter through αi\alpha_i in the full model.
Numeric check from the notes: shares of 0.2 and 0.3 with an outside share of 0.5 give δ1=ln⁡(0.2/0.5)=−0.92\delta_1 = \ln(0.2/0.5) = -0.92 and δ2=ln⁡(0.3/0.5)=−0.51\delta_2 = \ln(0.3/0.5) = -0.51.
ξjt\xi_{jt} is the error term in this regression, which is why it is called a structural error.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Estimation: back out the unobserved term, then use GMM
text:
Estimation: back out the unobserved term, then use GMM
Logit: the equation on the last slide is a linear instrumental-variables regression.
Random coefficients: shares have no closed form, so the estimator repeats a loop:

Guess the parameters that describe how tastes vary
Find the mean utilities δjt\delta_{jt} that make predicted shares equal observed shares
Regress δjt\delta_{jt} on price and characteristics using instruments; the residual is ξjt\xi_{jt}
Measure how far ξjt\xi_{jt} is from being uncorrelated with the instruments (the GMM objective)
Update the guess and repeat until the objective reaches a minimum

In a paper, this gets one paragraph. The steps go in an appendix.
Sources: Berry (1994); Nevo (2000a), pages 530 to 533.

Inference: report GMM standard errors for the parameters, and standard errors for the quantities the paper is about, such as elasticities.
Transition: estimation gives us numbers. Identification asks what in the data determines them.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: BLP identification has two parts: the price coefficient and substitution patterns
text:
BLP identification has two parts: the price coefficient and substitution patterns









Price coefficient
Substitution patterns




Parameters
Mean price sensitivity, α\alpha
How tastes vary across consumers


Problem
Endogeneity: price is correlated with ξjt\xi_{jt}
Market shares are aggregates, so they do not show who switched to what


What identifies it
Instruments that shift price
How shares respond across products and markets


Threats
Instruments correlated with demand shocks
Too little variation in prices, characteristics, choice sets, or demographics



Only the first part is an endogeneity problem. The second concerns which variation pins down the spread of tastes.

Source: Nevo (2000a), pages 528 to 530.


Nevo frames these as two questions: first, how to deal with prices that are set by firms using information the researcher lacks; second, what in the data distinguishes logit from random-coefficients logit.
There is one more endogeneity concern: unobserved characteristics may be correlated with observed ones. Nevo handles this with brand fixed effects.
Both parts are estimated together, from the same GMM objective. We take them in turn.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Random coefficients let tastes vary, which changes substitution patterns
text:
Random coefficients let tastes vary, which changes substitution patterns
(αiβi)=(αβ)+ΠDi+Σvi
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha_i \\ \beta_i \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha \\ \beta \end{pmatrix} + \Pi D_i + \Sigma v_i


α\alpha, β\beta: mean tastes
DiD_i: demographics, such as income, age, and children; Π\Pi: how tastes vary with them
viv_i: traits the researcher does not observe; Σ\Sigma: how much tastes vary with them
Logit sets Π=0\Pi = 0 and Σ=0\Sigma = 0
Consumers of a sugary cereal tend to like sugar, so when its price rises they move to other sugary cereals

Source: Nevo (2000), pages 519 and 526.

This is where the random coefficients enter. They are the terms ΠDi\Pi D_i and Σvi\Sigma v_i. They are called random because viv_i and DiD_i are drawn from a distribution; we never observe a specific consumer’s tastes.
Nevo’s example (page 523): Lucky Charms and Cap’n Crunch are both children’s cereals and Grape Nuts is a nutrition cereal. If Cap’n Crunch and Grape Nuts have similar shares, logit says a rise in the price of Lucky Charms raises both shares by the same amount. We expect more consumers to switch to Cap’n Crunch.
Why logit behaves this way: consumers differ only through the independent shock, so those who leave a product look like the average consumer, and their second choices follow market shares.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: In logit, lost sales follow market shares; with random coefficients, they follow similarity
text:
In logit, lost sales follow market shares; with random coefficients, they follow similarity

Lost sales from one cereal with 14 grams of sugar, in one market of the demo. Sugary rivals get 22.7% in logit and 40.5% with random coefficients.

Each point is a rival product. In the left panel, share alone determines a rival’s gain: rivals with similar shares gain about the same, whether or not they are sugary. In the right panel, sugar matters. Low-sugar rivals get 20.2 percent of lost sales in logit and 10.0 percent with random coefficients. The share going to no purchase falls from 57.0 to 49.5 percent. The product is F1B13 in market C01Q1; the demo page shows the calculation.
Why this matters: two products owned by merging firms are likely to be close substitutes. If the model cannot represent closeness, it misses the main force in the merger.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Identification of substitution patterns: compare how shares respond across products and markets
text:
Identification of substitution patterns: compare how shares respond across products and markets
Nevo’s example: products A and B are similar, and B and C have the same market share. The price of A rises.

Logit predicts equal changes in the shares of B and C
If B gains more than C, the data favor random coefficients, and the size of the gap identifies the parameters in Σ\Sigma
Demographics: the parameters in Π\Pi are identified by comparing markets with different demographics

Having many markets helps when they add variation in prices, characteristics, choice sets, and demographics. Nevo’s cereal data have no variation in the choice set across markets, which he offers as a reason his estimates of Σ\Sigma are imprecise.

Source: Nevo (2000a), pages 529 to 530 and 541.


The number of markets alone is the wrong test. What a section has to state is the comparison: which products, which changes, which markets. This is what “state which variation identifies which parameter” means in a structural paper.
Nevo adds that observing share changes as new products enter, or as characteristics change, is especially helpful.
In estimation, these comparisons enter through the same GMM moment conditions used for the price coefficient.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Results: a structural paper reports demand estimates, then simulation results
text:
Results: a structural paper reports demand estimates, then simulation results









Demand estimates
Simulation results




Comes from
Estimating the model on observed data
Solving the estimated model under a new scenario


Reports
Parameters and standard errors; elasticities; substitution; implied markups
Prices, quantities, profits, and consumer welfare under the scenario


Check
Are elasticities and markups sensible?
What is held fixed? Does the model predict well out of sample?


In BLP (1995)
Tables IV to VIII
Not simulated; Section 8 lists uses such as merger and trade policy



The demand estimates are also a result in their own right. A paper can stop there.
Sources: Berry et al. (1995), Sections 7 and 8; Nevo and Whinston (2010), pages 75 to 77.

Go slowly here if students have not seen BLP. The first column answers “what did we learn about consumers and firms?” The second answers “what would happen if?” Our demo does both: Steps 1 to 6 are demand estimates, and Step 7 is the simulation.
Coefficients alone are hard to interpret, so papers report what they imply. BLP report elasticities in Tables V and VI, substitution to the outside good in Table VII, and markups in Table VIII.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Simulation results: a merger simulation has four steps
text:
Simulation results: a merger simulation has four steps

Start from the demand estimates
Recover marginal costs from firms’ pricing conditions: p−mc=Ω−1s(p)p - mc = \Omega^{-1} s(p)
Change ownership: the merged firm sets the prices of both firms’ products
Solve for new equilibrium prices, then compute shares and welfare


State what is held fixed: current merger simulations hold products, firms, and pricing behavior fixed
Report results under a range of assumptions, such as cost savings
Validate the model: check that it predicts outcomes not used to estimate it


Sources: Nevo (2000b), pages 403 and 411; Nevo and Whinston (2010), pages 75 to 77.


Step 2 is the supply slide. Nevo computes the new equilibrium in each of the 45 cities using data from the last quarter of 1992, and reports medians.
Nevo and Whinston give a validation example: Peters (2006) compares merger simulations with what actually happened after airline mergers and finds the simulations missed the size of several price changes.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Demand estimates: product fixed effects triple the price coefficient, because quality was omitted
text:
Demand estimates: product fixed effects triple the price coefficient, because quality was omitted



Specification (all three are logit)
Price coefficient




OLS, no product fixed effects
−10.1


OLS, product fixed effects
−29.0


Instrumental variables, product fixed effects
−30.0




Better cereals cost more, so without fixed effects a high price partly signals high quality
Product fixed effects absorb a product’s fixed quality, which is part of ξjt\xi_{jt}
The instruments are for price. In Nevo (2001), they are prices of the same brand in other cities and cost proxies
Random coefficients come next; these rows address the price coefficient only


This is the selection problem from Lecture 6.1 in a demand setting: price and unobserved quality move together, so the comparison across products mixes the effect of price with the effect of quality.
The demo file has 20 instrument columns that are not labeled. In these simulated data they explain 97 percent of the within-product variation in price, so the instrumented price is close to the actual price. That is why the coefficient barely moves. In real data, instruments can change the estimate by much more.

Row three: when one product’s price rises, logit makes every rival respond in the same proportion (ratio of 1). With random coefficients, the most affected rival responds about 6 times as much as the least affected, in the median case, in one market.

The counterfactual depends on how the model lets consumers substitute, which is an assumption the section has to state and defend.

Why the merger result doubles: merging firms raise prices more when their products are close substitutes for each other, because more of the lost sales stay within the merged firm. Logit cannot represent that closeness. In market C01Q1, the median merging product sends 56 percent of lost sales to no purchase in logit and 42 percent with random coefficients, and 18 percent to the merger partner in logit and 22 percent with random coefficients.
The takeaway for writing: two models can fit one summary statistic and still disagree on the counterfactual. That is why a structural section states its assumptions and reports results under alternatives.

One market of the demo. Median predicted increase: 5.5% in logit and 9.1% with random coefficients.

section: Numerical estimation can stop early, so report how the model was solved
text:
Numerical estimation can stop early, so report how the model was solved
Estimation searches for the parameters that minimize the GMM objective. The optimizer stops when it is close enough, and that stopping rule is a choice.

How to read this: the coefficient moves a lot, and the elasticity barely moves

Source: Conlon and Gortmaker (2020), Table 7.


Conlon and Gortmaker re-estimate Nevo’s model on his simulated data three times. They report nearly identical elasticities and markups despite different parameter estimates, and they point to the Price × Income terms, which are nearly collinear in the data. The first row uses Nevo’s original settings; they note that those tolerances were too loose. “Better instruments” means an approximation to the feasible optimal instruments.
They also find that with these practices, estimates are stable across starting values and optimizers, which is better news than earlier work suggested (Knittel and Metaxoglou, 2014, as discussed in Conlon and Gortmaker 2020).
Transition: we now follow one structural paper from its question to its counterfactuals.

title: Cereal Demand Demo
section: Run the demo in VS Code
text:
Run the demo in VS Code
The demo uses PyBLP, a Python package (Conlon and Gortmaker 2020), so you need Python in addition to the R setup from Lecture 5.5. You only need Steps 1 to 5 once. The script ran in 34 seconds on a laptop with Python 3.13 and PyBLP 1.3.0 on Windows.

Install Python from python.org. On Windows, check the box “Add python.exe to PATH” in the installer.
Install the Python extension. In VS Code, open the Extensions view, search for Python, and install the extension from Microsoft.
Make a project folder with a short path, such as C:\arec570\cereal-demo, and download the script into it. Long paths, including many OneDrive folders, can make the install fail on Windows. Then choose File > Open Folder in VS Code and open that folder.
Create a virtual environment. This is a private set of Python packages for the project. Open a terminal with Terminal > New Terminal and run the lines for your computer.
Windows:
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
Mac:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
The terminal prompt now starts with (.venv). If Windows blocks the activate command, run Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass and try again.
Install the packages:
pip install pyblp pandas
Run the script:
python cereal-demand-demo.py
You can also open the script and click the Run button at the top right of the editor. If VS Code asks for an interpreter, choose the one in .venv.

If you open a new terminal later, run the activate line again before running the script.

title: Cereal Demand Demo
text:
Step 1: logit by OLS
This regression treats price as exogenous and controls only for a constant, sugar, and mushy.
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(products)), products.prices, products.sugar, products.mushy])
ols_no_fe = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0][1]
Price coefficient: -10.12

title: Cereal Demand Demo
text:
Step 5: compute elasticities and substitution
Coefficients are hard to interpret alone. This step converts them into what the model says about consumers: how demand responds to prices and where lost sales go. Steps 5 and 6 complete the demand results. Step 7 is the simulation.
E = results.compute_elasticities(market_id="C01Q1")
D = results.compute_diversion_ratios(market_id="C01Q1")
Each result is a table with one row and one column per product, computed here for market C01Q1.
Elasticities. The entry for products jj and kk is the percent change in the share of jj when the price of kk rises 1 percent. Take product F1B13 in this market, with a share of 0.0266, a price of 0.1370, and 14 grams of sugar. In the logit model, the formulas in the derivation notes use the coefficient from Step 3:
ηjj=−αpj(1−sj)=−30.05×0.1370×(1−0.0266)=−4.01
\eta_{jj} = -\alpha p_j (1 - s_j) = -30.05 \times 0.1370 \times (1 - 0.0266) = -4.01

ηkj=αpjsj=30.05×0.1370×0.0266=0.110
\eta_{kj} = \alpha p_j s_j = 30.05 \times 0.1370 \times 0.0266 = 0.110

So a 1 percent rise in this product’s price cuts its own share by 4.01 percent and raises the share of every rival by 0.110 percent. The rival’s identity does not appear in the formula. With random coefficients, PyBLP computes these derivatives for each simulated consumer and averages them, so rivals can respond differently. The own-price elasticity for this product becomes -4.91.
Diversion ratios. A diversion ratio is the share of the sales a product loses that go to each alternative. It is the most direct measure of substitution.



Where sales lost by F1B13 go
Logit
Random coefficients




11 sugary rivals (10 grams or more)
22.7%
40.5%


12 low-sugar rivals
20.2%
10.0%


No purchase (outside good)
57.0%
49.5%



In the logit model, each rival’s diversion equals its share divided by 1−sj1 - s_j, so lost sales follow market shares. With random coefficients, consumers who buy a sugary cereal tend to like sugar, so more of them switch to another sugary cereal.

title: Cereal Demand Demo
text:
Step 6: recover marginal costs
The data have no costs, so the model infers them. Firms set prices to maximize profit, and each firm’s first-order condition links its markup to the slopes of demand (Nevo 2001):
p−mc=Ω−1s(p)
p - mc = \Omega^{-1} s(p)

Here pp, mcmc, and ss are vectors of prices, marginal costs, and shares. The matrix Ω\Omega contains the demand derivatives from Step 5, with an entry set to zero when two products belong to different firms, because a firm only accounts for lost sales on its own products. Prices and shares are data and Ω\Omega comes from the estimates, so the equation can be solved for mcmc.
costs = results.compute_costs()
Logit: median price 0.124, median cost 0.084, median margin 31.6%
Random coefficients: median price 0.124, median cost 0.081, median margin 33.7%

title: Cereal Demand Demo
text:
Step 7: simulate the merger
The simulation merges firms 1 and 2, the two largest firms in the data (about 75 percent of sales). It holds demand and marginal costs fixed at the values from Steps 4 and 6 and changes one thing: who owns which product.

Rewrite Ω\Omega so that products of firms 1 and 2 count as one firm. The merged firm now accounts for sales that move between the two firms’ products.
Solve for the new prices p*p^{*} that satisfy p*−mc=Ωpost−1s(p*)p^{*} - mc = \Omega_{\text{post}}^{-1}\, s(p^{*}) for all firms at once.
Compute shares and consumer surplus at the new prices.

merged_firms = products.firm_ids.replace(2, 1).to_numpy()
new_prices = results.compute_prices(firm_ids=merged_firms, costs=results.compute_costs())
