Corn Flakes (Kellogg)
0.000
0.001



Under logit, every number in a column would be the same.

Source: Nevo (2000b), Table 3 (selected rows and columns; medians over 900 city-quarter markets).



Read across the first row: when Grape Nuts’ price rises 1%, Shredded Wheat’s share rises 0.115%, the largest response of any brand.
The diagonal entries are own-price elasticities.
This supports New York’s argument. The next slide asks whether it means a large price increase.
Transition: the counterfactual.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Result 2: the model predicts small price increases for Post-Nabisco, and they match what happened
text:
Result 2: the model predicts small price increases for Post-Nabisco, and they match what happened







Merger
Largest predicted price increase




Post and Nabisco (approved)
Shredded Wheat 3.1%; Grape Nuts 1.5%


General Mills and Nabisco (called off)
Shredded Wheat 7.5%


General Mills and Chex (approved)
Chex 12.2%




A 5% cut in marginal cost would offset the Post-Nabisco increase
Check against what happened: Shredded Wheat’s 1995 price was about equal to its 1993 price, close to the prediction with 5% cost savings
Being the closest substitute does not mean a large price increase: the amount of substitution was small


Sources: Nevo (2000b), pages 411 to 416, Tables 5 and 6.



Marginal costs come from the firms’ pricing conditions: the model infers them from prices and the demand estimates.
The called-off merger is something only a model can evaluate.
The check against later prices is informal; a difference-in-differences estimate like the one at the start would make it formal.
Transition: what this looks like in a written paper.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: What to think about for your proposal
text:
What to think about for your proposal

The question: can a design answer it, or does it need a model? Name the reason
The estimator: OLS, 2SLS, or a numerical method, and why
The assumptions: which ones drive the answer, and what happens if they change?
The evidence: what reduced-form estimate supports the model, or what could check it?



Most proposals in this course will be reduced form. Those students should be able to say why their question does not need a model.
Students with a structural question should name the estimator and the variation behind each key parameter.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
section: Result 2: small predicted price increases for Post-Nabisco, close to what happened
text:
Result 2: small predicted price increases for Post-Nabisco, close to what happened







Merger
Largest predicted price increase




Post and Nabisco (approved)
Shredded Wheat 3.1%; Grape Nuts 1.5%


General Mills and Nabisco (called off)
Shredded Wheat 7.5%


General Mills and Chex (approved)
Chex 12.2%




A 5% cut in marginal cost would offset the Post-Nabisco increase
Check against what happened: Shredded Wheat’s 1995 price was about equal to its 1993 price, close to the prediction with 5% cost savings
Being the closest substitute does not mean a large price increase: the amount of substitution was small


Sources: Nevo (2000b), pages 411 to 416, Tables 5 and 6.



Marginal costs come from the firms’ pricing conditions: the model infers them from prices and the demand estimates.
The called-off merger is something only a model can evaluate.
The check against later prices is informal; a difference-in-differences estimate like the one at the start would make it formal.
Transition: what this looks like in a written paper.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Lectures 6.1 and 6.2 estimated parameters. Machine learning predicts outcomes
text:
Lectures 6.1 and 6.2 estimated parameters. Machine learning predicts outcomes

In 6.1 and 6.2, the goal was a parameter: a treatment effect, a price coefficient, an elasticity
Machine learning answers a different question: given xx, what is the best guess of yy?
Mullainathan and Spiess: machine learning “not only provides new tools, it solves a different problem”
Today: three jobs machine learning does in economics papers, one paper for each, and what the methods section has to say


Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 87 to 88.



Start from what students know: the papers we read in 6.1 and 6.2 care about one coefficient and how it is identified.
Machine learning cares about how well it predicts yy for observations it has not seen.
Transition: the difference between the two goals, side by side.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Prediction and parameter estimation are judged differently
text:
Prediction and parameter estimation are judged differently









Prediction, ŷ\hat{y}
Parameter estimation, β̂\hat{\beta}




The question
What is yy for a new observation?
How does yy change when xx changes?


How it is judged
Accuracy on data the model did not see
Identification: the source of variation and its assumptions


Can you check it?
Yes: predictions and outcomes are both observed
No: rests on assumptions about how the data were generated


Typical method
LASSO, random forest, neural network
OLS, IV, difference in differences, structural models




Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 88 and 92.



Read the third row slowly. A prediction can be checked against outcomes. A causal effect cannot, because we never see the counterfactual.
That is why machine learning papers report accuracy, and causal papers report an identification strategy.
Transition: so how do economists use a tool built for prediction?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Machine learning does three jobs in economics papers
text:
Machine learning does three jobs in economics papers








Job
What machine learning does
Example paper




1. Prediction is the goal
Predicts an outcome, such as which households are food insecure
Zhao et al. (2025)


2. Prediction as a step
Chooses which variables enter an economic model or a treatment-effect regression
Li and Yu (2025); Belloni et al. (2014)


3. How effects vary
Estimates a separate treatment effect for each farm or household
Stetter et al. (2022)



In jobs 2 and 3, the paper still needs an identification strategy. Machine learning does not supply one.

Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017); Maruejols et al. (2025); Athey and Imbens (2019).



This table is the map for the rest of the lecture. Each job gets one section.
Jobs 2 and 3 connect to 6.1 and 6.2: machine learning sits inside a causal or structural analysis.
The last line is the most important point of the lecture.
Transition: two ideas students need before reading these papers.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Overfitting: a model can fit its own data well and predict new data badly
text:
Overfitting: a model can fit its own data well and predict new data badly

A flexible model can fit the noise in its data, so its in-sample fit overstates how well it predicts
Training and test data: fit the model on one part of the data (training), and measure accuracy on the rest (test)
Cross-validation: split the training data into KK parts, fit on K−1K-1, check on the one left out, and repeat; this chooses a model’s settings, such as how many variables to keep








Paper
How the data were split




Zhao et al. (2025)
70% training (756 households), 30% test (324 households)


Li and Yu (2025)
10-fold cross-validation to choose the LASSO penalty




Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 89 to 92; Bittmann (2025), Section 3.



Analogy: a student who memorizes last year’s exam answers scores perfectly on that exam and poorly on a new one.
The test set is the new exam. It is touched once, at the end.
If the data have time or place structure, the split should respect it: train on earlier years, test on later ones.
Transition: the two methods in today’s papers.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Two common methods: LASSO and random forests
text:
Two common methods: LASSO and random forests
LASSO is a regression with a penalty for the size of the coefficients:
minβ∑i=1n(yi−xi′β)2+λ∑j=1p|βj|
\min_{\beta} \; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(y_i - x_i'\beta\right)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j|


The first term is the usual OLS fit. The second term penalizes large coefficients
A larger λ\lambda sets more coefficients exactly to zero, so LASSO also selects variables
λ\lambda is chosen by cross-validation

Random forest: a regression tree splits the data into groups with similar outcomes; a forest averages many trees, each grown on a random sample of the data.

Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 90 to 97; Bittmann (2025), Section 4.



LASSO is OLS plus a cost for every variable it uses. With λ=0\lambda = 0 it is OLS.
Students do not need the tree algorithm. They need to know that a forest predicts by averaging many trees, and that it can find nonlinear patterns and interactions on its own.
Transition: job 1, where prediction is the whole point.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Zhao et al. (2025): predicting food insecurity among rural households in China
text:
Zhao et al. (2025): predicting food insecurity among rural households in China

Question: which rural households are food insecure (calorie poor)?
Data: 1,080 households in Jilin, Shandong, and Hubei; 3-day food consumption records; 61.1% are calorie poor
Methods: random forest and LASSO, compared with a logit baseline; 70% training, 30% test








Model (test data)
Accuracy




Random forest
65.7%


LASSO
61.1%


Logit (baseline)
58.9%


Predict “calorie poor” for every household
61.1%



Accuracy needs a comparison. The last row is the share of households that are calorie poor.

Source: Zhao et al. (2025), Sections 3 to 5 and Table 3. The last row is our calculation from the sample share.



The paper reports accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the ROC curve (0.62 for both forest and LASSO, where 0.5 is a random guess).
The last row is the most useful teaching point: a rule that labels every household calorie poor is right 61.1% of the time. The forest adds about 5 points.
The paper addresses this imbalance by oversampling the smaller class (SMOTE), and recommends choosing a cut-off based on a program’s coverage.
Transition: what can a prediction paper claim about why households are food insecure?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: A prediction paper can say which variables predict, but not what causes the outcome
text:
A prediction paper can say which variables predict, but not what causes the outcome

Zhao et al. rank predictors: household income and access to food markets come first in both models
These are predictors. A variable can predict well because it moves with an unobserved cause
LASSO’s choice of variables is unstable: Mullainathan and Spiess ran LASSO on ten random partitions of the same data, and the variables it kept changed from one to the next
Stetter et al. warn that their variable importance measure “should not be interpreted in a causal fashion”

To claim that income reduces food insecurity, the paper needs a design from 6.1.

Sources: Zhao et al. (2025), Section 5.2; Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), page 97, Figure 2; Stetter et al. (2022), page 740, footnote 17.



Zhao et al.’s discussion moves from “predicts” to “significantly influence.” That step is where a reader should stop and ask for an identification strategy.
Why LASSO’s selection is unstable: when two variables are correlated, LASSO may keep either one, and small changes in the sample change which.
Transition: job 2, where prediction serves an economic model.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Li and Yu (2025): LASSO chooses attributes, then a logit model estimates willingness to pay
text:
Li and Yu (2025): LASSO chooses attributes, then a logit model estimates willingness to pay

Setting: a choice experiment with 100 consumers in Göttingen; apples that vary in origin, size, organic, and price
Step 1, LASSO logit: 10-fold cross-validation chooses λ\lambda; price is always kept. LASSO drops Organic and Japan: respondents appear to ignore them
Step 2, conditional logit: the random utility model from 6.2; willingness to pay = −βk/βprice-\beta_k / \beta_{\text{price}}









Willingness to pay (€ per kg), relative to China
All attributes
After LASSO




France
1.20
1.53


Italy
1.42
1.40


Small apples
1.30
1.41


Organic
−0.04
dropped




Source: Li and Yu (2025), Sections 2 and 3, Tables 4, 6, and 7.



This is machine learning inside a structural model: the logit from 6.2. LASSO decides which attributes enter the utility function.
The economic estimate changes: France’s premium rises from €1.20 to €1.53.
A question for a reader: LASSO drops Organic for the whole sample. The paper can no longer report willingness to pay for organic apples, which is the policy question. Is that the right trade-off?
Transition: the same idea in a treatment-effect regression.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Belloni, Chernozhukov, and Hansen (2014): LASSO chooses control variables
text:
Belloni, Chernozhukov, and Hansen (2014): LASSO chooses control variables
With many candidate controls xix_i and a treatment did_i, double selection has three steps:

LASSO of the treatment did_i on xix_i: keep the controls that predict treatment
LASSO of the outcome yiy_i on xix_i: keep the controls that predict the outcome
OLS of yiy_i on did_i and the union of both sets of controls


Choosing controls only by how well they predict yy can drop a confounder that predicts treatment
Application: the effect of abortion on crime, 48 states over 12 years (576 observations), 251 candidate controls; LASSO keeps 8 to 14
Identification is unchanged: the effect is causal only if treatment is as good as random once the controls are included


Source: Belloni et al. (2014), Sections 1, 2.2, and 7.



Step 1 is the new idea. A confounder may predict treatment strongly and the outcome weakly; a prediction-only LASSO for yy would drop it, and the estimate would have omitted variable bias.
Their results: the property crime estimate stays close to the original study but is significant only at the 10% level; the violent crime and murder estimates become imprecise.
This is the selection-on-observables assumption from 6.1. LASSO makes the choice of controls systematic; it does not make the assumption true.
Transition: job 3.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Stetter et al. (2022): a causal forest estimates the effect of agri-environment schemes for each farm
text:
Stetter et al. (2022): a causal forest estimates the effect of agri-environment schemes for each farm
The target is the conditional average treatment effect: the effect for farms with characteristics xx,
τ(x)=E[Yi(1)−Yi(0)∣Xi=x]
\tau(x) = E\left[\,Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid X_i = x\,\right]


Data: 2,758 Bavarian farms in 2014; 1,641 joined an agri-environment scheme; more than 130 farm and county characteristics
Method: forests predict participation and each outcome, then a causal forest estimates τ(x)\tau(x) for each farm; settings chosen by cross-validation
Results: fertiliser spending falls significantly for 33% of farms (by €14 per hectare among them); land-use diversity rises for 55%; few significant effects on pesticides or greenhouse gas emissions


Source: Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 3 to 5 and Table 3.



Yi(1)Y_i(1) and Yi(0)Y_i(0) are the potential outcomes from 6.1: the farm’s outcome with and without the scheme.
The forest finds which characteristics make the effect larger or smaller. The paper uses this to argue for targeting payments by location, farm size, and yield potential.
€14 per hectare is about 13 kg of nitrogen per hectare, using the paper’s 2014 price.
Transition: where does identification come from?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: The causal forest needs the same identifying assumption as 6.1
text:
The causal forest needs the same identifying assumption as 6.1

Selection on observables: after conditioning on farm characteristics, participation is as good as random
Overlap: every farm has some chance of joining and of not joining; predicted probabilities run from 0.27 to 0.86, and 23 farms without overlap are dropped
The authors’ argument: with many characteristics, the forest captures unobserved factors such as a farmer’s environmental attitude
The limit, in their words: if a different group of confounders is missing from the data, “our estimates might still be biased”
They report placebo tests and simulated confounders as sensitivity checks


Source: Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 4.3 and 5.1.



Compare with Zhao et al.: here the authors name the identifying assumption and test its sensitivity. That is what makes it a causal paper.
The argument that many observed characteristics stand in for unobserved ones is an assumption. A reader should judge it the way they would judge any selection-on-observables design from 6.1.
Transition: what all three jobs require in the methods section.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: What the methods section states when a paper uses machine learning
text:
What the methods section states when a paper uses machine learning







Item
Example




1. The job: prediction, a step in a model, or heterogeneous effects
Zhao et al.: prediction is the goal


2. The target, the inputs, and a comparison model
Calorie poor; household and market characteristics; logit


3. How the data were split
70% training, 30% test


4. How settings were chosen
Cross-validation; number of trees


5. Performance on held-out data
Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, area under the ROC curve


6. For jobs 2 and 3: the identifying assumption and checks
Stetter et al.: selection on observables, overlap, placebo tests


7. Software and versions
Li and Yu: the glmnet package in R




Sources: Zhao et al. (2025); Li and Yu (2025); Stetter et al. (2022); Athey and Imbens (2019).



Items 1 to 5 apply to every paper that uses machine learning. Item 6 is what separates a causal claim from a prediction.
Item 7 matters for replication, as in Unit 5: machine learning results depend on random splits, so report the software and the random seed.
Transition: questions for your own proposal.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: What to think about for your proposal
text:
What to think about for your proposal

The job: is your question about predicting an outcome, choosing variables, or how an effect varies?
The claim: does your conclusion need a causal effect? If so, what is the design, and where does machine learning fit inside it?
The comparison: what simple model, or simple rule, should the method beat?
The evidence: which held-out performance measure, or which identification check, will you report?



Most students will not use machine learning in their proposal. They should still be able to read a paper that does and find items 1 to 7.
Students who do use it should name the job in one sentence at the start of the methods section.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Lectures 6.1 and 6.2 estimated parameters; machine learning targets prediction
text:
Lectures 6.1 and 6.2 estimated parameters; machine learning targets prediction

The designs in 6.1 and the models in 6.2 recover parameters: a treatment effect, a price coefficient, an elasticity
Supervised machine learning addresses a different objective: the most accurate prediction of yy given xx for observations outside the estimation sample
In Mullainathan and Spiess’s words, machine learning “not only provides new tools, it solves a different problem”
This lecture covers where these methods came from, the three roles they play in empirical economics, and how a methods section reports them


Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 87 to 88.



Frame the lecture around the distinction between estimating a parameter and predicting an outcome. Every later slide returns to it.
Transition: these methods developed largely outside economics, which explains much about how economists use them.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Machine learning developed in statistics and computer science, and entered applied economics recently
text:
Machine learning developed in statistics and computer science, and entered applied economics recently







Period
Development




1984 to 2001
Regression trees (Breiman et al., 1984), the LASSO (Tibshirani, 1996), and random forests (Breiman, 2001)


1990s
Neural networks studied in econometrics, but they “did not catch on at the time”


2001
Breiman’s “two cultures”: statistics relied on data models, while an algorithmic culture grew in other fields


2014
Early reviews for economists: Varian; Einav and Levin; Belloni, Chernozhukov, and Hansen


2017 to 2019
Mullainathan and Spiess; causal forests (Wager and Athey); Athey and Imbens’s review for economists


2020 to 2025
Reviews and special issues in agricultural and applied economics: Storm et al. (2020); Maruejols et al. (2025)



In applied economics, these methods have been in wide use for roughly a decade.

Sources: Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 686 to 688, 696 to 698, and 701; Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), page 87; Storm et al. (2020); Maruejols et al. (2025).



Athey and Imbens open with Breiman (2001): one culture “assumes that the data are generated by a given stochastic data model”; the other “uses algorithmic models and treats the data mechanism as unknown.” Econometrics belongs to the first culture.
Statistics has since absorbed the algorithmic approach; Athey and Imbens note that “the adoption of these methods in economics has been slower.”
The dates for the original methods come from the citations in Athey and Imbens.
Transition: why adoption was slow, and why it accelerated.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Economists adopted machine learning for new data and new questions, after its statistical properties were established
text:
Economists adopted machine learning for new data and new questions, after its statistical properties were established

New data: many units, many variables per unit, and unstructured sources such as satellite images and text
Prediction questions: some policy problems require an accurate forecast and no causal parameter
Many candidate variables: the analyst must choose controls or functional forms from a large set
Why adoption was slow: economics journals emphasize formal properties of estimators, such as consistency and asymptotic normality, which early machine learning methods did not provide
What changed: recent work established inference for adapted methods, including double selection and causal forests


Sources: Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 686 to 687; Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 88, 98, and 102.



Athey and Imbens: machine learning research focuses on “working properties of algorithms in specific settings,” with formal results such as error rates, while econometrics focuses on large-sample properties of estimators and tests.
The methods economists now use are often adaptations: they modify machine learning algorithms to deliver valid confidence intervals for causal parameters. Two appear later in this lecture.
Transition: how prediction and estimation are evaluated.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Prediction and parameter estimation are evaluated by different criteria
text:
Prediction and parameter estimation are evaluated by different criteria









Prediction, ŷ\hat{y}
Parameter estimation, β̂\hat{\beta}




Target
The outcome for a new observation
An effect or behavioral parameter


Evaluation
Accuracy on data not used in estimation
Identification: the source of variation and its assumptions


Verifiability
Directly testable: predictions and outcomes are both observed
Rests on assumptions about the data-generating process


Example question
What is this household’s risk of food insecurity?
How much did a program change outcomes?



The research question determines how a method is used. Later we will use machine learning tools inside an effect-estimation procedure

Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 88 and 92.



Prediction quality can be measured against held-out outcomes. A causal effect relies on assumptions because the counterfactual outcome is never observed
OLS can be used for prediction, and causal forests adapt tree methods to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects. The methods do not fall into exclusive categories
This is why machine learning papers report out-of-sample performance and causal papers report an identification strategy.
Transition: three ways economics papers combine the two.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Machine learning plays three roles in empirical economics
text:
Machine learning plays three roles in empirical economics








Role
What machine learning does
Example




1. Prediction as the objective
Predicts an outcome, such as household food insecurity
Zhao et al. (2025)


2. Prediction within a larger analysis
Selects the variables that enter an economic model or a treatment-effect regression
Li and Yu (2025); Belloni et al. (2014)


3. Heterogeneous treatment effects
Estimates how a treatment effect varies across farms or households
Stetter et al. (2022)



In roles 2 and 3, identification still comes from the research design. Machine learning does not supply exogenous variation.

Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017); Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 686 to 688; Maruejols et al. (2025).



This table organizes the rest of the lecture; each role has its own section.
Roles 2 and 3 connect directly to 6.1 and 6.2: the machine learning step sits inside a causal or structural analysis.
The final sentence is the main point of the lecture.
Transition: two concepts needed to read any of these papers.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Out-of-sample performance: training data, test data, and cross-validation
text:
Out-of-sample performance: training data, test data, and cross-validation

A flexible model can fit noise in its estimation sample, so in-sample fit overstates predictive performance (overfitting)
Training and test data: the model is estimated on one subset and evaluated on a held-out subset
Cross-validation: the training data are divided into KK folds; the model is estimated on K−1K-1 folds and evaluated on the remaining fold, in rotation, to select tuning parameters








Paper
Sample split




Zhao et al. (2025)
70% training (756 households), 30% test (324 households)


Li and Yu (2025)
10-fold cross-validation to select the LASSO penalty




Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 89 to 92; Bittmann (2025), Section 3.



Mullainathan and Spiess describe cross-validation as creating “an out-of-sample experiment inside the original sample.”
The test set is used once, for the final evaluation. If it informs model choices, it no longer measures out-of-sample performance.
With panel or spatial data, the split should respect that structure, for example by training on earlier years and testing on later ones.
Transition: the two methods used in the example papers.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Regularization: the LASSO and random forests
text:
Regularization: the LASSO and random forests
LASSO adds a penalty on the absolute size of the coefficients to the least squares objective:
minβ∑i=1n(yi−xi′β)2+λ∑j=1p|βj|
\min_{\beta} \; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(y_i - x_i'\beta\right)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j|


With λ=0\lambda = 0, the estimator is OLS; as λ\lambda increases, coefficients shrink and some are set exactly to zero
The LASSO therefore performs variable selection; λ\lambda is chosen by cross-validation

Random forests average the predictions of many regression trees, each estimated on a random subsample, which captures nonlinearities and interactions without specifying them in advance.

Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 90 to 97; Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 690 and 695 to 699; Bittmann (2025), Section 4.



Regularization trades a small increase in bias for a larger reduction in variance, which improves out-of-sample prediction.
Athey and Imbens note that ridge regression and the LASSO have antecedents in econometrics and statistics; the penalty is the shared idea.
Transition: the first role, where prediction is the objective.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Zhao et al. (2025) predict food insecurity among rural households in China
text:
Zhao et al. (2025) predict food insecurity among rural households in China
Objective: identify which rural households are calorie poor, using information a program could collect.

Measure the outcome: convert 3-day food consumption records for 1,080 households in Jilin, Shandong, and Hubei into calorie intake per person; households below the recommended intake are calorie poor (61.1%)
Assemble the inputs: household, decision-maker, village, and food-market characteristics
Split the sample: 756 households (70%) for training and 324 (30%) for testing
Fit the models on the training sample: a random forest (93 trees, chosen by out-of-bag error) and the LASSO, plus a logit benchmark
Evaluate on the test sample: accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the ROC curve


Source: Zhao et al. (2025), Sections 3 to 5.



Step 1 matters as much as the algorithm: the target is constructed from consumption records and a calorie threshold. A different threshold changes who counts as food insecure.
Out-of-bag error is the random forest’s built-in version of a hold-out sample: each tree is fit on a bootstrap sample, and the observations left out of that sample are used to measure its error.
The authors oversample the smaller class (SMOTE) because the two classes are unequal in size.
Transition: the results.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Predictive importance does not identify causal effects
text:
Predictive importance does not identify causal effects

Zhao et al. rank predictors; household income and access to food markets rank highest in both models
A variable may predict well because it is correlated with an unobserved determinant of the outcome
LASSO selections are unstable: across ten random partitions of the same data, Mullainathan and Spiess find that the selected variables change from one partition to the next
Stetter et al. caution that their variable importance measure “should not be interpreted in a causal fashion”

A causal claim about income would require an identification strategy of the kind discussed in Lecture 6.1.

Sources: Zhao et al. (2025), Section 5.2; Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), page 97, Figure 2; Stetter et al. (2022), page 740, footnote 17.



Zhao et al.’s discussion moves from variables that predict food insecurity to variables that “significantly influence” it. That shift is where a reader should ask for an identification strategy.
The instability arises because correlated predictors are close substitutes in prediction; small changes in the sample change which one the LASSO retains.
Transition: the second role, where prediction is one step in a larger analysis.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Li and Yu (2025) use the LASSO to select attributes before estimating willingness to pay
text:
Li and Yu (2025) use the LASSO to select attributes before estimating willingness to pay
Objective: estimate willingness to pay for apple attributes, allowing for attributes that respondents ignore (attribute non-attendance).

Collect choices: 100 consumers in Göttingen each choose among two apples and “no purchase” in 4 scenarios; apples vary in origin, size, production method, and price
Fit a LASSO logit of choices on all attributes; 10-fold cross-validation selects λ\lambda, and price is exempt from the penalty so it always stays in the model
Read the selection: the LASSO sets the coefficients on Organic and Japan to zero, which the authors interpret as attributes respondents ignore
Estimate a conditional logit (the random utility model from Lecture 6.2) with only the retained attributes
Compute willingness to pay for each attribute as −βk/βprice-\beta_k / \beta_{\text{price}}


Source: Li and Yu (2025), Sections 2 and 3.



Here machine learning operates inside a structural model: step 2 decides which attributes enter the utility function in step 4.
Willingness to pay is a ratio of marginal utilities: how many euros a consumer would give up for an attribute, holding utility constant.
Transition: how the estimates change.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Belloni, Chernozhukov, and Hansen (2014) use the LASSO to select control variables
text:
Belloni, Chernozhukov, and Hansen (2014) use the LASSO to select control variables
Objective: estimate a treatment effect when there are many candidate controls and the researcher must choose among them.
With a treatment did_i and candidate controls xix_i, double selection proceeds in three steps:

LASSO of the treatment did_i on xix_i, retaining controls that predict treatment
LASSO of the outcome yiy_i on xix_i, retaining controls that predict the outcome
OLS of yiy_i on did_i and the union of the two sets of controls


Selecting controls only for their ability to predict yy can omit a confounder that strongly predicts treatment
Application: abortion and crime; 48 states over 12 years (576 observations), 251 candidate controls, of which the LASSO retains 8 to 14
Identification: the estimate is causal only if treatment is as good as randomly assigned conditional on the controls


Source: Belloni et al. (2014), Sections 1, 2.2, and 7.



The first step is the methodological contribution. A confounder that predicts treatment strongly and the outcome weakly would be dropped by a LASSO for yy alone, producing omitted variable bias.
Their results: the property crime estimate remains close to the original study but is significant only at the 10% level; the violent crime and murder estimates become imprecise.
The identifying assumption is selection on observables, as in 6.1. The LASSO makes the choice of controls systematic and reproducible; it does not make the assumption more plausible.
Transition: the third role.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Stetter et al. (2022) estimate farm-level effects of agri-environment schemes with a causal forest
text:
Stetter et al. (2022) estimate farm-level effects of agri-environment schemes with a causal forest
The estimand is the conditional average treatment effect, the average effect for farms with characteristics xx:
τ(x)=E[Yi(1)−Yi(0)∣Xi=x]
\tau(x) = E\left[\,Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid X_i = x\,\right]


Data: 2,758 Bavarian farms in 2014; 1,641 participated in an agri-environment scheme; more than 130 farm and county characteristics; four environmental outcomes
Predict participation: a forest estimates each farm’s probability of participating, ê(x)\hat{e}(x)
Predict the outcome: a forest estimates each farm’s expected outcome, m̂(x)\hat{m}(x), ignoring participation
Remove the predictable parts: subtract ê(x)\hat{e}(x) from participation and m̂(x)\hat{m}(x) from the outcome
Estimate τ(x)\tau(x): a causal forest splits farms into groups where the effect differs most, and compares the remaining variation within each group


Source: Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 2.3, 4.1, and 4.2.



Yi(1)Y_i(1) and Yi(0)Y_i(0) are the potential outcomes from 6.1: a farm’s outcome with and without participation.
Steps 2 to 4 follow the logic of the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem: partial out the characteristics from both the treatment and the outcome, then relate what is left. The forests do the partialling out flexibly.
A regression tree splits to predict the outcome; a causal forest splits to separate farms with different treatment effects.
Settings are tuned by cross-validation. The participation and outcome forests use 5,000 trees each; the causal forest uses 100,000 for stable estimates.
Transition: what they find.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Causal forests rely on the same identifying assumptions as the designs in Lecture 6.1
text:
Causal forests rely on the same identifying assumptions as the designs in Lecture 6.1

Selection on observables: conditional on farm characteristics, participation is as good as randomly assigned
Overlap: every farm has a positive probability of each treatment status; estimated propensities range from 0.27 to 0.86, and 23 farms without overlap are excluded
The authors’ argument: a large set of characteristics allows the forest to proxy for unobserved factors, such as a farmer’s environmental attitude
The acknowledged limit: if a distinct group of confounders is absent from the data, “our estimates might still be biased”
Sensitivity analysis: placebo tests and simulated confounders


Source: Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 4.3 and 5.1.



In contrast to Zhao et al., the authors state the identifying assumption and test the sensitivity of their estimates to it. That is what makes the analysis causal.
The argument that many observed characteristics proxy for unobserved ones is itself an assumption, to be evaluated as any selection-on-observables design from 6.1 would be.
Transition: what a methods section must report in all three roles.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: What a methods section reports when it uses machine learning
text:
What a methods section reports when it uses machine learning







Item
Example




1. The role: prediction, a step in a larger analysis, or heterogeneous effects
Zhao et al.: prediction is the objective


2. The target, the inputs, and a benchmark model
Calorie poverty; household and market characteristics; logit


3. The sample split
70% training, 30% test


4. The choice of tuning parameters
Cross-validation; number of trees


5. Out-of-sample performance
Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, area under the ROC curve


6. For roles 2 and 3: the identifying assumption and its checks
Stetter et al.: selection on observables, overlap, placebo tests


7. Software and versions
Li and Yu: the glmnet package in R




Sources: Zhao et al. (2025); Li and Yu (2025); Stetter et al. (2022); Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 686 to 687.



Items 1 to 5 apply to every paper that uses machine learning. Item 6 distinguishes a causal claim from a prediction.
Athey and Imbens: researchers “should articulate clearly the goals of their analysis and why certain properties of algorithms and estimators may or may not be important.” Item 1 does that.
Item 7 matters for replication, as in Unit 5: results depend on random sample splits, so report the software, versions, and random seed.
Transition: questions for the proposal.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: What to consider for your proposal
text:
What to consider for your proposal

The role: does the question concern predicting an outcome, selecting variables, or how an effect varies?
The claim: does the conclusion require a causal effect? If so, what is the design, and where does machine learning enter it?
The benchmark: which simpler model or rule should the method outperform?
The evidence: which out-of-sample measure, or which identification check, will the paper report?



Most proposals in this course will not use machine learning, but every student should be able to locate items 1 to 7 in a paper that does.
Students who use these methods should state the role in the first sentence of the methods section.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Machine learning entered applied economics within the last decade
text:
Machine learning entered applied economics within the last decade







Period
Development




1984 to 2001
Regression trees (Breiman et al., 1984), the LASSO (Tibshirani, 1996), and random forests (Breiman, 2001)


1990s
Neural networks studied in econometrics, but they “did not catch on at the time”


2001
Breiman’s “two cultures”: statistics relied on data models, while an algorithmic culture grew in other fields


2014
Early reviews for economists: Varian; Einav and Levin; Belloni, Chernozhukov, and Hansen


2017 to 2019
Mullainathan and Spiess; causal forests (Wager and Athey); Athey and Imbens’s review for economists


2020 to 2025
Reviews and special issues in agricultural and applied economics: Storm et al. (2020); Maruejols et al. (2025)




Sources: Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 686 to 688, 696 to 698, and 701; Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), page 87; Storm et al. (2020); Maruejols et al. (2025).



The methods themselves are older; their wide use in applied economics dates from roughly the mid-2010s.
Athey and Imbens open with Breiman (2001): one culture “assumes that the data are generated by a given stochastic data model”; the other “uses algorithmic models and treats the data mechanism as unknown.” Econometrics belongs to the first culture.
Statistics has since absorbed the algorithmic approach; Athey and Imbens note that “the adoption of these methods in economics has been slower.”
The dates for the original methods come from the citations in Athey and Imbens.
Transition: why adoption was slow, and why it accelerated.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Why economists adopted machine learning, and why adoption was slow
text:
Why economists adopted machine learning, and why adoption was slow

New data: many units, many variables per unit, and unstructured sources such as satellite images and text
Prediction questions: some policy problems require an accurate forecast and no causal parameter
Many candidate variables: the analyst must choose controls or functional forms from a large set
Why adoption was slow: economics journals emphasize formal properties of estimators, such as consistency and asymptotic normality, which early machine learning methods did not provide
What changed: recent work established inference for adapted methods, including double selection and causal forests


Sources: Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 686 to 687; Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 88, 98, and 102.



Athey and Imbens: machine learning research focuses on “working properties of algorithms in specific settings,” with formal results such as error rates, while econometrics focuses on large-sample properties of estimators and tests.
The methods economists now use are often adaptations: they modify machine learning algorithms to deliver valid confidence intervals for causal parameters. Two appear later in this lecture.
Transition: how prediction and estimation are evaluated.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: How does Facebook recognize faces in photos?
text:
How does Facebook recognize faces in photos?
Algorithms use a large dataset of photos labeled as having a face or not to estimate a function f(x)f(x) that predicts the presence yy of a face from pixels xx.
This similarity to econometrics raises questions:

Are these algorithms merely applying standard techniques to novel and large datasets?
If there are fundamentally new empirical tools, how do they fit with what we know?
As empirical economists, how can we use them?


Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), page 87.



Mullainathan and Spiess open with this example because the setup is familiar to economists: an outcome yy, inputs xx, and a function to estimate.
The difference is in the goal. A face detector is judged only on whether it labels new photos correctly; no one asks for the coefficient on a particular pixel.
Transition: the next slide states that difference formally.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Parameter estimation (β̂\hat{\beta}) versus prediction (ŷ\hat{y})
Many economic applications revolve around parameter estimation: produce good estimates of parameters β\beta that underlie the relationship between yy and xx.
Supervised machine learning addresses a different objective: the most accurate prediction of yy given xx for observations outside the estimation sample.
This lecture covers where these methods came from, the three roles they play in empirical economics, and how a methods section reports them

Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 87 to 88.



The designs in 6.1 and the models in 6.2 recover parameters: a treatment effect, a price coefficient, an elasticity
Frame the lecture around the distinction between estimating a parameter and predicting an outcome. Every later slide returns to it.
Transition: these methods developed largely outside economics, which explains much about how economists use them.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Why economists adopted machine learning

More readily available access to “big data”

Properties: many units, many variables per unit, and unstructured sources such as satellite images and text
Challenge organizing and studying this type of data (or even to decide which variables to construct) without a simplifying conceptual framework
Better data allow for (1) sharper tests of existing models, (2) tests of theories that had previously been difficult to assess, and (3) assistance choosing controls or functional forms

Prediction questions

Some policy problems require an accurate forecast and no causal parameter



Sources: Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 686 to 687; Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 88, 98, and 102, Einav and Levin (2014)



Einav and Levin describe the shift from small government surveys to administrative and private-sector data with near-universal coverage. They argue that economic models become more useful with such data, because they tell the researcher which variables to construct.
An example of a prediction question, from Mullainathan and Spiess: a judge deciding on bail must predict whether a defendant will return for trial. The decision requires a forecast, and no causal parameter (Kleinberg et al., as discussed on page 102).
Transition: why economics was slower to adopt these tools than statistics.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Why adoption was slow
Economics journals emphasize formal properties of estimators, such as consistency and asymptotic normality, which early machine learning methods did not provide
However, recent work established inference for adapted methods, including double selection and causal forests

Sources: Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 686 to 687; Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 88, 98, and 102.



Athey and Imbens: machine learning research focuses on “working properties of algorithms in specific settings,” with formal results such as error rates, while econometrics focuses on large-sample properties of estimators and tests.
The methods economists now use are often adaptations: they modify machine learning algorithms to deliver valid confidence intervals for causal parameters. Two appear later in this lecture.
Transition: where machine learning sits among the AI-based methods economists now use.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Machine learning within the AI-based tool landscape
text:
Machine learning within the AI-based tool landscape


Source: Bahoo et al. (2025), Section 4.3 and Figure 6.



Bahoo et al. review 2,231 articles on AI in economics published from 1990 to 2024 and classify the methods those articles use. This figure is their summary.
This lecture covers supervised learning (prediction), ensemble learning (random forests), and causal machine learning.
The categories reflect how the literature labels its methods, and the boundaries are loose: their machine learning branch lists ARIMA forecasting under time series, and RCTs and difference in differences under causal inference. Those are standard econometric tools. The point to take from the figure is the breadth of methods now described as AI, more than the exact classification.
Transition: three roles machine learning plays in the papers students will read.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Examples of how machine learning is used in empirical economics
text:
Examples of how machine learning is used in empirical economics
1. Prediction as the objective: Predicts an outcome, such as household food insecurity
2. Prediction within a larger analysis: Selects the variables that enter an economic model or a treatment-effect regression
3. Heterogeneous treatment effects: Estimates how a treatment effect varies across farms or households

Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017); Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 686 to 688; Maruejols et al. (2025).



Each role has its own section later in the lecture, with one published paper.
In roles 2 and 3, the machine learning step sits inside a causal or structural analysis, so the identification questions from 6.1 still apply.
Transition: first, an application where predicting the outcome is the objective

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Out-of-sample prediction
Supervised machine learning algorithms seek functions that predict well out of sample.
For example, we might look to predict the value yy of a house from its observed characteristics xx based on a sample of nn houses (yiy_i, xix_i).
The algorithm would take a loss function L(ŷ,y)L(\hat{y}, y) as an input and search for a function f̂\hat{f} that has low expected prediction loss E(y,x)[L(f̂(x),y)]E_{(y, x)}[L(\hat{f}(x), y)] on a new data point from the same distribution.
With face detection:

A photo can be turned into a 100-by-100 array (vector) so that the resulting xx vector has 10,000 entries.
The yy value is 1 for images with a face and 0 for images without a face.
The loss function L(ŷ,y)L(\hat{y}, y) captures payoffs from proper or improper classification of “face” or “no face.”


Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), page 89



Walk through the three ingredients: an outcome yy, inputs xx, and a loss function that scores each prediction. The algorithm searches for the function f̂\hat{f} with the lowest expected loss on new data.
The key phrase is “a new data point from the same distribution.” Performance is defined on data the algorithm has not seen.
With squared-error loss, this is the familiar problem of minimizing mean squared prediction error.
Transition: what this looks like in practice, with house prices.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: An example: predicting house values with OLS and machine learning
text:
An example: predicting house values with OLS and machine learning




Using data on 51,808 homes from the American Housing Survey:

Fit OLS and several machine learning models using 10,000 homes and 150 characteristics
Predict values for the remaining 41,808 homes
Compare prediction accuracy using held-out R2R^2

Two findings:

Random forest: 45.5% held-out R2R^2, compared with 41.7% for OLS
Random forest: 85.1% training R2R^2, but only 45.5% held-out R2R^2



Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 89 to 90 and Table 1.



The outcome is log house value.
The first finding is that a flexible machine learning method can improve prediction accuracy relative to OLS.
The second finding is that performance on training data can substantially overstate performance on unseen observations.
The random forest’s training R-squared is 85.1%, compared with 45.5% for held-out observations.
The bracketed values in the table are 95% confidence intervals.
The improvement over OLS also differs across the distribution of house values.
Transition: What does a machine learning algorithm do differently from OLS to generate its predictions? Let’s start with a regression tree.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
How a regression tree predicts





Start with all houses in one group
Find the single yes-or-no split, on one variable, that best separates high-value from low-value houses (here, house type)
Repeat the search within each new group (bathrooms, then rooms or square footage)
Stop at a set depth; the prediction for a house in a final group (a leaf) is that group’s average value



Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 90 to 91 and Figure 1.



Read the leftmost path: a house of type 2, 3, or 7, with fewer than 1.5 bathrooms and fewer than 4.5 rooms, is predicted to have a log value of 9.2.
Mullainathan and Spiess show that each leaf is a product of dummy variables: x1=𝟏{Type=2,3,7}×𝟏{Baths<1.5}×𝟏{Rooms<4.5}x_1 = \mathbf{1}\{\text{Type} = 2,3,7\} \times \mathbf{1}\{\text{Baths} < 1.5\} \times \mathbf{1}\{\text{Rooms} < 4.5\}, with coefficient 9.2. A tree is therefore a regression on interactions that the algorithm chooses itself.
This is the advantage over OLS, where the researcher must decide which interactions to include.
Transition: the risk that comes with that flexibility.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: A tree that grows too deep overfits, so depth is limited
text:
A tree that grows too deep overfits, so depth is limited

The problem: a deep enough tree puts every house in its own leaf; it fits the training data perfectly and predicts new houses poorly
Regularization: restrict the complexity of the function, here the depth of the tree
The trade-off: a shallower tree fits the training data less well, because each leaf averages over many houses, but it overfits less, because that averaging removes idiosyncratic noise
Tuning: the best depth is chosen with the data, by cross-validation (next slide)








Method
What limits its complexity




Regression tree
Depth; minimum number of observations per leaf


LASSO
Sum of the absolute values of the coefficients


Random forest
Depth of each tree; number of trees; variables tried at each split




Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 91 to 93 and Table 2.



Mullainathan and Spiess call a tree that fits each observation “perfect overfit.”
Every machine learning method has some measure of complexity to restrict. The table shows three; their Table 2 lists more.
Transition: how the level of complexity is chosen.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Choosing the level of complexity with cross-validation
text:
Choosing the level of complexity with cross-validation

Set aside a test sample that is not used until the end
Split the rest (the training sample) into KK equal parts, or folds; 5 or 10 is common
For each candidate setting (for example, tree depths 2, 3, 4, …): fit the model on K−1K-1 folds, predict the left-out fold, and record the error; repeat so each fold is left out once
Pick the setting with the lowest average error across the KK folds
Refit with that setting on the full training sample, then report performance once on the test sample


Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 92 to 93; Bittmann (2025), Section 3.



Mullainathan and Spiess describe this as creating “an out-of-sample experiment inside the original sample.”
It works because prediction quality is observable: both the prediction and the outcome are in the data. Parameter estimation has no equivalent check.
The test sample is used once. If it informs the choice of settings, it no longer measures out-of-sample performance.
With panel or spatial data, folds should respect that structure, for example by training on earlier years and testing on later ones.
Transition: one expression that covers trees, the LASSO, and forests.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Most machine learning methods solve the same problem
text:
Most machine learning methods solve the same problem
minf∈ℱ∑i=1nL(f(xi),yi)subject toR(f)≤c
\min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \; \sum_{i=1}^{n} L\big(f(x_i), y_i\big) \quad \text{subject to} \quad R(f) \le c


In-sample loss: how well the function fits the training data
Function class ℱ\mathcal{F}: linear functions, trees, or averages of trees
Complexity restriction R(f)≤cR(f) \le c: chosen by cross-validation

The LASSO combines squared-error loss, linear functions, and the restriction ∑j|βj|≤c\sum_j |\beta_j| \le c. Written with a penalty λ\lambda:
minβ∑i=1n(yi−xi′β)2+λ∑j=1p|βj|
\min_{\beta} \; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(y_i - x_i'\beta\right)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j|

A random forest averages many trees, each fit on a bootstrap sample with a random subset of variables (700 trees in Table 1).

Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 92 to 94 and Table 2; Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 690 and 695 to 699.



This is Mullainathan and Spiess’s “most of machine learning in one expression.” Every method on the previous slides is a choice of loss, function class, and complexity restriction.
For the LASSO: with λ=0\lambda = 0 it is OLS; as λ\lambda rises, coefficients shrink and some become exactly zero, so the LASSO also selects variables.
Athey and Imbens note that penalized regression has antecedents in econometrics and statistics; ridge regression uses the squared coefficients in place of their absolute values.
Transition: the first role, where prediction is the objective.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: The random forest predicts best, but improves only modestly on a simple rule
text:
The random forest predicts best, but improves only modestly on a simple rule

Accuracy is informative only relative to a benchmark; the final row is the majority-class rate.

Source: Zhao et al. (2025), Sections 3 to 5 and Table 3. The final row is our calculation from the sample share.



The paper also reports sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the ROC curve (0.62 for both the forest and the LASSO, against 0.5 for random classification).
The final row shows why benchmarks matter: assigning every household to the majority class is correct 61.1% of the time, so the forest improves on that rule by about 5 percentage points.
The authors recommend choosing the classification cut-off according to a program’s coverage: a lower cut-off catches more food-insecure households at the cost of more false alarms.
Transition: what a prediction paper can conclude about the determinants of food insecurity.

Source: Li and Yu (2025), Section 3, Tables 6 and 7.



The economic estimates change: the premium for French apples rises from €1.20 to €1.53 per kilogram, and the premium for small apples from €1.30 to €1.41.
Dropping Organic and Japan lowers the log-likelihood only slightly (from −403.62 to −409.61), which the authors take as evidence the two attributes add little.
A question for discussion: the LASSO excludes Organic for the whole sample, so the paper cannot report willingness to pay for organic apples, the attribute most relevant to policy. Is that trade-off appropriate?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: The effects of agri-environment schemes vary across farms and are limited on average
text:
The effects of agri-environment schemes vary across farms and are limited on average







Outcome
Farms with a significant effect in the intended direction




Fertiliser expenditure

Effects are larger or smaller by location, farm size, and yield potential, and the authors argue for targeting payments on these characteristics


Source: Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 5.2, 5.3, and 6 and Table 3.



€14 per hectare corresponds to about 13 kg of nitrogen per hectare at the paper’s 2014 price.
The authors use Shapley values to measure how much each group of characteristics contributes to the variation in estimated effects; farm type contributes little.
The share of farms with significant effects depends on the precision of each farm-level estimate; a farm without a significant effect may still have a nonzero effect.
Transition: the source of identification.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Machine learning in a nutshell
If you take away one idea today: ML is a prediction method learns from observations we already have, then we check how well it predicts observations it has not seen

Choose the outcome to predict and the information available when a prediction is made
Fit a prediction rule using one group of observations
Compare its predictions with actual outcomes in a separate group
Report how much better it performs than a simple benchmark

In a causal study, machine learning can help account for differences between groups before estimating an effect


A prediction rule might be a regression, a tree, or an average of many trees
The separate group provides evidence about performance on new observations from a similar setting
Prediction accuracy alone does not identify a causal effect

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: How a house-price prediction rule learns
text:
How a house-price prediction rule learns
Imagine we have recent home sales and want to predict the sale price of another house

For each sold house, record its sale price and characteristics such as size and location
Set aside some houses before fitting a model
Use the remaining houses to fit a rule that turns characteristics into predicted prices
Measure each mistake by comparing a prediction with the actual sale price

For a house that sold for $300,000, a prediction of $320,000 misses by $20,000
Is this rule sufficient, or should it be adjusted to reduce the average mistake on the houses used for fitting?

Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), page 89



The observed price is yy, the house characteristics are xx, and the fitted prediction is f̂(x)\hat f(x)
A loss function gives a score to each mistake. Absolute error scores this example as 20,000 dollars. Squared error gives larger mistakes more weight
The observations used for fitting form the training sample

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Why we keep some houses aside
text:
Why we keep some houses aside
Expected loss is average loss on future houses. We cannot calculate it directly because their sale prices are unknown

Train: choose the rule that reduces average loss on the houses used for fitting, called empirical loss
Test: predict the prices of the houses set aside earlier
Compare: use their average loss to estimate performance on new houses

The next paper reports held-out R2R^2 as a summary of predictive fit. Higher held-out R2R^2 means better predictions relative to predicting the same average for every house

Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 89 to 90



The reading calls the average error on training observations empirical loss and the desired average error on new observations expected loss
The held-out houses provide an estimate of out-of-sample loss, provided they represent the houses to which we will apply the rule
Set the test houses aside before choosing the prediction method or its settings

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Why stop a tree from dividing further?
text:
Why stop a tree from dividing further?

A tree can keep dividing the training houses into smaller groups
With enough divisions, it can nearly memorize their sale prices
Those very specific groups may predict poorly for houses the tree has not seen
We limit the number of divisions and require several houses in each final group

Fitting the training houses closely while predicting new houses poorly is called overfitting

Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 91 to 93 and Table 2.



Mullainathan and Spiess call a tree that fits each observation “perfect overfit”
Limiting the number of divisions is a form of regularization: the method gives up some training fit to improve predictions on new observations
The forest’s large drop in R2R^2 from training to test data illustrates this concern

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: How do we choose when a tree should stop?
text:
How do we choose when a tree should stop?

Keep the test houses aside until the final evaluation
Divide the training houses into several groups
Fit a short tree on all but one group, then check its predictions for the group left out
Repeat with each group left out, then repeat the process for deeper trees
Choose the depth with the smallest average prediction error
Fit a tree of that depth on all training houses and evaluate it once on the test houses

This repeated check within the training data is called cross-validation

Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 92 to 93; Bittmann (2025), Section 3.



Mullainathan and Spiess describe this as creating “an out-of-sample experiment inside the original sample”
The training groups are called folds, often five or ten
It works because prediction quality is observable: both the prediction and the outcome are in the data. Parameter estimation has no equivalent check.
The test sample is used once. If it informs the choice of settings, it no longer measures out-of-sample performance.
With panel or spatial data, folds should respect that structure, for example by training on earlier years and testing on later ones.
Transition: one expression that covers trees, the LASSO, and forests.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: What changes when we use another method?
text:
What changes when we use another method?
The steps stay the same: fit on training data, choose how flexible the rule can be, and check predictions on held-out data








Method
Prediction rule
How flexibility is limited




OLS
A linear combination of house characteristics
Researcher chooses the characteristics and interactions


Regression tree
A sequence of yes-or-no splits
Limit the number of splits and houses per final group


LASSO
A linear combination of characteristics
Shrink coefficients and set some to zero


Random forest
An average of many trees
Limit each tree and average their predictions




Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 92 to 94 and Table 2; Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 690 and 695 to 699.



Mullainathan and Spiess summarize these methods as a choice of prediction error measure, class of rules, and limit on complexity
Cross-validation helps choose settings such as tree depth or the amount of LASSO shrinkage
LASSO uses a penalty on the absolute sizes of coefficients. A larger penalty shrinks more coefficients toward zero and can remove variables from the fitted rule
A forest fits many trees on different samples and subsets of characteristics, then averages their predictions
Transition: the first role, where prediction is the objective.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Zhao et al. (2025): predicting which households are calorie poor
text:
Zhao et al. (2025): predicting which households are calorie poor
The question is whether information a program could collect can identify rural households with inadequate calorie intake

Use three days of food records to calculate calorie intake for each of 1,080 households
Mark a household as calorie poor if its intake falls below the study’s threshold
Record household, village, and food-market characteristics that might help predict that outcome
Fit a random forest, LASSO, and a logit model using 756 households
Predict calorie poverty for the other 324 households and compare predictions with their measured outcomes


Source: Zhao et al. (2025), Sections 3 to 5.



Step 2 matters as much as the algorithm: a different calorie threshold changes who counts as calorie poor. The households are in Jilin, Shandong, and Hubei, and 61.1% of the full sample meets the paper’s definition
The forest uses 93 trees, chosen using observations left out when each tree was fit. The paper also reports sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the ROC curve
Out-of-bag error is the random forest’s built-in version of a hold-out sample: each tree is fit on a bootstrap sample, and the observations left out of that sample are used to measure its error.
The authors oversample the smaller class (SMOTE) because the two classes are unequal in size.
Transition: the results.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: How much does the random forest improve prediction?
text:
How much does the random forest improve prediction?







Model (test sample)
Accuracy




Random forest
65.7%


LASSO
61.1%


Logit benchmark
58.9%



Accuracy is the share of test households classified correctly. The forest exceeds the logit benchmark by 6.8 percentage points

Source: Zhao et al. (2025), Sections 3 to 5 and Table 3



The paper also reports sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the ROC curve (0.62 for both the forest and the LASSO, against 0.5 for random classification).
The paper reports that 61.1% of the full sample is calorie poor. A rule that always predicts calorie poor could serve as another benchmark, but its accuracy in the test sample is not reported
The authors recommend choosing the classification cut-off according to a program’s coverage: a lower cut-off catches more food-insecure households at the cost of more false alarms.
Transition: what a prediction paper can conclude about the determinants of food insecurity.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: What can a predictor ranking tell us?
text:
What can a predictor ranking tell us?
Zhao et al. find that household income and access to food markets help predict calorie poverty

A predictor can be useful because it moves with another factor that the data do not measure
Correlated predictors can replace one another, so the variables chosen by LASSO may change when the training sample changes
The ranking tells us which information helps classify households in this dataset


Sources: Zhao et al. (2025), Section 5.2; Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), page 97, Figure 2; Stetter et al. (2022), page 740, footnote 17.



Zhao et al.’s discussion moves from variables that predict food insecurity to variables that “significantly influence” it. That shift is where a reader should ask for an identification strategy
Mullainathan and Spiess show that LASSO selects different variables across ten random partitions of the same data. Stetter et al. also warn against a causal reading of variable importance
The instability arises because correlated predictors are close substitutes in prediction; small changes in the sample change which one the LASSO retains.
Transition: the second role, where prediction is one step in a larger analysis.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Li and Yu (2025): selecting apple attributes before estimating willingness to pay
text:
Li and Yu (2025): selecting apple attributes before estimating willingness to pay
The question is how much consumers value apple attributes such as origin, size, and production method

Ask 100 consumers to choose among two apples and a no-purchase option in four scenarios
Record each apple’s attributes and price in every choice
Use LASSO to identify attributes that help explain the choices, while always retaining price
Fit the choice model from Lecture 6.2 using the retained attributes
Use that model’s attribute and price coefficients to calculate willingness to pay

In this sample, LASSO removes Organic and Japan from the final choice model

Source: Li and Yu (2025), Sections 2 and 3.



The paper interprets the removed attributes as evidence of attribute non-attendance, meaning that respondents may not use those attributes in their choices
Ten-fold cross-validation chooses the amount of LASSO shrinkage; price is exempt from shrinkage. The final model is a conditional logit
Willingness to pay for attribute kk is −βk/βprice-\beta_k/\beta_{\text{price}}: how many euros a consumer would give up for the attribute, holding utility constant
Transition: how the estimates change.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Belloni et al. (2014): choosing controls for a treatment-effect model
text:
Belloni et al. (2014): choosing controls for a treatment-effect model
The question is which controls to include when there are many plausible candidates

Start with the treatment, the outcome, and 251 possible controls
Use LASSO to find controls that predict the treatment
Use LASSO again to find controls that predict the outcome
Include every control selected in either step in the final OLS treatment-effect model

This is called double selection. A control that predicts treatment can matter even when it adds little to outcome prediction
The application uses 576 state-year observations on abortion and crime. A causal interpretation still requires the identifying assumption from Lecture 6.1

Source: Belloni et al. (2014), Sections 1, 2.2, and 7.



A confounder that predicts treatment strongly and the outcome weakly could be dropped by a LASSO for the outcome alone, producing omitted-variable bias
The application covers 48 states over 12 years; LASSO retains 8 to 14 of the 251 candidate controls
Their results: the property crime estimate remains close to the original study but is significant only at the 10% level; the violent crime and murder estimates become imprecise.
The identifying assumption is selection on observables, as in 6.1. The LASSO makes the choice of controls systematic and reproducible; it does not make the assumption more plausible.
Transition: the third role.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Stetter et al. (2022): do program effects differ across farms?
text:
Stetter et al. (2022): do program effects differ across farms?
Research question: Does participation in an agri-environment scheme change farm outcomes, and do those effects vary across farms?

Observe 2,758 Bavarian farms in 2014, including 1,641 program participants
Collect farm characteristics, program participation, and environmental outcomes
Use machine learning to account for observed differences between participating and nonparticipating farms
Estimate heterogeneous treatment effects using a causal forest

The authors examine four outcomes, including fertiliser expenditure, pesticide expenditure, land-use diversity, and emissions.

Source: Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 2.3, 4.1, and 4.2.



The study uses more than 130 farm and county characteristics.
Participation and outcome models are estimated using random forests.
The causal forest estimates conditional average treatment effects.
The aim is to identify whether effects differ by observable farm characteristics.
Settings are tuned using cross-validation.
The authors use large forests to obtain stable estimates.
Transition: What do the authors find?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Which farms have estimated benefits from the schemes?
text:
Which farms have estimated benefits from the schemes?







Outcome

Fertiliser expenditure
