Estimated effects vary by location, farm size, and yield potential. The authors use these differences to discuss how payments might be targeted

Source: Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 5.2, 5.3, and 6 and Table 3.



“Detectable” means the reported confidence interval excludes zero. The emissions outcome is greenhouse gas emissions
€14 per hectare corresponds to about 13 kg of nitrogen per hectare at the paper’s 2014 price.
The authors use Shapley values to measure how much each group of characteristics contributes to the variation in estimated effects; farm type contributes little.
The share of farms with significant effects depends on the precision of each farm-level estimate; a farm without a significant effect may still have a nonzero effect.
Transition: the source of identification.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: What must hold for a causal interpretation?
text:
What must hold for a causal interpretation?
The causal forest compares farms after accounting for their recorded characteristics. The interpretation still depends on two assumptions from Lecture 6.1

Comparable farms: after accounting for recorded characteristics, participation is as good as randomly assigned
Both options are possible: farms with similar characteristics could participate or stay out of the program

The authors exclude 23 farms that lack a suitable comparison and check how their findings respond to alternative assumptions about missing factors

Source: Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 4.3 and 5.1.



The formal names are selection on observables and overlap. Estimated participation probabilities range from 0.27 to 0.86 for retained farms
The authors argue that many recorded characteristics can stand in for unobserved factors such as environmental attitudes. They acknowledge that omitted confounders could still bias the estimates
They report placebo tests and simulations with omitted confounders
Transition: what a methods section must report in all three roles.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: What to report in a machine learning methods section
text:
What to report in a machine learning methods section







Item
Example




1. What the method does in the study
Zhao et al. use it to predict calorie poverty


2. What is predicted and which information is used
Calorie poverty from household and market characteristics


3. Which observations are used for fitting and testing
70% training, 30% test


4. How method settings are chosen
Cross-validation; number of trees


5. How well it performs on test observations
Classification accuracy, compared with logit


6. If effects are claimed, what supports the causal comparison
Stetter et al. discuss comparable farms and overlap


7. How another researcher could repeat the analysis
Software, package versions, random seed, and code




Sources: Zhao et al. (2025); Li and Yu (2025); Stetter et al. (2022); Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 686 to 687.



Items 1 to 5 describe the prediction step. Item 6 is essential when the paper interprets a result as an effect
Athey and Imbens: researchers “should articulate clearly the goals of their analysis and why certain properties of algorithms and estimators may or may not be important.” Item 1 does that.
Item 7 matters for replication, as in Unit 5: results depend on random sample splits, so report the software, versions, and random seed.
Transition: questions for the proposal.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
How do the methods differ?
Each method learns a prediction rule from training data, but differs in how it generates predictions and controls complexity.








Method
How it predicts
How it controls flexibility




OLS
Estimates a linear combination of characteristics
Researcher specifies variables and interactions


Regression tree
Divides observations into groups
Limits on tree depth and group size




Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 92 to 94 and Table 2; Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 690 and 695 to 699.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
text:
Structural models in a nutshell
If you take away one idea today: A structural model describes how people or firms make choices, estimates the parameters of that behavior from data, and uses the estimated model to study a change

State who chooses what and what shapes those choices
Use observed choices to estimate parameters such as price sensitivity
Change the policy or market setting in the model
Solve the model again to predict choices, prices, or welfare under that change

For a proposed cereal merger, this means estimating how shoppers substitute between brands, then predicting prices under new ownership

Sources: Nevo and Whinston (2010), pages 73 to 77; Nevo (2000b), pages 395 to 397.



The model’s behavioral assumptions and the variation used to estimate its parameters determine how credible the prediction is
Some parameters can be estimated with OLS or 2SLS; other models require a numerical search
The merger example carries these four steps through the lecture

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: How does prediction help estimate an effect?
text:
How does prediction help estimate an effect?
Suppose an agri-environment program encourages farmers to reduce fertiliser use.
The research question is: Do programs have the same effect on every farm?
The average treatment effect tells us how participation changes fertiliser use across farms.
But the effect may differ depending on:

Farm size
Location
Crop production and yield potential
Other farm characteristics


Sources: Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 701 to 704; Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 2.3 and 4.1 to 4.3.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Example papers in this lecture

Background: Einav and Levin (2014); Bahoo et al. (2025)
Overview for agribusiness: Maruejols et al. (2025)
Prediction: Zhao et al. (2025)
Prediction within a larger analysis: Li and Yu (2025); Belloni et al. (2014)
Heterogeneous treatment effects: Stetter et al. (2022)
Further reading: Bittmann’s guide from OLS to causal machine learning (Bittmann 2025)



Timing: 10 minutes on background, 10 on core concepts, 40 on the three roles (about 13 each), 15 on reporting.
The aim is for students to read, evaluate, and write the methods section of a paper that uses these tools, whether or not they use them in their own work.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Evaluating predictions and parameters









Prediction, ŷ\hat{y}
Parameter estimation, β̂\hat{\beta}




Target
The outcome for a new observation
An effect or behavioral parameter


Common techniques
LASSO, random forests, and other prediction methods
OLS, IV, difference in differences, and structural models


Evaluation
Accuracy on data not used in estimation
Identification: the source of variation and its assumptions


Verifiability
Directly testable: predictions and outcomes are both observed
Rests on assumptions about the data-generating process




Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 88 and 92.



Prediction quality can be measured against held-out outcomes. A causal effect relies on assumptions because the counterfactual outcome is never observed
For prediction, ask what a household’s risk of food insecurity is. For parameter estimation, ask how much a program changed outcomes
OLS can also predict, and causal forests adapt tree methods to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects. The table classifies methods by their usual role in this lecture
The research question determines how a method is used. Later we will use machine learning tools inside an effect-estimation procedure
This is why machine learning papers report out-of-sample performance and causal papers report an identification strategy.
Transition: three ways economics papers combine the two.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Two goals: prediction and parameter estimation
text:
Two goals: prediction and parameter estimation
Many economic applications estimate a parameter, such as a treatment effect or price sensitivity
Supervised machine learning methods are often designed to predict an outcome accurately for new observations
Economists can also use prediction methods within procedures that estimate effects
This lecture covers where these methods came from, the three roles they play in empirical economics, and how a methods section reports them

Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 87 to 88.



The designs in 6.1 and the models in 6.2 recover parameters: a treatment effect, a price coefficient, an elasticity
Prediction is the direct goal in Role 1 and a component of the effect-estimation procedure in Role 3
Transition: these methods developed largely outside economics, which explains much about how economists use them.

title: Lecture 6.2: Structural Models
text:
Overview

An economic research design (a source of variation and an identifying assumption) is meant to answer causal questions
Some questions cannot be answered that way:

the change has not happened yet
the answer has to be in dollars of welfare
you need to know why an outcome changed

For these, papers write down an economic model and estimate it: a structural model



Start from what students know: a design gives a credible estimate for a change that happened in the data.
Read the three cases slowly. Each one returns later in the lecture.
Transition: we will use one question all day, about a merger.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Machine learning’s use in applied economics grew over the past 20 years
text:
Machine learning’s use in applied economics grew over the past 20 years







Period
Development




1984 to 2001
Regression trees (Breiman et al., 1984), the LASSO (Tibshirani, 1996), and random forests (Breiman, 2001)


1990s
Neural networks studied in econometrics, but they “did not catch on at the time”


2001
Breiman’s “two cultures”: statistics relied on data models, while an algorithmic culture grew in other fields


2014
Early reviews for economists: Varian; Einav and Levin; Belloni, Chernozhukov, and Hansen


2017 to 2019
Mullainathan and Spiess; causal forests (Wager and Athey); Athey and Imbens’s review for economists


2020 to 2025
Reviews and special issues in agricultural and applied economics: Storm et al. (2020); Maruejols et al. (2025)




Sources: Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 686 to 688, 696 to 698, and 701; Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), page 87; Storm et al. (2020); Maruejols et al. (2025).



The methods themselves are older; their adoption in applied economics grew across the 2000s and 2010s.
Athey and Imbens open with Breiman (2001): one culture “assumes that the data are generated by a given stochastic data model”; the other “uses algorithmic models and treats the data mechanism as unknown.” Econometrics belongs to the first culture.
Statistics has since absorbed the algorithmic approach; Athey and Imbens note that “the adoption of these methods in economics has been slower.”
The dates for the original methods come from the citations in Athey and Imbens.
Transition: why adoption was slow, and why it accelerated.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: How do we score a house-price prediction?
text:
How do we score a house-price prediction?
Suppose a house sold for $300,000 and our model predicted $320,000.








Loss function
Score for this house
What it emphasizes




Absolute error
|320−300|=20\lvert 320-300\rvert=20
The size of each mistake


Squared error
(320−300)2=400(320-300)^2=400
Larger mistakes receive more weight



A loss function measures how wrong a prediction is for one observation.
For squared error:
L(f̂(xi),yi)=(yi−f̂(xi))2
L(\hat{f}(x_i),y_i)=(y_i-\hat{f}(x_i))^2

Here, yiy_i is the actual price and f̂(xi)\hat{f}(x_i) is the predicted price.

Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), page 89



Prices are measured in thousands of dollars; squared errors have squared units.
The loss function assigns a penalty to each prediction error.
Squared error is used in ordinary least squares.
Different loss functions may favor different prediction rules.
Transition: One prediction error tells us very little about how well a model performs overall. We want a rule that makes small errors across many houses.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Li and Yu (2025): selecting apple attributes
text:
Li and Yu (2025): selecting apple attributes
Research question: How much are consumers willing to pay for apple attributes such as origin, size, and production method?

Ask 100 consumers to choose between apples with different attributes and a no-purchase option
Use LASSO to identify which attributes help predict consumer choices
Estimate a conditional logit model using the selected attributes
Calculate willingness to pay from the estimated coefficients

Role of ML: Select variables to include in an economic model.

Source: Li and Yu (2025), Sections 2 and 3.



Each respondent completes four choice scenarios.
The authors use LASSO to select apple attributes, while always retaining price.
Tenfold cross-validation determines the LASSO penalty.
The final conditional logit estimates relationships between attributes and choice probabilities.
Willingness to pay is calculated as the negative ratio of the attribute and price coefficients.
The prediction step helps specify the economic model rather than serving as the final result.
Transition: Which attributes does LASSO retain?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Why are Organic and Japan omitted?
text:
Why are Organic and Japan omitted?
LASSO shrinks attribute coefficients toward zero. The authors choose the penalty using tenfold cross-validation
At the chosen penalty, Organic and Japan reach zero. They contribute the weakest additional signals for predicting choices after the other recorded attributes are considered
Price stays in the model because the authors exempt it from the penalty. The price coefficient is needed to calculate willingness to pay
This selection describes the fitted model for these respondents. It does not establish that every respondent ignored either attribute

Source: Li and Yu (2025), Section 3.1, Figure 2, and Table 4



The authors’ Shapley-value check also ranks Japan and Organic lowest among the attributes
Tenfold cross-validation selects the penalty that minimizes mean cross-validated error
The authors suggest attribute non-attendance as one interpretation, but selection alone cannot establish an individual respondent’s reasoning

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Why select controls for both equations?
text:
Why select controls for both equations?
Belloni et al. revisit the relationship between earlier abortion rates and later crime rates across states
A state characteristic may be related to both rates. For example, an initial state condition could predict how abortion rates change and how crime rates change over time
If controls are selected only for predicting crime, the procedure might omit a variable that strongly predicts abortion rates and also matters for crime
Double selection retains controls selected from either prediction step before estimating the abortion-rate coefficient

Source: Belloni et al. (2014), Sections 1 and 7



Earlier abortion rates are constructed to reflect the age groups associated with later crime; the application reports violent crime, property crime, and murder separately
The concern is omitted-variable bias: a shared state factor can make the abortion-rate coefficient absorb part of that factor’s association with crime
An initial condition is a state’s starting level of a variable, such as its initial abortion rate or income

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Belloni et al. (2014): double selection in practice
text:
Belloni et al. (2014): double selection in practice
The application has 576 state-year observations and 251 candidate controls, including initial conditions, interactions, and trends

Use LASSO to find controls that predict the relevant abortion rate
Use LASSO again to find controls that predict the crime rate
Combine the controls selected in either step
Regress the crime rate on the abortion rate and those controls using OLS

The final models include 8 to 14 of the 251 candidate controls, depending on the crime outcome
The estimates for violent crime and murder become imprecise after the selected controls are included

Source: Belloni et al. (2014), Sections 1, 2.2, and 7.



The application covers 48 states over 12 years. The 251 controls supplement time effects included in every model
The property crime estimate remains close to the original study but is significant only at the 10% level; the violent crime and murder estimates become imprecise
Selection on observables is the identifying assumption. LASSO makes the choice among a large set of proposed controls systematic and reproducible
Transition: the third role.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: How do the authors support the comparison?
text:
How do the authors support the comparison?
The causal forest compares farms after accounting for their recorded characteristics. The authors examine two conditions

Comparable farms: after accounting for recorded characteristics, participation is as good as randomly assigned
Both options are possible: farms with similar characteristics could participate or stay out of the program

The authors exclude 23 farms that lack a suitable comparison and check how their findings respond to alternative assumptions about missing factors

Source: Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 4.3 and 5.1.



The formal names are selection on observables and overlap. Estimated participation probabilities range from 0.27 to 0.86 for retained farms
The authors argue that many recorded characteristics can stand in for unobserved factors such as environmental attitudes. They acknowledge that omitted confounders could still bias the estimates
They report placebo tests and simulations with omitted confounders
Transition: what a methods section must report in all three roles.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Different goals: prediction and parameter estimation
text:
Different goals: prediction and parameter estimation
Many economic applications estimate a parameter, such as a treatment effect or price sensitivity
Causal inference in a RF sense asks us to predict outcomes under conditions that were not observed, trying to replicate the gold standard of a RCT
Supervised machine learning methods are often designed to predict an outcome accurately for new observations
Note: Economists can also use prediction methods within procedures that estimate effects
This lecture covers where these methods came from, the three roles they play in empirical economics, and how a methods section reports them

Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 87 to 88.



The designs in 6.1 and the models in 6.2 recover parameters: a treatment effect, a price coefficient, an elasticity
Prediction is the direct goal in Role 1 and a component of the effect-estimation procedure in Role 3
Transition: these methods developed largely outside economics, which explains much about how economists use them.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: What are we trying to minimize?
text:
What are we trying to minimize?
We want a prediction rule that makes the smallest mistakes, on average, for new houses.
This is called expected loss:
E(Y,X)[L(f̂(X),Y)]
E_{(Y,X)}[L(\hat{f}(X),Y)]

For squared error:
E(Y,X)[(Y−f̂(X))2]
E_{(Y,X)}[(Y-\hat{f}(X))^2]


LL measures the loss for one house.
EE takes the average loss across the population.
f̂(X)\hat{f}(X) predicts price using house characteristics.

The goal: Find the prediction rule f̂\hat{f} that minimizes expected loss.

Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), page 89



Expected loss extends the idea of a loss function from one observation to the population.
The expectation is taken over the joint distribution of house prices (Y) and characteristics (X).
We want a rule that predicts well for future houses drawn from the same population.
Expected loss is a population quantity. We cannot calculate it exactly because we do not observe the entire population.
Transition: If we cannot calculate expected loss directly, how do we determine whether a prediction rule is any good?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: How do we evaluate a prediction rule?
text:
How do we evaluate a prediction rule?
We cannot directly calculate expected loss because we do not observe every possible future house.
Instead, we use the data we have:

Training data: Choose a prediction rule that minimizes average loss across observed houses. This is called empirical loss.
1n∑i=1nL(f̂(xi),yi)
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}L(\hat{f}(x_i),y_i)



Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 89 to 90

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: How does a regression tree predict house values?
text:
How does a regression tree predict house values?
Unlike OLS, a regression tree does not require us to specify a linear relationship. Instead, it divides houses into groups with similar values.





Start with all houses in one group
Find the yes-or-no split that produces the greatest reduction in squared prediction error (here, house type)
Repeat within each new group, using characteristics such as bathrooms, rooms, and square footage
Predict the value of a house using the average value of houses in its final group (a leaf)



Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 90 to 91 and Figure 1.



Table 1 showed that machine learning methods can outperform OLS on held-out observations. We now examine how these methods construct prediction rules, beginning with regression trees.
OLS estimates coefficients for a specified set of variables and interactions. A regression tree searches for splits that group houses with similar outcomes.
Each split is selected to reduce squared prediction error in the training data.
Read the leftmost path: a house of type 2, 3, or 7, with fewer than 1.5 bathrooms and fewer than 4.5 rooms, is predicted to have a log value of 9.2.
The prediction at each leaf is the average log house value among the training observations in that group.
A regression tree effectively selects interactions among characteristics without requiring the researcher to specify them in advance.
Random forests build on this idea by combining predictions from many trees.
Transition: If each additional split can improve the fit to training data, why not keep dividing houses into smaller groups?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Why not keep dividing the tree?
text:
Why not keep dividing the tree?
Each additional split allows a regression tree to fit the training houses more closely.

More splits create smaller groups of similar houses
Smaller groups can reduce prediction errors in the training data
But very specific groups may capture patterns unique to those houses
Those patterns may not hold for new observations

Overfitting occurs when a model fits the training data closely but predicts poorly on new data.
Regularization limits model flexibility to improve out-of-sample prediction.

Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 91 to 93 and Table 2.



Each split is selected to reduce training error, but reductions in training error do not necessarily improve predictions on new observations.
A sufficiently deep tree can nearly memorize the training observations.
This helps explain why the random forest’s training R-squared is so much higher than its held-out R-squared, although the gap alone does not establish which tree settings are optimal.
Regularization constrains model complexity.
For regression trees, we can limit tree depth, the number of splits, or the minimum number of observations in a leaf.
Restricting flexibility may increase training error while improving held-out performance.
Transition: How do we determine the appropriate amount of flexibility?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: How do we choose the right tree depth?
text:
How do we choose the right tree depth?
A deeper tree may fit the training data better, but how deep should it be?
Cross-validation evaluates different model settings using only the training data.

Divide the training data into several groups (folds)
Fit the model using all but one fold
Predict outcomes for the excluded fold and calculate prediction error
Repeat until every fold has been excluded once
Choose the tree depth with the lowest average prediction error

Then fit the selected model on all training data and evaluate it on the held-out test data.

Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 92 to 93; Bittmann (2025), Section 3.



Cross-validation creates repeated prediction exercises within the training sample.
For example, in five-fold cross-validation, the model is trained five times, each time leaving out a different fifth of the training observations.
Repeat the process for different tree depths and compare their average validation errors.
After selecting the depth, refit the model using the entire training sample.
The final test sample is reserved for evaluating performance after model selection.
Cross-validation helps select model settings, but it does not guarantee that the selected model will perform well in a different population.
With panel or spatial data, cross-validation should respect the structure of the observations.
Transition: The same principle applies to other methods. What differs is how each method constructs and constrains its prediction rule.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Zhao et al. (2025): predicting calorie poverty
text:
Zhao et al. (2025): predicting calorie poverty
Research question: Can household and market characteristics help identify households at risk of inadequate calorie intake?

Use three days of food records to measure calorie intake for 1,080 rural households
Classify each household as calorie poor or not calorie poor
Use household, village, and food-market characteristics to predict that classification
Fit a random forest, LASSO, and logit model using 756 households
Evaluate predictions on the remaining 324 households

Unlike house values, the outcome is binary: a household is either classified as calorie poor or not.

Source: Zhao et al. (2025), Sections 3 to 5.



This is supervised learning because the outcome is observed and used to train the prediction models.
The outcome is binary rather than continuous, so the authors evaluate classification accuracy rather than regression R-squared.
The calorie-poverty threshold determines which households receive the label.
The households are in Jilin, Shandong, and Hubei. Approximately 61.1% of the full sample is classified as calorie poor.
The authors use SMOTE to address class imbalance and out-of-bag observations to help tune the forest.
Transition: Does the random forest classify households more accurately than conventional approaches?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Does machine learning improve classification?



Model
Test-sample accuracy




Random forest
65.7%


LASSO
61.1%


Logit benchmark
58.9%



Accuracy measures the percentage of households classified correctly.
The random forest improves accuracy by 6.8 percentage points relative to logit.
But accuracy does not tell us which households were misclassified.

False positive: A household is predicted to be calorie poor when it is not
False negative: A calorie-poor household is not identified


Source: Zhao et al. (2025), Sections 3 to 5 and Table 3.



The methods are evaluated on the same held-out observations.
A model’s accuracy depends on the classification threshold.
For a food assistance program, false negatives may be especially consequential because eligible households could be overlooked.
The paper also reports sensitivity, specificity, and area under the ROC curve.
The full-sample calorie-poverty prevalence is 61.1%; that is not necessarily the accuracy of a majority-class classifier in the test sample.
Transition: The authors also examine which variables are most useful for prediction. What can we learn from those rankings?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Do important predictors identify causes?
Zhao et al. find that household income and access to food markets help predict calorie poverty.
But a variable that improves prediction is not necessarily a cause of the outcome.

A predictor may be correlated with other factors that affect calorie poverty
Highly correlated predictors may provide similar information
LASSO may select one predictor and exclude another, depending on the sample

Predictor importance tells us what helps classify households, not what would happen if we changed that characteristic.

Sources: Zhao et al. (2025), Section 5.2; Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), page 97, Figure 2; Stetter et al. (2022), page 740, footnote 17.



The distinction is between predicting an outcome and identifying a causal effect.
Income may predict calorie poverty, but this analysis does not identify the effect of increasing income.
Mullainathan and Spiess demonstrate that LASSO may select different variables across different partitions of the same data.
This is especially relevant when predictors are highly correlated.
Prediction can help identify households for assistance without establishing why those households experience inadequate calorie intake.
Transition: In the next examples, prediction is not the final objective. Instead, machine learning helps researchers estimate economic relationships.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
How does LASSO select attributes?
LASSO estimates coefficients while penalizing their absolute magnitude.
As the penalty increases, some coefficients shrink to zero.
In Li and Yu (2025):

Tenfold cross-validation determines the penalty
Organic and Japan have coefficients of zero at the selected penalty
Price remains because the authors exclude it from the penalty

The excluded attributes provide little additional predictive information in this fitted model, given the other attributes.
Does a coefficient of zero mean consumers do not value the attribute?

Source: Li and Yu (2025), Section 3.1, Figure 2, and Table 4.



LASSO minimizes prediction error plus a penalty on coefficient magnitude.
A larger penalty generally produces a simpler model.
Cross-validation selects the penalty based on predictive performance.
A zero coefficient is a model-selection result, not evidence that every consumer ignores the attribute.
Correlated attributes may substitute for one another.
The authors also use Shapley values to evaluate attribute importance.
Transition: How does this selection affect the economic estimates?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: How does a causal forest differ from a regression tree?
text:
How does a causal forest differ from a regression tree?
A regression tree divides observations into groups to predict an outcome.
A causal forest seeks groups with different treatment effects.

Predict treatment participation using observed characteristics
Predict the outcome using observed characteristics
Account for those predicted relationships when comparing treated and untreated farms
Use many trees to estimate how treatment effects vary across farm characteristics

The goal: Estimate treatment-effect heterogeneity rather than minimize ordinary outcome prediction error.

Sources: Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 701 to 704; Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 2.3 and 4.1 to 4.3.



Standard prediction forests estimate relationships between predictors and observed outcomes.
Causal forests adapt tree-based methods to estimate variation in treatment effects.
In Stetter et al., machine learning estimates treatment participation and expected outcomes as intermediate steps.
The causal forest uses adjusted comparisons to estimate heterogeneous effects.
The method does not automatically eliminate selection bias.
The credibility of the estimates depends on the identification assumptions.
Transition: Let’s look at an application to agri-environment programs.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Which farms have detectable program effects?
text:
Which farms have detectable program effects?







Outcome
Share of farms with a statistically detectable effect




Fertiliser expenditure
33% show reductions


Land-use diversity
55% show increases


Pesticide expenditure
7% show improvements


Emissions
Under 1% show reductions; about 4% show increases



Among farms with detectable reductions in fertiliser expenditure, the estimated reduction averages €14 per hectare. Estimated effects vary by location, farm size, and yield potential. Policy relevance: Differences in estimated effects may inform how program payments are targeted.

Source: Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 5.2, 5.3, and 6 and Table 3.



A statistically detectable effect means the reported confidence interval excludes zero.
The percentages describe statistical detectability, which depends on both estimated effect magnitude and precision.
An insignificant estimate does not mean the true treatment effect is zero.
The effects vary across farm characteristics, suggesting that average effects can hide meaningful heterogeneity.
The authors examine how these differences might inform program targeting.
These are estimates from an observational study, so the identifying assumptions remain important.
Transition: How do the authors justify interpreting these differences as treatment effects?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: What makes a causal forest estimate credible?
text:
What makes a causal forest estimate credible?
A causal forest can estimate differences in treatment effects, but machine learning alone does not establish causality.
The analysis relies on two important assumptions:

Selection on observables: After accounting for recorded characteristics, treated and untreated farms are comparable in their potential outcomes
Overlap: Farms with similar characteristics have a positive probability of participating or not participating

Stetter et al. exclude 23 farms that lack suitable comparisons and examine sensitivity to unobserved confounding.
The distinction: Machine learning helps estimate relationships; causal identification determines whether they can be interpreted as treatment effects.

Source: Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 4.3 and 5.1.



Selection on observables assumes that the recorded characteristics account for the confounding relevant to treatment assignment.
Overlap requires comparable treated and untreated farms across the covariate region used for estimation.
The retained farms have estimated participation probabilities between 0.27 and 0.86.
The authors use placebo tests and simulations involving omitted confounders.
Sensitivity analysis can investigate robustness but cannot establish that all relevant confounders were observed.
Machine learning provides flexible estimation, not an identification strategy by itself.
Transition: What should we look for when assessing machine learning in an empirical economics paper?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: What role does machine learning play in economic research?
text:
What role does machine learning play in economic research?








Role
Research objective
Contribution of ML




Prediction
Identify households at risk of calorie poverty
Improve classification accuracy


Model selection and estimation
Estimate preferences or a coefficient of interest
Select variables and controls


Heterogeneous treatment effects
Estimate how program impacts differ across farms
Flexibly estimate differences in treatment effects




Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017); Athey and Imbens (2019); Zhao et al. (2025); Li and Yu (2025); Belloni et al. (2014); Stetter et al. (2022).

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Testing the prediction rule

Test data: Apply the fitted rule to houses that were set aside and not used to train the model.
Evaluate: Calculate average loss on the test houses to estimate how well the rule predicts new observations.

Why? A rule that performs well on training data may not predict well on new data.
The next paper reports held-out R2R^2 as a summary of predictive fit. Higher held-out R2R^2 means better predictions relative to predicting the same average for every house

Source: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 89 to 90



Empirical loss is the average observed loss in the sample.
When squared-error loss is used, empirical loss is the mean squared error (MSE).
The algorithm uses training data to fit the prediction rule.
Evaluating the rule on the same data used to train it can produce an overly optimistic assessment of predictive performance.
Test observations provide an estimate of out-of-sample performance, assuming they represent the population of interest.
Set test observations aside before model selection and tuning.
The next paper uses held-out R-squared to summarize predictive performance.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
How do the methods differ? (continued)








Method
How it predicts
How it controls flexibility




LASSO
Estimates a linear combination of characteristics
Penalizes coefficients, shrinking some to zero


Random forest
Averages predictions from many trees
Randomization, averaging, and tree settings



Common goal: Minimize prediction error on new, unseen observations.

Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017), pages 92 to 94 and Table 2; Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 690 and 695 to 699.



The methods differ in the class of prediction rules they consider and how they limit complexity.
OLS specifies the functional form in advance. Its flexibility depends on the variables and interactions included.
Regression trees discover splits and interactions from the data.
LASSO adds a penalty to the least-squares objective. Larger penalties shrink coefficients toward zero, and some become exactly zero.
Random forests fit many trees using randomized observations and predictors, then average their predictions.
Cross-validation can help select the amount of LASSO penalization, tree depth, and other model settings.
All methods can be evaluated using the same held-out prediction metrics, such as MSE or R-squared.
Transition: We have seen how machine learning methods improve prediction. Next, we consider how they can be used in economic research.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: What changes when LASSO selects attributes?
text:
What changes when LASSO selects attributes?
After removing the selected attributes, estimated willingness to pay changes for some of the remaining characteristics.
LASSO selects variables based on their contribution to the model’s predictive objective, subject to its penalty.
But the variables that produce the best predictions are not necessarily the variables we need to estimate a particular economic parameter.

Source: Li and Yu (2025), Section 3, Tables 6 and 7.



The comparison is between a conditional logit model containing all attributes and a model excluding the attributes selected for removal by LASSO.
Willingness to pay for French apples increases from €1.20 to €1.53 per kilogram.
The estimate for Italian apples changes little.
Organic willingness to pay is no longer estimated in the selected specification.
Selecting variables for predictive performance does not automatically produce unbiased estimates or valid inference for every economic parameter.
Discussion: If organic production is a primary research interest, should the researcher allow LASSO to exclude it?
The variables included in a model affect its estimated coefficients and willingness-to-pay estimates. Selecting variables for prediction does not necessarily produce the best model for answering an economic research question.
Transition: What if we use machine learning to select control variables when estimating a treatment effect?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Conditional average treatment effects
Conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) describe how estimated treatment effects differ across farms with different characteristics.
τ(x)=E[Y(1)−Y(0)∣X=x]
\tau(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x]


Sources: Athey and Imbens (2019), pages 701 to 704; Stetter et al. (2022), Sections 2.3 and 4.1 to 4.3.



This extends the potential-outcomes framework introduced earlier in the course.
Y(1) is the potential outcome under program participation; Y(0) is the potential outcome without participation.
The average treatment effect summarizes the mean difference across the population.
The conditional average treatment effect describes how that difference varies with observed characteristics.
The objective is not simply to predict fertiliser use, but to estimate differences in treatment effects.
Transition: How can machine learning help estimate these differences?

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Three questions to ask when reading a paper
text:
Three questions to ask when reading a paper

What is the quantity the researchers want to estimate?
What does machine learning contribute to that objective?
What assumptions are needed to interpret the results?


Sources: Mullainathan and Spiess (2017); Athey and Imbens (2019); Zhao et al. (2025); Li and Yu (2025); Belloni et al. (2014); Stetter et al. (2022).



Prediction accuracy is the primary objective in the first example.
In the second role, ML is used to support an economic model or the estimation of a particular parameter.
In the third role, ML helps estimate treatment-effect heterogeneity.
Better prediction does not necessarily imply better parameter estimates or more credible causal inference.
The research objective determines how the model should be evaluated.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Why estimate heterogeneous treatment effects?
The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) measures the average effect of participation across all farms:
ATE=E[Y(1)−Y(0)]
ATE=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]

But the program may affect farms differently depending on their size, location, or production practices.
The Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) measures the average effect for farms with particular characteristics:
τ(x)=E[Y(1)−Y(0)∣X=x]
\tau(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x]

ML application: Causal forests can identify patterns in treatment-effect heterogeneity without requiring researchers to specify every interaction in advance.


ATE summarizes the average effect across the target population.
CATE describes how the average effect varies with observed characteristics.
In a conventional regression, we would need to specify treatment interactions with farm characteristics.
Causal forests provide a flexible way to estimate these differences.
CATE estimation still requires credible causal identification assumptions.
Transition: How do causal forests estimate these differences across farms?

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
section: How to read a methods section
text:
How to read a methods section
Follow the argument from the research question to the conclusion

What quantity is the study trying to learn about
Which observations and measures represent that quantity
What comparison or variation supports the estimate
How are the estimate and its uncertainty calculated
Which claims do the data and assumptions support


The first three questions connect to Lectures 5.1, 5.5, and 6.1. Thursday surveys how reviewers check the whole argument. Unit 7 develops the referee report in detail.

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
section: Make two passes through the section
text:
Make two passes through the section








Pass
Read for
Mark in the paper




1. Purpose
The estimand, population, and outcome
One sentence stating what is estimated


2. Evidence
Sample, variation, assumptions, and inference
The paragraph or table supporting each claim



Then ask where the paper explains the largest threat to its interpretation

The estimand is the quantity the research question calls for. Depending on the paper, it may be a treatment effect, preference parameter, prediction target, or pattern in an open-ended account.

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
section: First check: what is being estimated?
text:
First check: what is being estimated?
An estimand names the target quantity



Part
Example for a water-pricing study




Population
Farms served by participating irrigation districts


Outcome
Monthly irrigation water use


Comparison
Use under a revised price and under the prior price


Period
The first two years after the price change



A reviewer looks for a result that answers the question stated in the introduction

Sources: Gibson (2019); Lecture 6.1

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
section: Gibson: check whom the data describe
text:
Gibson: check whom the data describe
Gibson describes studies of local residents that use administrative records of registered residents
Registration and actual residence can differ when people move
Ask which population the data cover, who is missing, and whether the difference matters for the proposed estimate

Source: Gibson (2019), pages 331 to 332

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
section: Gibson: check what the measure records
text:
Gibson: check what the measure records
A household survey may record purchases during one week. A household can report zero purchases and still consume food from its existing stocks
For every central variable, ask

What event or quantity is recorded
What period does it cover
How does the paper construct it
Does it represent the concept in the research question


Source: Gibson (2019), discussion of food purchases and consumption

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
section: What reviewers check in the data
text:
What reviewers check in the data







Item
Question




Sample
How were units selected and which were excluded


Observation
What does one row represent


Measures
How were the outcome and explanatory variables constructed


Timing
Were the relevant measures observed before or after exposure


Missingness
Which observations are absent and why



For survey data, also check the sampling frame, response process, and weights

Sources: Gibson (2019); Lecture 5.1

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
section: Methods answer different kinds of questions
text:
Methods answer different kinds of questions







Research task
Example of evidence or method




Estimate a policy effect
Experiment or credible observational comparison


Estimate preferences
Choice data with an economic model


Predict a future outcome
Held-out evaluation of a prediction rule


Understand a decision process
Interviews, fieldwork, or case studies


Isolate a proposed mechanism
Controlled laboratory variation




Ask students to find the task in the paper before evaluating the technique. A paper can combine approaches when each contributes to a stated question.

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
text:
Starr: open-ended evidence
Interviews and fieldwork can reveal how people describe a decision and which considerations the researcher had not anticipated
Read for the recruitment rule, interview protocol, record keeping, and method of analyzing responses
Ask how the authors compare accounts with other evidence and address cases that challenge their explanation

Source: Starr (2014), Sections 2 and 3

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
text:
When methods are combined







Sequence
What the added method contributes




Interviews before a survey
Clarify concepts and improve survey questions


Survey before interviews
Investigate patterns or unexpected responses


Concurrent evidence
Compare accounts with measured outcomes



A methods section should explain how the components inform the same research question

Source: Starr (2014), Section 2

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
text:
What makes a comparison credible?
For an effect estimate, locate four statements in the paper

The groups, places, or periods being compared
The source of variation in the explanatory factor
The assumption that gives the comparison its interpretation
The main ways that assumption could fail

Then examine how the authors investigate those threats

Examples from Lecture 6.1 include parallel trends for difference in differences, exclusion for an instrument, and continuity around a regression discontinuity cutoff.

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
text:
What details permit replication?







Methods detail
What a reader needs




Equation or rule
Outcome, explanatory variables, and target parameter


Sample
Units, period, restrictions, and missing-data rules


Estimation
Estimator, controls, and model settings


Inference
Standard errors, clustering, and tests


Checks
Planned sensitivity and alternative specifications




The methods section and repository can divide the work. The paper states the choices and why they were made. Code and documentation implement them.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
False positives and false negatives








Decision
Null is true
Specified effect is present




Reject the null
False positive or Type I error
Detect the effect


Do not reject
Correct non-rejection
False negative or Type II error



The Type I error rate is α\alpha. Power is the probability of detecting a specified effect, 1−β1-\beta

Source: Kim (2019), Section 2


Type II error and power require an effect size or a specific alternative. Interpret a nonsignificant estimate using its confidence interval and the effect sizes the study had power to detect.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Power begins with an effect worth detecting
text:
Power begins with an effect worth detecting
Choose the smallest effect that would matter for the research or policy decision
Power for that effect depends on

Outcome variation and measurement quality
The number of usable observations in each group
Clustering, treatment allocation, and the planned estimator
The test level and the direction of the test

State the assumed effect size and design when reporting a power calculation

Source: Kim (2019), Sections 2 and 3.5

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Survey size has two different uses
text:
Survey size has two different uses







Goal
Planning question




Describe a population
How precise must a proportion or mean be


Compare groups or test a hypothesis
What effect should the study be able to detect



Plan for completed responses. Expected nonresponse and clustered sampling can increase the number that must be contacted
The sampling frame and response process determine which population the completed survey represents

Sources: Lecture 5.1; Kim (2019), Section 3.5

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
An illustrative survey calculation
Suppose a study compares adoption rates of 50% and 60% in two independent groups
With a two-sided 5% test and 80% power, a standard calculation calls for about 388 completed responses per group
At an expected 80% response rate, that is about 485 invitations per group. Clustering and ineligible contacts require further planning

Illustrative calculation using base R power.prop.test(p1 = .50, p2 = .60, sig.level = .05, power = .80)


This is a normal-approximation calculation for independent groups of equal size. It is not a sample-size recommendation for a particular student’s project. A 10 percentage point difference was specified before calculating sample size. Response rates and cluster effects must be estimated for the actual design.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Repeated tests create more chances for a false positive
text:
Repeated tests create more chances for a false positive
If 20 independent null hypotheses are each tested at the 5% level, the chance of at least one false positive is
1−(1−0.05)20≈0.64
1-(1-0.05)^{20}\approx 0.64

The value changes when tests are dependent. A reader should look for the full set of tests, the planned hypotheses, and any adjustment for multiple comparisons

Source: Kim (2019), discussion of multiple testing

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: What changes with a large sample?
text:
What changes with a large sample?
For a valid test with a fixed 5% level, the nominal Type I error rate remains 5% under the null
Power rises for a specified nonzero effect. Estimates can become precise enough to detect effects too small to matter for the decision
Sampling, measurement, and model bias still require attention

Source: Kim (2019), Sections 2 and 3; statistical clarification in notes


Kim calls rejection of a substantively negligible effect a false positive in a broader practical sense. Keep that distinct from the technical Type I error rate. At fixed alpha, sample size alone does not raise the nominal Type I rate of a valid test.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Read the interval with the estimate
text:
Read the interval with the estimate
Suppose the estimated effect is −2 units, with a 95% interval from −7 to 3
The data are compatible with zero change and with a reduction of 5 units, which might matter for policy
A reviewer asks whether the interval rules out effects that matter, and whether the sample had adequate power for that question

This is an illustrative estimate. An interval’s interpretation depends on the estimator, sampling design, and assumptions used to construct it.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: When is an effect small enough to set aside?
text:
When is an effect small enough to set aside?
An equivalence analysis starts by defining a substantively negligible range, such as (−Δ,Δ)(-\Delta,\Delta)
The research question determines Δ\Delta. Evidence for equivalence requires an interval sufficiently narrow to support an effect inside that range
Report the estimated effect and interval so a reader can apply a different decision threshold

Source: Kim (2019), Section 3.7

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
text:
Practice: read this methods paragraph

We survey 300 farms in 12 irrigation districts before and after a revised water charge. Six districts adopt the charge. We estimate a difference-in-differences model of self-reported monthly water use, controlling for acreage and crop mix. Standard errors are clustered by district. The estimated change is −0.8 acre-feet, with a 95% interval from −2.2 to 0.6.

Illustrative classroom example

Give students time to mark the estimand, sample, treatment, outcome, estimator, and inference procedure. The next slide asks for the missing information a reviewer would request.

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
section: What would a reviewer ask next?
text:
What would a reviewer ask next?

How were farms and districts selected
What supports the parallel-trends assumption
How was monthly water use reported and checked
Are 12 districts enough for the stated inference procedure
What effect size would matter, and what can the interval rule out

Connect each question to a claim in the methods paragraph

The example deliberately leaves these answers open. Twelve clusters merit care with conventional cluster-robust standard errors. The interval includes zero and reductions that could matter; interpretation needs a substantive benchmark.

title: Lecture 6.4: Reading a Methods Section
text:
Return to Tuesday’s methods draft

Underline the sentence that states your target quantity or question
Mark where you describe the sample, measures, comparison, and analysis
Add the assumption or design choice that needs the most explanation
State how you will report uncertainty, precision, or power

Use the workshop feedback to decide which part of the methods section to develop next

title: Methods workshop preparation
text:
Bring 1–2 pages of written notes about the methods you currently plan to use for your research project. You can bring a printed copy or a document you can share in class. You do not need slides.
Use these five headings:

Question and hypotheses — State your research question and one or two hypotheses you want to examine
Data — Name the source, the people or units observed, the place and period, and what one observation represents
Measures — Name your outcome and the main explanatory variables, and say how you will construct them
Analysis — Explain the comparison or pattern you will use to examine each hypothesis, and name the method you expect to use. Include a simple equation if it helps you explain the plan
Open decision — Identify one assumption, data limitation, or methods choice on which you want feedback

Write what you know now. If a data source, measure, or method is still undecided, say so and describe the options you are considering. Be ready to explain your plan briefly and ask your group one focused question.
Review your notes from Lecture 5.1 on sampling and surveys, Lecture 5.5 on data reporting, and the methods lectures on econometric models, structural models, and machine learning as useful for your project. There is no new assigned reading for Tuesday.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Quantitative and qualitative evidence








Approach
Evidence
Research use




Quantitative
Numerical measures from surveys, records, or experiments
Estimate patterns, effects, parameters, or predictions


Qualitative
Interviews, field observations, or documents
Document decisions and the processes that produce them


Mixed methods
Numerical and qualitative evidence
Examine a question using measured outcomes and accounts of decisions




The table distinguishes three forms of evidence.
Quantitative. Numerical measures from surveys, administrative records, or experiments, used to estimate patterns, effects, parameters, or predictions.
Qualitative. Interviews, field observations, or documents, used to document how decisions are made and the processes behind them.
Mixed methods. Both forms of evidence in one study.
These categories describe evidence rather than whole studies. A survey can contain numerical and open-ended questions, and an experiment can include interviews. For any source, the relevant questions are how the units were selected, how the concepts were measured, and how the evidence was analyzed.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Where Unit 6 has taken us

6.1 Used reduced-form comparisons and worked from a research question to an estimating equation and identifying assumption
6.2 Modeled behavior to estimate structural parameters and consider counterfactuals
6.3 Used machine learning for prediction and as a component of other analyses

Today we add experimental design, qualitative and mixed methods, and the statistical decisions that shape what an estimate can support
Experimental and observational designs can both produce quantitative data

Lecture 6.1 also introduced the written empirical strategy section. Today focuses on additional approaches and decisions that students may use in their workshop plans.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Match a method to the research task
text:
Match a method to the research task







Research task
Example of evidence or method




Estimate a policy effect
Experiment or credible observational comparison


Estimate preferences
Choice data with an economic model


Predict a future outcome
Held-out evaluation of a prediction rule


Understand a decision process
Interviews, fieldwork, or case studies


Isolate a proposed mechanism
Controlled laboratory variation




Ask students to find the task in the paper before evaluating the technique. A paper can combine approaches when each contributes to a stated question.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: An experiment creates a planned comparison
text:
An experiment creates a planned comparison
Suppose irrigation districts randomly offer some farms a monthly water-use report

Define the eligible farms and assign the offer at random
Measure subsequent water use for both assigned groups
Compare the groups to estimate the effect of being offered the report
Check whether assignment, follow-up, and measurement worked as planned

The result describes the sampled farms and intervention. Generalizing to other places or to a mandatory program requires further reasoning

Distinguish assignment to an offer from actual receipt and use of the report. The intention-to-treat comparison estimates the effect of the offer. Randomization supports the comparison when assignment is implemented and outcome follow-up is adequate. Cluster randomization by district would change the effective sample size and inference.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Laboratory experiments make choices observable
In a gift-exchange experiment, researchers can vary a wage offer and observe effort while specifying the decision rules and information available to participants
When reading an experiment, identify

What the researcher varies
What is held fixed
What participants choose and what is observed
Which populations and settings the result is meant to inform


Source: Falk and Heckman (2009), discussion of the gift-exchange experiment

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Qualitative evidence can explain a decision process
text:
Qualitative evidence can explain a decision process
Suppose farms respond differently to a new water charge. Interviews could ask how they understood the charge and which irrigation choices were feasible

Select participants to cover relevant differences in farm size, crop, water rights, and location
Use a consistent interview guide while allowing follow-up questions
Record how interviews were documented and analyzed
Examine accounts that challenge the initial explanation

State whose experiences the sample covers and how the analysis supports each interpretation

Source: Starr (2014), Sections 2 and 3


Purposeful selection can be appropriate when the aim is to understand a process or variation in experiences. It does not create a probability sample for estimating population prevalence. Interviews may suggest mechanisms and inform measurement; the design must support any causal or population claim made from them.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Combine methods for a stated purpose
text:
Combine methods for a stated purpose







Sequence
What the added method contributes




Interviews before a survey
Clarify concepts and improve survey questions


Survey before interviews
Investigate patterns or unexpected responses


Concurrent evidence
Compare accounts with measured outcomes



A methods section should explain how the components inform the same research question

Source: Starr (2014), Section 2

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Across methods, ask what the evidence represents
text:
Across methods, ask what the evidence represents
Before interpreting a result, establish

Population Whose decisions or outcomes are observed
Measure What the recorded variable or account captures
Comparison What variation or selection supports the interpretation
Limits Which alternative explanations or unobserved cases could change the conclusion

Gibson’s examples make the first two questions concrete. Kim addresses statistical uncertainty and repeated tests for quantitative estimates

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Who is represented in the data?
text:
Who is represented in the data?
Gibson describes studies of local residents that use administrative records of registered residents
Registration and actual residence can differ when people move
Ask which population the data cover, who is missing, and whether the difference matters for the proposed estimate

Source: Gibson (2019), pages 331 to 332

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
What does the measure record?
A household survey may record purchases during one week. A household can report zero purchases and still consume food from its existing stocks
For every central variable, ask

What event or quantity is recorded
What period does it cover
How does the paper construct it
Does it represent the concept in the research question


Source: Gibson (2019), discussion of food purchases and consumption

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: A quantitative claim has an estimate and uncertainty
text:
A quantitative claim has an estimate and uncertainty
Suppose a study estimates that a water-use report reduces monthly use by 2 units

The estimate summarizes the observed comparison
An interval shows which effect sizes remain compatible with the data and the inference procedure
A decision about the null hypothesis can produce a false positive or a false negative

The next slides connect these errors to power, sample size, and the number of tests

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Return to the water-use report example
text:
Return to the water-use report example
Suppose the estimated effect is −2 units, with a 95% interval from −7 to 3

Which farms were eligible and which provided follow-up data
Does the water-use measure include all sources of irrigation water
Could a reduction of 5 units matter for policy
Did the planned sample have reasonable power to detect that reduction

The interval and the design determine the claim the study can make

Use this example to connect the experimental design, Gibson’s measurement concerns, and Kim’s inference concerns. The interval includes zero and a reduction of 5 units. It does not establish that the intervention has no effect. The example is illustrative, with no asserted study result.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Report from Tuesday’s methods workshop
Students who did not receive feedback on Tuesday can report their current methods plan

Reserve the final 20 to 25 minutes. Allow about two minutes for each report and a few minutes for feedback, adjusting to the number of students who still need a turn.
Return first to those who did not receive feedback in Tuesday’s lab.

State the research question and one hypothesis
Describe the observations, central measures, and proposed method
Name one design or inference decision on which you want feedback

After each report, discuss the outcome measure, proposed comparison, and one design choice that needs further work

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Methods covered in Unit 6

6.1 Used reduced-form comparisons and developed an estimating equation and identifying assumption from a research question
6.2 Estimated structural parameters from a model of behavior and used the model to examine counterfactuals
6.3 Used machine learning for prediction and within other empirical analyses

6.4 covers experiments, qualitative and mixed methods, and the measurement and statistical decisions that support a conclusion

6.1 to 6.3. The first three meetings of Unit 6 worked with observational data: a reduced-form comparison with a stated identifying assumption in 6.1, structural estimation and counterfactuals in 6.2, and machine learning for prediction in 6.3.
6.4. Today adds designs in which the researcher creates the variation (experiments) or collects accounts of how decisions are made (interviews). It also covers the measurement and statistical decisions that determine whether a result supports a conclusion. Both apply to the empirical strategy section of the workshop plans.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Select a method to match the research task
text:
Select a method to match the research task







Research task
Evidence or method




Estimate a policy effect
Random assignment or an observational comparison with a stated identifying assumption


Estimate preferences
Choice data and a model of consumer or producer behavior


Predict a future outcome
A prediction rule evaluated with held-out observations


Document a decision process
Interviews, fieldwork, or case studies


Test a response to an incentive
A field or lab experiment




The research task determines the method. The rows connect today’s material to earlier meetings.
Estimate a policy effect. Random assignment, or an observational comparison with a stated identifying assumption (6.1).
Estimate preferences. Choice data and a model of behavior (6.2).
Predict a future outcome. A prediction rule evaluated on held-out observations (6.3).
Document a decision process. Interviews, fieldwork, or case studies.
Test a response to an incentive. A field or lab experiment.
The districts’ question falls in the first row. Because the districts decide which farms receive the report, they can assign it at random, and the next three slides develop that field experiment.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Experimental design: random assignment
The irrigation districts use their customer lists to assign the report offer at the farm level

Define eligible farms and randomly assign the offer
Survey both groups about subsequent monthly water use
Compare mean water use to estimate the effect of being offered the report
Document report delivery, survey response, and departures from the assignment protocol

The estimate applies to the offer among farms included in the experiment. Extrapolation to other districts or a mandatory reporting program requires evidence about those settings

The intention-to-treat comparison estimates the effect of the offer. Farms may receive the report without using it. Randomization supports the comparison when assignment is implemented and outcome follow-up is adequate. Assignment by district would change the effective sample size and inference.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Laboratory experiments: controlled variation
Falk and Heckman’s gift-exchange experiment examines whether workers respond to higher wages with higher effort

Participants act as firms or workers
A firm offers a wage that the worker can accept
A worker who accepts sees the wage and chooses an effort level that is costly to provide
The experiment specifies the available choices, minimum effort, and payoff rules

Researchers observe wages and effort under these rules and examine whether effort rises with the wage offered

Source: Falk and Heckman (2009), discussion of the gift-exchange experiment

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Qualitative methods: interviews and fieldwork
Research use: Interviews can document whether farms received and understood the report, how they used it, and which irrigation changes were feasible
Study procedures

Recruit across farm size, crop, water rights, and location
Document the interview guide and follow-up questions
Describe recording, transcription, and coding
Examine accounts that challenge the proposed explanation

Reporting: State the recruitment criteria and evidence for each interpretation

Source: Starr (2014), Sections 2 and 3


Purposeful selection can document variation in decisions and experiences. Population prevalence requires a sampling design that supports that estimate. Interviews may also identify mechanisms and improve survey measures. Interpret each result according to the recruitment and analysis procedures.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Mixed methods designs
Interviews (qualitative) combined with the follow-up survey (quantitative) in different sequences







Sequence in the water-use study
Contribution




Interviews before the survey
Identify how farms track water use and refine the survey measure


Interviews after the survey
Investigate why some farms used the report and others did not


Concurrent interviews
Compare accounts of irrigation changes with reported water use



The interviews examine how farms responded to the report. The survey comparison estimates the effect of offering it

Source: Starr (2014), Section 2


Opening line. In this example, mixed methods means interviews (qualitative) combined with the follow-up survey (quantitative). The timing of the interviews determines what they contribute.
Before the survey. Interviews show how farms track water use, which helps the team write a survey question that farms can answer accurately.
After the survey. Interviews can explain a result, for example why some farms acted on the report and others did not.
Concurrent. Interviews conducted alongside the survey allow a comparison between farms’ accounts of what they changed and the water use they report.
Last line. The two parts answer different questions. The interviews describe how farms responded, and the survey comparison estimates the effect of the offer.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Population, measurement, comparison, and limits


Population

Definition: Units the study aims to learn about
Example: Farms on participating districts’ customer lists

Measure

Definition: Recorded variable representing a concept
Example: Survey-reported monthly water use


Comparison

Definition: Groups used to estimate a difference
Example: Farms assigned the report offer and comparison farms

Limits

Definition: Features restricting the claim
Example: Missing survey responses and farms outside the customer lists


Farms that complete follow-up form the analytic sample, which may differ from the eligible population

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Population represented in the data

Included: Farms served by participating districts appear on the customer lists
Possibly excluded: Farms relying entirely on private wells or other suppliers may be absent
Population claim: An estimate for farms on the lists requires additional evidence before applying it to all farms in the region

Gibson’s distinction between registered and resident households illustrates how a data source can omit members of the population named in the research question

Source: Gibson (2019), pages 331 to 332


Included. The customer lists cover farms that receive water from the participating districts.
Possibly excluded. Farms that rely only on private wells, or that buy water from other suppliers, do not appear on the lists.
Population claim. The experiment estimates the effect for listed farms. Applying the estimate to every farm in the region would require evidence that unlisted farms respond in the same way.
Gibson’s example. A list of registered households differs from the households actually living in a place, so a sample drawn from the registry misses residents who are not registered. The general point is to check whether the data source covers the population named in the research question.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Measurement and interpretation
The outcome of interest is total irrigation water use. Suppose instead the follow-up survey asked only about district deliveries. That question records one source of water and omits withdrawals from private wells
If farms substitute groundwater for district water after receiving the report, district deliveries could decline while total water use remains unchanged
Gibson’s food example makes the same point: one week’s purchases omit food consumed from household stocks

Source: Gibson (2019), discussion of food purchases and consumption


First paragraph. The design calls for total irrigation water use. This slide considers what would happen if the survey asked only about water delivered by the district.
Second paragraph. Many farms also pump groundwater. A farm that receives the report could reduce its district deliveries and pump more from its own well. Deliveries would fall and the study would report a reduction, even though total water use did not change. The estimate could be precise and still fail to answer a question about total water use.
Third paragraph. Gibson’s food example has the same structure. One week of food purchases omits food consumed from stocks the household already held, so purchases differ from consumption.
The survey wording determines which quantity the estimate measures, so the wording should be checked against the concept in the research question.

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Statistical estimates and uncertainty
In the water-use report experiment, an estimated difference of −2 units gives the direction and magnitude of the observed difference
A confidence interval reports uncertainty around that estimate. A hypothesis test evaluates the data under a specified null hypothesis. Both calculations depend on the sample, outcome measure, and study design
Power concerns the probability of detecting a specified effect. Multiple testing concerns the chance of a false positive across the tests conducted

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
text:
Statistical power and effect size
A power calculation specifies the effect size the study is designed to detect. For a policy analysis, this may be the smallest effect that would change the decision
For a specified effect, power depends on

Outcome variation and measurement quality
The number of usable observations in each group
Clustering, treatment allocation, and the planned estimator
The test level and the direction of the test

Report the assumed effect size, sampling design, and planned test with the calculation

Source: Kim (2019), Sections 2 and 3.5

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Survey sample size and research objectives
text:
Survey sample size and research objectives







Goal
Planning question




Describe a population
How precise must a proportion or mean be


Compare groups or test a hypothesis
What effect should the study be able to detect



Calculate the required number of completed responses. Expected nonresponse and clustered sampling can increase the number of people who must be contacted
The sampling frame and response process determine which population the completed survey represents

Sources: Lecture 5.1; Kim (2019), Section 3.5

title: Lecture 6.4: Experiments, Qualitative Evidence, and Inference
section: Example: sample size for a difference in proportions
text:
Example: sample size for a difference in proportions
Suppose a study compares adoption rates of 50% and 60% in two independent groups
With a two-sided 5% test and 80% power, the calculation requires about 388 completed responses per group
At an expected 80% response rate, that is about 485 invitations per group. Clustering and ineligible contacts require further planning
